item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber's hands-on look at Apple's new Full Disk Access privacy controls, squarely in Apple security territory. (score 9)

From Daring Fireball.

On Monday, when the second betas of the v27.3 OSes came out, I posted about Apple adding the new privacy controls they had promised a month prior, in the wake of Meta’s Muse app surprising some users with what information it had access to (e.g., incoming iMessages) after being granted Full Disk Access — which authorization some users just clicked right through. I also posted a link to Apple’s corresponding new support documents. My initial take on Monday:

I’m installing it now, but from what I’ve seen so far, these changes not only alleviate my concerns that Apple might over-tighten the screws, I actually think they add clarity and give users more, not less, control over their Macs.

After a week, I’m willing to call it: this overhaul of these settings and permissions is a win. I really like the way that, for apps asking for Full Disk Access, users can now grant access to a list of folders instead. That’s what I mean about these new settings giving users more control.

Are these new dialog boxes “scarier”? Yes, and the point is, they should be. You should be slightly jolted into attention when an app prompts for any of these permissions. The question is whether they are unnecessarily scary. I would say no, not at all. The descriptions are fair and accurate. Is it unnecessarily scary to show you thumbnails of your personal photos before permitting Full Disk Access that would grant an application unfettered access to your personal photos? No! It’s a bit of a jolt to see them, but that’s just reducing the abstraction. The words “full disk access” feel different than actually seeing a snapshot of what full disk access entails.

Might this discourage some Mac users from granting Full Disk Access to AI agent apps? Yes. And it should! Users who actually understand the stakes will not be dissuaded by these new permissions — when granting them is what they know they want to do. Additionally, I think these new dialog boxes represent very good UI design. They look like a new modern take on MacOS “system chrome” design — not skinny iPhone-sized alerts.

My only gripe about the new stuff is the prominent menu bar indicator that now appears when one app is controlling another. You can’t turn it off (except via an undocumented hidden defaults setting), and it’s distracting on most Macs, and extra distracting on the new MacBook Pros with PROLED displays because on those Macs, it appears in the Dynamic Island! Chance Miller, on Threads (with screenshots):

Most of the changes in macOS 27.3 are reasonable, but this Live Activity thing for system access has got to go. It’s way too aggressive.

It takes over the Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro!

As I write this article on a new MacBook Pro review unit, I have 8 of these indicators in my Dynamic Island: Scroll Reverser, Keyboard Maestro Engine, HazeOver, SteerMouse Manager, Moom, Chest (a promising new utility for managing menu bar icons), System Events, and a new text snippet expansion utility I’m beta testing.

Every one of these apps is running all of the time for me. This indicator being on, all the time, for every one of them isn’t helping me notice unusual activity. If anything, if Apple doesn’t rethink this idea, it’s going to make me miss the indication if an app is taking advantage of access permissions in an unwanted or unexpected way.

Zac Hall, Miller’s colleague at 9to5Mac, published an article on Tuesday showing the command-line defaults incantation to disable this. That’s better than not being able to disable it at all, but I expect Apple to revisit this based on feedback. It seems like a well-intentioned feature that was designed by people who didn’t realize how many always-on utilities “control other apps”.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Months of undetected prompt theft at AI inference providers, including Zero Data Retention traffic, is a real lesson in AI supply chain trust. (score 8)

From The Hacker News.

Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.

Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.

OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.

The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.

The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.

The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.

The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.

On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.

"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.

The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.

The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.

One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.

A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.

A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint.

Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt.

In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings.

OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.

The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties.

The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week.

Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers.

Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted.

What the Providers Have Disclosed

An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections.

Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated.

A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window.

At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July.

The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts.

Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers.

Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three.

The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week.

What Users Should Do

The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price.

Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check.

Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys.

A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: Apple now spells out paid iCloud+ tiers for heavier Apple Intelligence use, a notable shift in how Apple charges for AI. (score 7)

From Daring Fireball.

By John Gruber

Ivy: Plan. Do. Reflect.
The to-do list that ends.

  • Apple Documents Extra Apple Intelligence Usage Limits Per iCloud+ Paid Tier

  • Apple Support:

    Starting with the 2027 software releases, Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are available for free for users with a supported device set to a supported language. Some features rely on powerful server models and have limits where increased access is available with eligible iCloud+ plans, starting with the 27.3 release. These include, but aren’t limited to, features in these categories:

    • Siri AI
    • Images: Intelligent Photo Editing Tools including Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing, and Image Playground
    • Workflows and automation: AFM Cloud and Cloud Pro models in Shortcuts
    • Third-party apps using Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute

    [...]

    When you hit your daily usage limit for a particular feature category, you’ll be notified. Each device has its own daily usage limit per feature category. Once you reach a limit, you can wait until your daily usage limit resets on that device or immediately increase your limit by upgrading to an eligible iCloud+ plan.

    Here’s Apple’s table with the usage limits by tier:

item.title: Nothing Brite about it
item.author: And now it’s all this
item.description:
Why: Dr. Drang's thoughtful take on how Siri AI finally keeps conversational context, and where it still falls short. (score 7)

From And now it’s all this.

Siri’s great failing over the past decade and a half has been its contextual ignorance . It treated every request you made as if it were the first chalk markings on a great blank slate, a slate that was immediately washed clean after it answered you. That’s no longer the case with Siri AI. It now keeps track of your conversations, and it can dig through your apps to find information. This is, without question, a tremendous improvement, but I did run into a problem with it about a week ago.
item.content:encoded:
Why: Dr. Drang's thoughtful take on how Siri AI finally keeps conversational context, and where it still falls short. (score 7)

From And now it’s all this.

Siri’s great failing over the past decade and a half has been its contextual ignorance. It treated every request you made as if it were the first chalk markings on a great blank slate, a slate that was immediately washed clean after it answered you. That’s no longer the case with Siri AI. It now keeps track of your conversations, and it can dig through your apps to find information. This is, without question, a tremendous improvement, but I did run into a problem with it about a week ago.

I was out on a walk, listening to one of Apple Music’s built-in playlists, and “I’m Just a Singer (In a Rock and Roll Band)” by the Moody Blues came on. I wasn’t paying close attention, but after a while I realized that I didn’t know who the lead singer was. I knew only that it wasn’t Justin Hayward, who did most of their lead vocals. So I asked Siri, “Who’s singing lead vocals on this song?”

This was a test. I would never have asked the pre-2025 Siri this kind of question. I have asked similar questions over the past year or two, but only because I figured Siri would pass the question along to ChatGPT. And in those cases, I made the question more explicit—something like “Who is the lead singer on the Moody Blues song ‘I’m Just a Singer (In a Rock and Roll Band)’?”—because Siri usually wouldn’t tell ChatGPT what I was listening to.

Siri AI passed the test, telling me it was John Lodge. Great! I decided to do this more often.

A couple of minutes later, “Do It Again” by Steely Dan started playing.1 I had a vague memory of seeing a video of them performing this song on some TV show, with Skunk Baxter playing bongos. Was that just for the TV show, or did he also play bongos on the record? So I asked Siri, “Who’s playing percussion2 on this song?”

Siri answered that Graeme Edge played percussion on “I’m Just a Singer (In a Rock and Roll Band).” A correct answer, but not what I was looking for. I wondered if Siri was running slow and hadn’t updated itself to know what the current song was. So I asked again and got the same answer. Then I asked for the lead vocalist and got an answer of John Lodge again. What the hell?

Then I realized that I had been caught by conversational context. After my first question, in which Siri correctly interpreted “this song” as the song that was currently playing, it treated my later questions as part of an extended conversation about “I’m Just a Singer” and interpreted “this song” accordingly. So I changed my question to “Who is playing percussion on the currently playing song?” This switched Siri’s context, and I got the right answer. (It was V. Feldman, not Skunk Baxter, although Baxter did play guitar on the track.)

I suspect that if more time had passed between the two songs (and my questions), Siri would have changed its interpretation of “this song.” How much time? I have no idea. Despite what George Harrison told us, “this song” has something tricky about it.

  1. No, the music you listen to is shit. ↩

  2. I thought “percussion” was more likely than “bongos” to be in the song credits. ↩

item.content:encoded:
Why: A Big Think essay on Epicurean decision-making, the kind of good-life philosophy Jack saves. (score 7)

From Big Think.

You are able to make good decisions about how to live your life.

I hate to open a new newsletter with a twee self-help aphorism covered in fortune cookie crumbs, but it’s probably the most important thing to start with. Because Epicureanism is an ancient Greek philosophy, and like almost all its contemporaries, it places responsibility on you. You are the overseer of your life. You can think things through, make good choices, and get things right. You are not some child, carried about by adult hands, blinking at a world blurring by. In the eyes of Greek philosophers, you are a rational, intelligent, deliberative human being. You control your life.

Epicureanism argues that a good life is one where we develop strategies to either cure or endure pain — both physical and emotional — while seeking out opportunities to enjoy ourselves more. It says that a happy life means savoring simple pleasures where you are, right now, and with the people who matter. But to do that, we need to make better decisions. We need to willfully choose an Epicurean life. We need to work at happiness.

Some of you might be wondering why there’s a cute little crab scuttling along our freshly minted logo. Well, that’s a hermit crab. In my upcoming book, The Art of Enough, I use the hermit crab motif to represent one of the most important ideas in Epicureanism. Because I think it embodies a certain skill we all need to nurture if we are to live a good life.

This article is for Big Think members only. Become a member to read it in full.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Seth Godin on why engagement has to be earned, useful for leading teams and PMs. (score 7)

From Seth's Blog.

The single most important factor in learning is whether the student is actively engaged in the process.

Eyes bright, hands up, curious and eager for the insight on the other side.

Ask any teacher–students like this are a delight.

The same is true for the work of professionals–from doctors to cashiers. Wanting to be there, open to interaction, eager for change–these are so obvious that we usually overlook them.

In fact, the real work of anyone building an institution of learning or an organization that seeks to serve is simple: create the conditions for people to choose to actively participate.

The lazy method is to wait for the self-motivated and take credit for the results when they show up. The hard work is to build the systems and culture that makes it more likely that you’re attracting, motivating and transforming the people who want to go where you can take them.

Everything else is a bonus.

item.author: Behind the Craft
item.description:
Why: Microsoft's Charles Lamanna on how engineering changes when AI writes the code, from inside Jack's own company. (score 7)

From Behind the Craft.

Watch now (19 mins) | Microsoft’s EVP for Copilot on what happens when coding is free, plus 5 unfiltered takeaways from my roundtable with Satya Nadella
item.content:encoded:
Why: Microsoft's Charles Lamanna on how engineering changes when AI writes the code, from inside Jack's own company. (score 7)

From Behind the Craft.

Dear subscribers,

According to Charles (Microsoft’s EVP for Copilot and Agents), the best engineers don’t hand write code anymore but also never had to think harder. We had a great chat about what engineers should focus on when coding is nearly free, what multiplayer AI can look like, and how Microsoft is rebuilding Office around Copilot.

I also joined a small private roundtable with Satya at Microsoft Ignite and wrote my unfiltered takeaways below.

Watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify.

Charles and I talked about:

  • (00:00) Agents will be software's main users

  • (02:19) Why agents are the harshest customers

  • (03:25) Will Copilot replace Office?

  • (07:46) AI is overfit to solo programmers

  • (11:44) Stop sending out 10-page AI slop

  • (12:31) I’m writing less code but thinking harder than ever

  • (15:25) Building is free, but alignment isn't

  • (16:52) Don't debate A vs. B—just ship

I’m proud to partner with Granola

The world’s best teams, including Ramp, Linear, Replit, Brex, and more, use Granola to take notes and focus more in meetings. I’ve tried many meeting apps myself but keep coming back to Granola. Get 3 months free via my link below.

Try Granola for Free

My top takeaways from Charles and Satya

  1. “I've never had to think harder than I do right now.” That's what Charles's most AI-pilled engineers tell him. Instead of hand writing code, they now focus on architecture, testing, and scaling themselves via agents. Charles believes that engineers have always moved to solving higher order problems: “Even ignoring AI, if you went to a software engineer in 1990 and showed them what you can do in Azure, AWS, they’d be like, ‘Whoa, 90% of what I do has been replaced.’”

  1. “All ICs are now managers of agents with a token budget.” Microsoft has 200K+ employees but Satya believes that the best internal teams run like a startup. “There's a founder. The founder has a token budget. Then the founder hires somebody, and they get a token budget too.” For example, Copilot Cowork was built by only 11 engineers and 1 engineer maintains the entire GitHub Copilot runtime.

4 unfiltered takeaways from my roundtable with Satya

item.content:encoded:
Why: BYU survived Kansas in triple overtime on a two-point conversion, a big result going into the finale. (score 7)

From Vanquish The Foe.

You probably said some choice words, but a Bear Bachmeier two-point conversion completion to JoJo Phillips in triple overtime lifted BYU in a 31-29 win over Kansas Saturday in Lawrence.

BYU went into half down 6-3, but two third quarter interceptions from the defense allowed BYU to pull ahead 16-6 going into the fourth quarter. Kansas tied the game, and Matthias Dunn shanked a kick on the last play of regulation.

Kansas has played teams tight this year, but it doesn’t feel good to scrape by a 4-6 team. LJ Martin played most of the game, and while he was bottled up for much of the game, came through in the end and ran for 127 yards. Bear Bachmeier passed for 173 yards and added 59 rushing yards and 2 rushing TDs.

Stats were even across the board, which is not surprising considering the result. Both teams had 2 turnovers and outgained Kansas 381-359.

Next we’ll see how the committee treats BYU after the result. Regardless, BYU’s CFP and Big 12 title game hopes remain alive when BYU hosts Cincinnati next Saturday in the final regular season game.

item.title: Verstappen wins breathless Las Vegas GP as Ferraris collide
item.author: Formula 1 - The Race
item.description:
Why: Verstappen won a wild Las Vegas GP with 20-plus lead changes while the Ferraris collided. (score 7)

From Formula 1 - The Race.

Max Verstappen delivered a masterclass to win a peloton-style Las Vegas GP, while George Russell crashed and the Ferrari drivers collided
item.content:encoded:
Why: Verstappen won a wild Las Vegas GP with 20-plus lead changes while the Ferraris collided. (score 7)

From Formula 1 - The Race.

Verstappen wins breathless Las Vegas GP as Ferraris collide

Max Verstappen delivered a masterclass in defensive driving to win a peloton-style Las Vegas Grand Prix for Red Bull, while main challenger George Russell crashed and the Ferrari drivers collided amid their recent struggles.

The first 15 laps were manic with the slipstream proving so powerful that constant changes of position took place, as Russell took the lead three times at the Turn 14 chicane only to be repassed before or into Turn 1 by Verstappen each time.

Isack Hadjar had also ran second and attacked Verstappen, and begged Red Bull to instruct Verstappen not to defend so that they could pass and repass each other to try to break away, but he predicted on the radio he was about to be passed by Russell and so it proved.

The yo-yoing changed on lap 15 because the top five at that point - Verstappen, Russell, Hadjar, Pierre Gasly and Kimi Antonelli - stopped fighting long enough to break clear of Arvid Lindblad, creating a buffer to the rest of the field and allowing these cars to escape before a safety car for Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara's collision at Turn 14, which left Perez in the barrier.

After a seven-lap delay for barrier repairs that included a full set of pitstops, immediately after the restart Hadjar's front wing failed taking him out of contention, and Verstappen and Russell went at it with another three lead changes, as Lando Norris - 11th earlier in the race - and Antonelli, on an opposite tyre strategy on the softs to finish the race, took turns in the lead before being dispatched again.

On Russell in particular, Verstappen pulled off two incredible instances of going around the outside at Turn 2 and one dive at Turn 5 to retake the lead, completing most of his overtaking in the corners versus many others doing most of their work on the straights.

Antonelli established himself as Verstappen's main threat in the closing stages, especially after Russell locked up and went into the barrier at Turn 5 with three laps to go, remarkably getting going again to finish in the points.

And then Antonelli lost positions to both McLarens going into Turn 1 on the final lap, suffering for lifting to stay behind Verstappen, which had deployment consequences.

That buffer gave Verstappen - who laughed and mocked Russell (with whom he'd clashed in FP3 on Friday) on the radio with a "well done" after his crash - a crucial one-second lead that he was able to eke out into victory across the line.

During the safety car McLaren CEO Zak Brown sounded defeated when speaking to Sky Sports F1 after Norris had dropped as low as 11th, but the fastest lap in the first stint showed the McLaren driver's pace and an excellent recovery from him and Piastri - up 14 places - was rewarded with a double-podium. "Who would have thought?" said Norris at that result.

Antonelli just held on for fourth after his power issues, repassing Gasly into the chicane on the final lap to secure the position.

Fifth was nevertheless Gasly's best result of the season, while Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto was elevated to sixth in the final classification as the team clawed back 18 points against Racing Bulls.

Lewis Hamilton ended as the top Ferrari driver in seventh in a bitter display for the Scuderia as its drivers both lost a sack full of positions and crashed into each other during this race as their teamwork issues continue.

The Ferraris had bickered in the first stint as Hamilton had an expletive-led rant about how Leclerc needed to work with him to overtake, while Leclerc accused Hamilton of "squeezing" him and said that would "end badly" if it carried on.

Hamilton was given a 10-second penalty for going off track in a battle with Norris, which he served under the safety car, and fought back to lead Leclerc afterwards, before Leclerc spun Hamilton out at Turn 7 - which the stewards gave Leclerc a 10-second penalty for.

Leclerc had been sixth on the road before the penalty.

His dropping down to 10th helped Carlos Sainz give Williams its joint-best result of the year at one of the few tracks it hadn't written off at the end of the season, while his team-mate Alex Albon was not able to start the race.

Russell was just behind him in ninth and Leclerc rounded out the top 10 after his penalty, ahead of the Audis of Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto.

Lindblad had been fifth in the queue under the safety car but spun while trying to generate heat in his tyres and ultimately retired from the race, meaning Racing Bulls failed to score any points - Liam Lawson starting the race a lap down and recovering to 15th, one place behind Hadjar.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Signal is defending end-to-end encryption against on-device AI agents in iOS 27, a new frontier for private messaging. (score 8)

From The Hacker News.

Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete."

The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen.

It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature.

Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

"The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy."

The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk.

Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android).

"However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said.

"Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system."

Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data.

Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users -

  • Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience
  • Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing

The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup.

On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications.

In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post.

"We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said.

"In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents."

Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings.

Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: A one-page attack on an AI assistant's memory and connected credentials shows how agent security is breaking down. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.

The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.

The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.

There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.

Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage."

In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up.

From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown.

That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent.

The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines.

Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through.

The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in.

The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: A critical bug in the library most apps use to handle OpenPGP keys, triggered just by importing a hostile key. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.

The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.

Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.

The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.

Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says.

The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG.

When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details.

The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier.

What to Update

The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

What to install depends on where the library sits:

  • Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory.
  • Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible.
  • Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch.
  • Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases.
  • GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed.

The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

Google News,

item.title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access
item.author: The Hacker News
item.description:
Why: Amazon reports attackers using autonomous AI agents to find and exploit a zero-day, a real milestone for offensive AI. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week. The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup,
item.content:encoded:
Why: Amazon reports attackers using autonomous AI agents to find and exploit a zero-day, a real milestone for offensive AI. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.

The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.

The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.

MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.

The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.

The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.

Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.

Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.

The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.

Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.

A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.

That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.

In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.

The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.

Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.

The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw.

What to Do Now

With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach:

  • Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs.
  • Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default.
  • Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to.
  • Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched.
  • If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used.

The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described.

The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

Google News,

item.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
item.author: Krebs on Security
item.description:
Why: A ransomware recovery firm that claimed crypto magic was just paying the attackers, a great Krebs cautionary tale. (score 7)

From Krebs on Security.

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
item.content:encoded:
Why: A ransomware recovery firm that claimed crypto magic was just paying the attackers, a great Krebs cautionary tale. (score 7)

From Krebs on Security.

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

item.content:encoded:
Why: MacSparky reads the tea leaves on Apple's recent turn toward delight and whimsy under John Ternus. (score 7)

From MacSparky.

If you’re paying attention, there’s something weird going on at Apple lately.

On the most recent MacBook Pro, the PROLED model, they put the glowing Apple logo back in the lid. The CEO, John Ternus, even commented on that in a recent interview with Steven Levy, where he bragged about it.

When Siri AI released, a lot of us were complaining that it didn’t have enough third-party support and third-party app developers had their hands tied. Applying our traditional Apple thinking caps, we all figured that at the soonest we’d get a little bit more access next June, but this would take years. Yet that expanded third-party access is already showing up in the point release betas.

After the iPhone Duo released, a lot of people complained they wished it had Face ID. Well, the device doesn’t have hardware for that, but it does have a front-facing camera. And in the latest point release for the iPhone Duo, Apple’s turned on a form of face identification. It doesn’t work for everything because it’s not as secure as Face ID, but it is something a user can select to get to their phone more quickly.

It just seems Apple lately is a lot more nimble with their updates and responsiveness.

Maybe this is just a weird set of coincidences. But I’d like to attribute it to John Ternus. He is, after all, a product guy. And I can’t help but think that he uses and cares about these things more than Tim Cook did.

This isn’t meant to be a dig on Tim Cook. He did his job. And the company became a lot bigger and more profitable under his watch, but I’m not in it for the stock price. I’m in it for the user experience, and lately I’m noticing things.

I almost didn’t create this newsletter out of fear that I would jinx it all, but we may be entering a new phase with Apple products where things are a bit more delightful. I sure hope that’s the case.

The post There’s Something Weird Going On at Apple appeared first on MacSparky.

The TV industrial complex was based on the effectiveness of advertising, and the ads that […]
item.content:encoded:
Why: Seth Godin on how systems grow surprising side effects, a useful lens for anyone shaping a platform. (score 7)

From Seth's Blog.

Emergent properties

No system stays the way it began, and all systems evolve characteristics that surprise us.

The rise of the automobile system led to roads and gas stations, of course, but also parking lots, drive-through fast food restaurants and drunk driving.

The TV industrial complex was based on the effectiveness of advertising, and the ads that were among the most profitable were for beverages and snack foods, which made those industries ever more efficient and led to convenience foods and also widespread obesity.

And factory farming feeds billions of people. Competitive pressures led to a rise in fertilizer use and a destruction of topsoil, which also dramatically shifts the climate.

Any complex system will soon surprise us with its unanticipated effects.

item.title: Penalised Antonelli beats Verstappen with both Ferraris out in Q2
item.author: Formula 1 - The Race
item.description:
Why: Las Vegas GP qualifying chaos puts Verstappen on pole despite Antonelli's top lap, ahead of tonight's race. (score 7)

From Formula 1 - The Race.

Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying at F1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, but Max Verstappen will start from pole position, and both Ferraris missed the pole battle
item.content:encoded:
Why: Las Vegas GP qualifying chaos puts Verstappen on pole despite Antonelli's top lap, ahead of tonight's race. (score 7)

From Formula 1 - The Race.

Penalised Antonelli beats Verstappen with both Ferraris out in Q2

Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, but Max Verstappen will start from pole position because of the Mercedes driver’s grid penalty, and both Ferraris failed to make the pole fight.

Antonelli has a five-place grid penalty for taking the updated Mercedes ADUO turbocharger this weekend, but he minimised the damage of that beautifully in Q3.

Antonelli gambled by dropping back from a squabbling pack of cars on the final runs as he ended up crossing the line with only a couple of seconds to spare.

But that turned out perfectly as he was in the ideal track position to pick up a huge slipstream from multiple cars at the end of the lap to set a 1m33.893s.

That was two and a half tenths quicker than Max Verstappen, who couldn’t improve on his second Q3 run.

But he’ll start from pole position because of Antonelli’s penalty and will share the front row of the grid with the man he clashed with in practice, George Russell.

Russell asked Mercedes for a tow from Antonelli, which didn’t transpire.

Lando Norris was fourth for McLaren ahead of Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls, who was a career-best sixth.

Oscar Piastri was seventh but he has to serve a 10-place grid penalty.

Liam Lawson was eighth ahead of Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, who had been second in Q2. Team-mate Franco Colapinto rounded out the top 10, after brushing the wall.

Both Ferraris out in Q2

The biggest shock of qualifying proved to be a double Ferrari Q2 elimination, the first time the team has failed to get a car into Q3 since Imola last year.

Lewis Hamilton was struggling throughout FP3 and qualifying, and looked vulnerable to an early exit from the start.

But team-mate Charles Leclerc ended up joining him in the danger zone after he made an error into Turn 7, ruined his lap and then fell short of making the chequered flag for another attempt.

As others improved, that meant Leclerc and Hamilton were shuffled down to 11th and 12th.

Behind them were the Audis and Williams, with Nico Hulkenberg leading Carlos Sainz, Gabriel Bortoleto and Alex Albon.

Rafael Camara was knocked out in 17th in his second-ever F1 qualifying session, seven hundredths away from a second successive Q2 session.

Sergio Perez was 18th for Cadillac - his best qualifying since Monaco - even though he was left without a tow from his team-mate Valtteri Bottas on his lap, as in Bottas’s words, “We lost each other.”

Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll were 19th and 20th for Aston Martin, ahead of Bottas and Bearman, who sacrificed his qualifying session to tow Camara, because of his huge grid penalty.

Q3 classification

1 Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) 1m33.893s
2 Max Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.258s
3 George Russell (Mercedes) +0.331s
4 Lando Norris (McLaren) +0.351s

8 Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) +1.197s
9 Pierre Gasly (Alpine) +1.212s
10 Franco Colapinto (Alpine) +1.421s

Out in Q2

11 Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) 1m35.197s +0.111s (gap to Q3)
12 Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.167s
13 Nico Hulkenberg (Audi) +0.374s

Out in Q1

item.content:encoded:
Why: Apple can finally confirm the UK backdoor demand behind pulling Advanced Data Protection, a landmark encryption policy story. (score 9)

From Six Colors.

Apple can at last admit what everyone knew about its restriction in February 2025 on iCloud’s Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for new users in the United Kingdom: the government made us do it.

ADP provides end-to-end, device-based encryption for most iCloud data, and it was a remarkable bump up in privacy protection when Apple released it suddenly in December 2022. The February 2025 announcement offered no details as to why Apple made this enrollment change.

Reporting in April 2025 revealed that the UK government had demanded Apple build a backdoor for access to iCloud data under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which also prevented Apple from revealing this demand. Apple instead disabled the feature for new users.

On Thursday, the UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent body that allows challenges to government surveillance orders, said—paraphrasing—it was ridiculous for Apple to be unable to discuss something widely known in public.

Apple challenged an original broad order that would have jeopardized privacy for users worldwide, and a second one that more narrowly set the scope for British citizens. The company told some media outlets that it “welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.”

Go to the linked site.

Read on Six Colors.

item.title: Scope down permissions of existing sessions using AWS STS GetScopedCredentials
item.author: AWS Security Blog
item.description:
Why: New STS API to scope down session credentials for AI agents, a least-privilege pattern relevant to agent security. (score 7)

From AWS Security Blog.

When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it.
