item.content:encoded:
Why: New STS API to scope down session credentials for AI agents, a least-privilege pattern relevant to agent security. (score 7)

From AWS Security Blog.

When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it. GetScopedCredentials is a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that you can use to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security credentials. You can assign each agent, sub-agent, or process its own set of credentials that keep the caller’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity but carry reduced permissions, a shorter session duration, or both.

You can call GetScopedCredentials with the temporary security credentials you already use, such as those from aws login, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance profile, or an AWS Lambda function. In each call, you pass a scope down policy, a shorter session duration, or both. A scope down policy is an inline policy that describes the maximum permissions for the new credentials. The resulting permissions are the intersection of your session’s effective permissions and the scope down policy, so they can only be reduced. Similarly, the session duration you request can’t exceed the remaining duration of the calling session. You can also call GetScopedCredentials again with the resulting credentials to scope down permissions or reduce session duration even further.

GetScopedCredentials is designed as a building block. Because it scopes down permissions on the credentials you already have, you can build it into agent frameworks, services that issue credentials to other components, continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, and your own applications. You can also call it again with scoped-down credentials, so an orchestrating agent can give each sub-agent narrower access than its own.

In this post, we walk through a few common use cases to get you started, show you how to call GetScopedCredentials, and explain how to manage access to it.

Example use cases

You can use GetScopedCredentials whenever a workload needs narrower access than the session that starts it. Examples include limiting what AI agents can do, scoping down permissions based on runtime context, and granting just-in-time access. We cover two of the most common use cases in more detail in this section.

Limit what AI agents can do

When you pass credentials to an agent, the agent can use any permission those credentials carry. An agent decides which actions to take at runtime, often based on prompts or tool output. If its credentials are overly permissive, an agent that makes a mistake can act beyond the task you gave it.

Before you pass credentials to an agent, you can use GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions to only what its tasks require, such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. You could also take the opposite approach and keep most of its permissions while removing only the actions the agent should never perform, such as deleting resources. An orchestrating agent can do the same for each sub-agent it starts. Because a scope down operation can only narrow permissions, a sub-agent never has more access than the agent that started it. To help ensure that your agents only have access to the scoped-down credentials, run them in isolated or sandbox environments such as AWS Strands Box.

Scope down permissions based on runtime context

Many workloads run under a single IAM role but need different, narrower permissions for each task they perform. The right set of permissions for a task often depends on information the workload learns only at runtime, such as who sent a request.

Consider a multi-tenant application that stores each tenant’s files under a separate prefix in one S3 bucket. This application uses a single IAM role to serve all its tenants, so the role can access every tenant’s prefix. However, each request should reach only the files of the tenant who sent it, and the application learns which tenant that is only after it authenticates the request. At that point, a trusted credential broker in the application takes the tenant details from the authenticated session and calls GetScopedCredentials with a scope down policy that allows access only to that tenant’s prefix. It passes only the scoped-down credentials to the worker that handles the request, so Amazon S3 denies that worker access to other tenants’ prefixes even though the original role covers them all.

How to call GetScopedCredentials

This section walks through the process of scoping down permissions for an existing session. Before you call GetScopedCredentials, make sure you have valid temporary security credentials and that they have the permissions to call the API. The following identity based policy grants that permission.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "sts:GetScopedCredentials",
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}

To call GetScopedCredentials, use the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language.

Step 1: Define a scope down policy

Write a scope down policy that describes the maximum permissions the resulting credentials should have. At launch, GetScopedCredentials accepts one inline scope down policy of up to 2,048 characters. You can write a scope down policy in many ways, such as authoring a policy from scratch, reusing or modifying an existing policy, or asking an AI assistant to draft one. This section covers two such approaches.

Option A: Write the policy yourself

If you know which actions and resources your task needs, write the policy directly. The following sample policy allows the resulting credentials to only read objects from a single S3 bucket.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"
  }]
}

Make sure to include every action the task needs, including dependent actions. For example, if your task uses Amazon Athena to query data in Amazon S3, the policy must also allow s3:GetObject on that data, because Athena reads it with your credentials.

To keep most of the calling session’s permissions and remove only a few sensitive ones, use an Allow statement with NotAction. This statement doesn’t grant additional access, because a scope down policy can only reduce permissions. The resulting credentials keep the calling session’s permissions except the actions you list, which makes this a quick way to set guardrails without listing each action a task needs. The following sample policy blocks identity and account management, assuming other roles, and deleting some critical resources.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "NotAction": [
      "iam:*",
      "organizations:*",
      "account:*",
      "sts:AssumeRole*",
      "s3:DeleteBucket",
      "ec2:TerminateInstances",
      "rds:DeleteDBInstance",
      "dynamodb:DeleteTable"
    ],
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}

Option B: Generate the policy with IAM Policy Autopilot

You can also use IAM Policy Autopilot to generate a scope down policy. IAM Policy Autopilot is an open source tool from AWS that analyzes the AWS SDK calls in your code and identifies the permissions it requires to run successfully. You can run it from the command line or as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in your AI coding assistant. To install it, see the Getting Started instructions for IAM Policy Autopilot.

We’ll use the following Python code to generate a scope down policy using IAM Policy Autopilot. It records a report’s status in an Amazon DynamoDB table.

import json
import logging
import os

import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb")
table_name = os.environ["TABLE_NAME"]


def _response(status_code, message):
    return {"statusCode": status_code, "body": json.dumps({"message": message})}


def handler(event, context):
    try:
        request = json.loads(event.get("body") or "{}")
        report_id = request["reportId"]
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError):
        return _response(400, "Request body must be JSON with a reportId")

    if not isinstance(report_id, str) or not report_id:
        return _response(400, "reportId must be a non-empty string")

    try:
        dynamodb.put_item(
            TableName=table_name,
            Item={
                "reportId": {"S": report_id},
                "status": {"S": "READY"},
            },
            ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(reportId)",
        )
        return _response(200, "Report status saved")
    except ClientError as error:
        code = error.response["Error"]["Code"]
        if code == "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
            return _response(409, "Report status already exists")

        logger.error("PutItem failed: %s", code)
        return _response(500, "Unable to save the report status")

Save the code as report_status.py and run the following command. If the generated policy exceeds the 2,048 character limit, set the max-policy-size and allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size options to 2048. IAM Policy Autopilot then replaces groups of actions with wildcards to fit that size and warns you if it can’t.

iam-policy-autopilot generate-policies ./report_status.py \
  --region us-west-2 \
  --account 123456789012 \
  --service-hints dynamodb \
  --max-policy-size 2048 \
  --allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size 2048 \
  --pretty

IAM Policy Autopilot returns the following policy.

{
  "Id": "IamPolicyAutopilot",
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "dynamodb:PutItem",
        "dynamodb:WriteDataForReplication"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/*"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:ViaService": [
            "dynamodb.us-west-2.amazonaws.com"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

IAM Policy Autopilot generates a starting policy that can include wildcards, either because specific resources can’t be inferred from the code, such as with the table/* and key/* resources in this example, or because an optional parameter that limits policy size replaced actions with wildcards. Review the generated policies and replace the wildcards with the actions and resources your task should access.

However you create the policy, save it as scope-down-policy.json. If you want to continue calling GetScopedCredentials with the resulting credentials, also include the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in the Allow block of the permission policy.

Step 2: Call GetScopedCredentials

Pass the scope down policy you created to GetScopedCredentials. The following command also uses the optional duration-seconds parameter to limit the resulting session duration and the optional scoped-session-description parameter to record context for the scoped-down credentials. If you omit the duration-seconds parameter, the credentials keep the calling session’s remaining duration.

aws sts get-scoped-credentials \
  --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"}]}' \
  --duration-seconds 300 \
  --scoped-session-description report-status-job \
  --region us-west-2

The response includes a new set of temporary security credentials, a SessionInfo element, and some helpful information about session size and contents.

{
  "Credentials": {
    "AccessKeyId": "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE",
    "SecretAccessKey": "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY,
    "SessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...",
    "Expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z"
  },
  "SessionInfo": {
    "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane",
    "ScopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane"
  },
  "SessionTokenUtilization": 17,
  "SessionTokenSize": 724,
  "ScopedPoliciesCount": 1
}

Notice that the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the SessionInfo element matches the ARN of your calling session. The scoped-down credentials retain the identity of the calling session, including the role session name, session tags and context keys.

The ScopedPoliciesCount value in the response shows how many scope down policies apply to the session. It increases only when a recursive call adds a new scope down policy and not when a call only shortens the session duration.

Each GetScopedCredentials call is logged in AWS CloudTrail. The following event, shortened for readability, shows the call from this example.

{
    "eventVersion": "1.11",
    "userIdentity": {
        "type": "AssumedRole",
        "principalId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:janee",
        "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane",
        "accessKeyId": "ASIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE",
        ...
    },
    "eventTime": "2026-10-12T02:55:00Z",
    "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com",
    "eventName": "GetScopedCredentials",
    "awsRegion": "us-west-2",
    ...
    "requestParameters": {
        "policy": "{\"Version\":\"2012-10-17\",\"Statement\":[{\"Effect\":\"Allow\",\"Action\":\"s3:GetObject\",\"Resource\":\"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*\"}]}",
        "scopedSessionDescription": "report-status-job",
        "durationSeconds": 300
    },
    "responseElements": {
        "credentials": {
            "accessKeyId": "ASIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE",
            "sessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...",
            "expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z"
        },
        "sessionInfo": {
            "scopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane",
            "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane"
        },
        "sessionTokenUtilization": 17,
        "sessionTokenSize": 724,
        "scopedPoliciesCount": 1
    },
    "readOnly": false,
    ...
}

The scopedSessionDescription value in the CloudTrail event records the text you passed to the API call earlier. Later calls made with the scoped-down credentials show the scoped down session’s access key ID in userIdentity.accessKeyId, which can be used to trace back to its immediate parent session.

Step 3 (optional): Scope down the credentials again

You can call GetScopedCredentials recursively with the scoped-down credentials to narrow permissions or reduce session duration even further. You can apply a maximum of three scope down policies to a session, and each new scope down policy intersects with all prior ones. Recursive calls that only shorten the session duration and don’t add a scope down policy don’t count toward this limit. For a recursive call to succeed, every earlier scope down policy must allow the sts:GetScopedCredentials action.

Managing access to GetScopedCredentials

You can control access to the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in all relevant policy types. You can also use the sts:DurationSeconds condition key to limit the session duration of scoped-down credentials, and global condition keys such as aws:PrincipalArn, aws:PrincipalTag, and aws:SourceVpce to restrict who can call the API and from where.

Availability and request quota

GetScopedCredentials is available in all AWS commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. The API has a dedicated request quota of 200 requests per second per account in each Region at launch. You can use scoped-down credentials with most AWS services. For a list of services that aren’t supported, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference.

Conclusion

GetScopedCredentials gives you a building block for reducing permissions at runtime. This is particularly helpful when you want to give each agent, sub agent or workload only the access it needs.

For more information about GetScopedCredentials, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference. To learn how permissions are evaluated for scoped-down credentials, see Permissions for GetScopedCredentials and Policy evaluation for requests within a single account. Now go build!

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or contact AWS Support.

Vaishnavi Merugu

Vaishnavi is a Senior Technical Product Manager in AWS Identity. Her work focuses on products that simplify identity and access management for customers. Outside of work, she enjoys traveling and exploring new cultures and food.

Ryan Peng

Ryan is a Software Development Engineer in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), where he builds the short-term credential vending systems that customers rely on to grant and constrain access to their AWS resources. Most recently, he has focused on how workloads and AI agents can run with the narrowest set of permissions they need. Outside of work, Ryan enjoys watching and playing sports, and staying active outdoors.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Hands-on with Siri Recap, Apple's privacy-isolated conversation summaries on Apple Watch. (score 7)

From MacRumors: Mac News and Rumors - All Stories.

With the watchOS 27.3 beta, Apple started testing Siri Recap. ‌Siri‌ Recap lets the Series 12 and Ultra 4 Apple Watch models listen to conversations to generate a brief summary of what was discussed. Actual audio is sectioned off from apps, Apple, and the rest of the OS, and then discarded after a summary is generated.


It's a privacy-forward way of tracking what's going on around you, but after two weeks of testing, it's clear that the privacy safeguards limit its usefulness. Overly brief summaries, lack of speaker labeling, and no original audio to compare against make ‌Siri‌ Recap unreliable.

Before I get into my experience, I want to make it clear that ‌Siri‌ Recap is a beta feature in beta software. It hasn't been released yet, Apple hasn't finished refining it, and it won't be available to the public until watchOS 27.3 launches in December. Still, the bones are in place. Some of the issues I encountered could improve before release, but others are the result of the way it's built.

My first recaps were from YouTube videos and Instagram Reels. ‌Siri‌ Recap can tell when I'm watching TV shows and movies, but it can't distinguish a YouTube video from a real-life conversation. I was surprised it summarized dialogue I wasn't involved in instead of waiting until it recognized my voice (which ‌Siri‌ can do). Listening in on ambient conversations makes it feel a little stalker-like. When ‌Siri‌ Recap is turned on, it's listening, and there's no indication for the people around you.


Most of my other recaps summarized short, inconsequential conversations with my partner that I don't need or want to revisit. I don't need to remember that my breakfast on Friday had one too many pieces of vegan bacon, or that my cat was playing with a silica packet. I don't need to remember discussions about Grand Theft Auto VI or that I saw a rabbit in the driveway the other day. There is an option to only have ‌Siri‌ Recap on at certain times of the day or in certain locations, which would eliminate that issue. Ironically, ‌Siri‌ did the best at summarizing shorter interactions I don't care about.


I've taken my cats to a few vet appointments recently, so I had an opportunity to test ‌Siri‌ Recap with genuinely important conversations where I get a flood of information. After the first visit, I learned ‌Siri‌ and I don't have the same opinion on the details that matter, and I found that summaries of longer conversations are just too concise and inaccurate to be helpful.

I told the vet my cat is picky and will only eat one kind of dry food, but stays hydrated because she drinks a lot of water. In a separate part of the conversation, I said she was gaining weight even though her prescription food isn't for kittens. ‌Siri‌ combined those two parts of the conversation into a summary that doesn't make sense, and I had that issue in almost every long conversation.

A few minutes later, I asked for a recommendation on heartworm medication because I've read about some problematic products that can make cats sick. The vet relayed a story about needing a particular brand for her cat because she has a rabbit at home, and rabbits are sensitive to a lot of medications. ‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't label speakers, so the summary of that conversation turned into a confusing amalgamation suggesting I have a rabbit at home. Inappropriately combining unrelated concepts is likely something that can be fixed, but the lack of speaker labels is intentional.


During a pre-surgery consultation, I think I ran into another limitation. Apple says potentially harmful content isn't summarized, which could cover a broad range of topics. Important parts of the conversation with the vet aren't in the summary, like some of the scarier surgical risks and resuscitation preferences. ‌Siri‌ doesn't say if anything was skipped because of the content, so I don't know if that information wasn't considered important or if it was filtered out.


Some of what ‌Siri‌ recapped was useful. If conversations were fact-heavy, ‌Siri‌ did a good job getting everything down, especially when dates were involved. I scheduled a follow-up appointment and ‌Siri‌ got the date right and the exact total of the bill when it was spoken aloud. Apple does say ‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't include financial info, so I'm not sure what counts. ‌Siri‌ is also surprisingly good at interpreting spoken medication names like benazepril and clopidogrel and correctly guessing what they're meant to be.


During a third vet visit, the recap did get many of the major points, but going over those notes made me realize this kind of summarization may not work, even when accurate. I had my own memory of the conversation and knew what I thought was important, but some of what ‌Siri‌ kept wasn't what mattered to me.

Those ‌Siri‌ details I re-read were cemented in my memory over other information when I revisited the conversation later in the week, subtly changing how I remember the appointment. I worry having notes that aren't my own will overwrite what I would have remembered without them. It's almost like having a picture of something that happened in my head, and then having someone tell me it happened differently.


‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't record full conversations for privacy reasons, but that leaves ‌Siri‌ to decide what to keep in a discussion and what's not. I don't trust ‌Siri‌ to make that kind of decision, personally. There's no option to go back and check what ‌Siri‌ left out since there are no recordings. I wouldn't want a version of ‌Siri‌ Recap that records full conversations because of the privacy concerns, but I'm not sure Apple has delivered a version that's both useful and privacy-forward.

‌Siri‌ picks and chooses what matters, and in my two-week test, ‌Siri‌ merged concepts and conversations in ways that were more confusing than helpful over and over again. ‌Siri‌ Recap isn't a feature I'm going to use, and it's not a feature I'd recommend to others.
Related Roundups: watchOS 26, watchOS 27
Tag: Siri
Related Forum: Apple Watch

This article, "Siri Recap Hands-On: Private, But Not Very Useful" first appeared on MacRumors.com

item.content:encoded:
Why: A threatened tax on offshore AI data centers could reshape where cloud providers like Azure build. (score 7)

From The Verge.

President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.

Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US

While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”

Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”

Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.

Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:

Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.

We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.

So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Preview of 10th ranked BYU's high-stakes road game at Kansas Saturday. (score 7)

From Vanquish The Foe.

BYU plays their final true road game of the regular season in Lawrence on Saturday. The Cougars and Jayhawks kick off at 10:00am MT on ESPN.

We don’t need to remind BYU fans of the importance of this game or the demons that come to life when the Cougars play Kansas. 10th-ranked BYU’s College Football Playoff hopes are very much alive. And they very much are at stake when these two teams square off at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium.

Let’s dive into five questions ahead of the matchup.

What demons are the Cougars facing against the Jayhawks?

For starters, BYU has never beaten Kansas in football in three tries. Somehow, the Cougars have had more success against Kansas in basketball than football. The matchup everyone seems to be pointing to is the one in 2024. It’s a very similar situation. The Jayhawks traveled to Provo in mid-November with BYU at 9-0 with College Football Playoff hopes very alive. Kansas came with an unremarkable 3-6 record but had just beaten a ranked Iowa State team. BYU turned the ball over twice and committed one of the worst special teams blunders imaginable. A punt in a short field by Kansas while BYU was up three bounced off Evan Johnson’s helmet. Kansas recovered the muff and scored a few plays later to take the lead. It was one of the most devastating losses in recent BYU history.

Before that, Kansas and BYU met up in 2023, the Cougars’ last trip to Lawrence before this weekend. After leading 17-14 at halftime, BYU allowed 24 second half points as they unraveled, losing what was their first official Big 12 Conference game.

The demons didn’t start there either. The first meeting between the Cougars and Jayhawks was the Aloha Bowl in 1992. Kansas won on a late field goal and subsequent interception from Tom Young.

Just how dynamic is Kansas’ offense?

Scoring-wise, Kansas is 49th in the FBS in points per game. That might not have BYU shaking in their boots, but the Jayhawks can move the ball in many ways. Quarterback Isaiah Marshall only threw three incompletions all game against West Virginia last week. Receivers Nik McMillan and Cam Pickett do most of the damage, accounting for nearly half of the receptions on the team by themselves. Watch out for Nahzae Cox, who is averaging 26.5 yards per catch as a deep threat.

At quarterback, Marshall certainly can hurt defenses with his legs. The signal caller totaled a whopping 164 rushing yards on 19 attempts against the Mountaineers, for an 8.6 yard average. He ranks second in the Big 12 in rushing yards by a quarterback. It’s not just a one-man show on the ground either. Five different Jayhawks carried the football in their 37-14 win over West Virginia. Three different ballcarriers collected at least 14 carries. All this amounts to Kansas boasting the 16th-ranked rushing offense in the FBS.

Where is BYU’s biggest advantage on offense?

Like Kansas, BYU wants to run the ball. LJ Martin is getting healthier each week. Even after not playing during the second half against Baylor, Martin should be good to go for a bigger workload. When facing conference opponents, Kansas ranks 89th in rushing defense, allowing nearly 170 rushing yards per game against Big 12 foes. Kansas’ defense has been generally solid, but this seems like a weak point. The combination of Bear Bachmeier and Martin should get the run game going enough to control the game. BYU also has allowed the third-least sacks among all Power Four teams. The offensive line should be able to hold up against a middling Kansas pass rush.

Kansas is better against the pass, ranking 16th in completion percentage allowed and 47th in passing yards allowed (out of 138).

Are BYU’s road struggles a concern?

BYU’s two losses this season have both come on the road. First, they inexplicably lost to unranked UCF in Orlando. A few weeks ago, Utah defeated the Cougars at Rice-Eccles Stadium. However, those aren’t the only examples of the Cougars struggling on the road this season. Their last road win came in Fort Worth against TCU. TCU came into the game 2-2 and outmatched. Yet it was 7-7 at halftime and the Cougars won by just seven, 17-10.

The Cougars mustered just 216 total yards of offense including a miniscule 62 passing yards. Granted, the weather was very wet and suboptimal for offense. Still, BYU played just as sloppy as the weather, with seven penalties as well. The road struggles are a real thing. That is something BYU needs to overcome. This will not be the most hostile crowd BYU has faced this year, but the Cougars have shown they can come out flat when the game isn’t in Provo.

Do style points matter for BYU?

To put it bluntly, yes. In fact, it might be required. If BYU scrapes by the Jayhawks, the unpredictable committee may punish BYU for playing too close to a 5-6 Kansas team. The spread currently sits at 5.5 points in favor of the Cougars. Winning this game by six points to cover the spread may not be enough. This is because there are two teams just behind BYU in the College Football Playoff rankings hot on their tail. Wake Forest sits at No. 11 with just one loss and a possible trip to the ACC Championship Game in their future. Texas Tech is at 12, likely headed to Arlington. If both of those teams blow out their remaining opponents while BYU inches by Kansas or Cincinnati, the committee may allow one of those teams just behind them to leapfrog the Cougars. The Cougars need to win by double digits.

Prediction: BYU 27, Kansas 23

item.title: F1's new V8 engine agreed – five things you need to know
item.author: Formula 1 - The Race
item.description:
Why: F1 locks in a return to V8 engines for 2030, a big rules story. (score 7)

From Formula 1 - The Race.

F1 will adopt V8 engines in 2030 now key stakeholders have unanimously agreed on key details that will underpin the new rules
item.content:encoded:
Why: F1 locks in a return to V8 engines for 2030, a big rules story. (score 7)

From Formula 1 - The Race.

F1's new V8 engine agreed – five things you need to know


Formula 1 will adopt V8 engines in 2030 now key stakeholders have unanimously agreed on the key details that will underpin the new regulations. 

A framework has been unanimously agreed by the FIA, Formula 1, the teams and the engine manufacturers to bring in a 2.1-litre, turbocharged V8 with a reduced electric element.

This switch will be made one year earlier than planned, bringing an early end to the V6 turbo-hybrid rules that only started a controversial new era this season with a switch to a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electric power.  

The FIA World Motor Sport Council will rubber-stamp the plan at a Shanghai meeting next month. 

How key final progress was reached

A meeting of the F1 Commission on Monday, November 16 led to agreement in principle over the framework. 

But it required some final progress to be made for the engine manufacturers themselves to accept ending the current rules cycle in 2029 and be satisfied with the switch. 

The manufacturers are Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull/Ford, Audi Honda and future engine supplier General Motors - which was aiming to belatedly join the current rules cycle before the end of the decade (more on that shortly). 

After the Commission, a meeting with the manufacturers – which are represented in the Commission but have their own key discussion group with the other stakeholders – went through key feedback to resolve what was necessary to push the proposal to the next stage. 

This is what facilitated Friday's announcement of unanimous agreement of the technical framework. 

GM will delay engine to fit

A key consequence of the change of timeline is what it means for GM’s plans. 

Its Cadillac team, which GM is a minority owner of alongside TWG Motorsports, joined the grid this year as a Ferrari customer on the condition it becomes a full works entry. 

GM had been planning to debut that engine built to the current rules in 2029, which it was willing to accept even though it would be only two seasons before all-new rules came in as originally planned. 

To accommodate the next rules era starting earlier, though, GM will delay its manufacturer debut so it does not have to design and build a V6 for one season only.

It is expected to remain a Ferrari customer for an extra year and the rules being agreed is well timed as the purpose-built GM engine facility opens in mid-December this year, which means the full might of its development push can be devoted to the new 2030 rules instead of a split project. 

"For a period of time, we were working on both,” TWG boss Dan Towriss said in Las Vegas. “So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8. There are a number of designs that are in motion now.”

The key details

Officially, the proposed 2030 engine will be a 2.1-litre turbo V8 that carries over “some geometrical specifics”, will feature limited hybridisation” as well as sustainable fuels, and be married to a lighter chassis. 

This is all part of the plan to make the engines simpler, cheaper and louder – although the extent of that last point is still unclear given it will not be a normally aspirated engine. 

“I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps – it's just that high-pitch squeal that I'm missing from this era,” said Mercedes driver George Russell.

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri cautioned “I don't know if they'll be exactly like the V8 engines that I grew up watching, necessarily”, but added “I think it's firstly great that we've been listened to”. 

The turbocharger stays partly to satisfy manufacturer demand but also to assist with fuel efficiency, avoid larger tanks and more fuel usage at the start of races. 

This also helps with the stated aim of making the car and engine around 80kg lighter with almost half of that coming on the engine side. 

More details of this will surely come from the “detailed regulatory framework” that will go to the WMSC in Shanghai next month.

However, it does appear to represent a satisfactory compromise between what some manufacturers want in terms of hybridisation and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem’s initial desire for an even bigger, loud engine without a turbo. 

“The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide,” said Ben Sulayem. 

“Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.”

What’s still to be confirmed

The FIA did not specify the hybrid element, which has been known for some time to be heading towards a 100kW base electric power contribution with an extra 100kW available as effectively a push-to-pass overtaking aid. 

It will give the engine more than 1,000bhp at full power but crucially, compared to the current engines, not be dependent on the electric element and therefore not at the mercy of the energy limitations that have dogged the 2026 rules since their debut. 

Why the hybrid element has not been exactly specified is unclear – “maybe it have some KERS or stuff like that”, as Alpine boss Flavio Briatore put it – but it stands to reason that this is being delayed until more detail can be shared about how it will work. 

With the 2026 rules, the engine regulations were designed first, then the chassis and sporting regulations were contorted around them - leading to a fundamentally compromised product, all because the engine rules had to be set early to get all the targeted manufacturers committed. 

This time the core V8 engine plan should be much simpler to align with the car design and operation, but there are still elements to decide - like exactly how a push-to-pass system should be managed and whether the active aero with movable front and rear wings is worth retaining when that was primarily adopted to assist with making the current cars more efficient on the straights.

Drivers are excited - with minor caveats

Every single driver on the F1 grid has, publicly or privately, expressed their displeasure with the 2026 engines and their consequences. 

So, unsurprisingly, all who have been asked about the return of V8s have welcomed the plan - from the general concept to the fact that there was a good degree of consultation with the drivers themselves. 

Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar said he was very excited for a “full attack racing car” and went as far as adding “I don't see why that would not be the most fun cars of all time in 2030”. 

His team-mate, four-time world champion and vocal 2026 rules critic Max Verstappen, indicated he would have liked it to go further though. 

"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever,” he said. “That sounds even better, but I know that that's not something realistic.

“So this is good, this is for sure in the right direction."

Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton’s own caveat related to the detail of the as-yet undefined regulations that will define how the engines actually work – although what he hopes for most should naturally be achieved simply by stripping back the electric side so much. 

“It's all good and well going to V8, it depends on how they design it, regulation wise,” he said.

“And going back to the good sound because that's I think been lacking since we've been in the V6 era. Bring back the smaller exhaust and get that sound back.

“And as long as we don't have the engine dying halfway down the straight, then I think that will be better.”

item.content:encoded:
Why: On your always-include list. (score 10)

From Cliff Mass Weather Blog.

Examine the climatological precipitation map for Washington State, and the heaviest precipitation is on the western slopes of the Cascades and Olympic Mountains (see below)

This is expected because most of our precipitation comes from moist air moving eastward off the Pacific.  Air that is forced to rise, cool, and precipitate on the west-facing major slopes of our region.

But something VERY different occurred during the 36 hours ending Thursday evening (see below).  The heaviest precipitation was on the EASTERN slopes of the Cascades and the southeastern slopes of the Olympics (see below)

Very little on the western slopes of the Cascades.


The visible satellite image on Thursday morning shows clouds east of the Cascade crest. Nearly clear on the western side.


Substantial snow fell on the eastern slopes of the Cascades, as shown by an image provided by the NW Avalanche Center for a location just east of Stevens Pass.   I am tempted to get out my skis!




Even as far west as Crystal Mountain, a fresh cover of the white stuff was apparent.


Want to be really impressed with the changes?  Below is the change in snowpack during the past three days.   Massive increase in snow east of the Cascade crest of Oregon and Washington.


The UW WRF modeling system predicted this east-side precipitation (see below) days before (see below).


It also forecast the eastern slopes getting snow (see below).


So why the precipitation reversal?

Easy to explain.  

A low center passed south of us, pushing moisture north into eastern Washington, and then swinging the moisture toward the west on the eastern slopes of the Cascades.   

This is illustrated by the 850 hPa (about 5000 ft) and 500 hPa (about 18,000 ft) maps below for 4 PM Wednesday (below).  You can see the easterly (from the east) winds approaching the Cascades.

850 hPa pressure, 5000 ft


500 hPa 18,000 ft

This pattern, with lows going into our south, has occurred several times during the last few weeks, but the latest forecasts suggest a substantial pattern shift with precipitation falling preferentially on the western slopes during the next week or so.



Looking east from the Cascades crest.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Six Colors on Siri AI writing controls in Mail, a favorite writer on timely Apple news. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

There I was, drafting an email reply in macOS 27.2.1, when I was greeted by this fresh hell:

I’ve been on record since the 27 releases as saying that I find Siri’s writing tools across the platform updates to be unnecessarily aggressive, and they certainly haven’t gotten less so.

Look, I’m a professional writer. I do not need help writing a three-sentence email. If there are people who find these features useful, have at! But I would love the ability to dispatch them with extreme prejudice, and I can find no options anywhere in Mail to say “begone with you!”

But all hope is not lost. After complaining on Mastodon1, Andrew Kemp offered this suggestion:

Lo and behold, yes! If you open up System Settings and go to Screen Time > Content & Privacy, then turn on the Content & Privacy switch, you can then go into the Siri sub-menu and turn off Writing Assistance. (You can also disable other Siri options in here, such as Broad World Knowledge, Image Creation, and Realistic Images, all of which probably make more sense for the parental controls for which Screen Time is designed.)

I had to close and re-open my draft message, but when I did, it was back to just the formatting bar. Phew.

I don’t love having to turn to Screen Time for this feature any more than I like the idea of using accessibility features for aesthetic alterations to the OS, but any port in a storm, I suppose.

I know we’re in the era of “shove AI into everything!” but I have generally appreciated Apple’s more conservative stance here. I just wish they would give us more granular options for turning off the parts of these features we don’t want that doesn’t require parenting ourselves.

  1. Something I’m all too capable of doing, even on paternity leave. ↩

item.content:encoded:
Why: KVM flaw exposing host memory from a guest VM matters for cloud security and confidential computing. (score 8)

From The Hacker News.

A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years.

In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities.

What to Do

The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted.

Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range.

Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected.

Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change.

Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it:

  • Check the setting with 
    cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested
    . A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on.
  • If the host cannot be updated yet, add 
    options kvm_amd nested=0
    to the host's module configuration.
  • Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with 
    uname -r
    and by reading the nested setting again.

The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: AI agents autonomously finding a zero-day is a notable security and AI shift. (score 8)

From AWS Security Blog.

Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

Discovery

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

Cairn and an overview of this campaign

Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. The following operations show both the persistence and the capability of autonomous AI agents.

Persistence against a hardened target

The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.

When those attempts failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded.

A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login.

Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction.

Zero-day discovery

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

Subsequent use

In another session, the threat actor stepped in. After the agents discovered the zero-day, the actor then provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network. The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel. The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.

Attribution

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor based on the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time script timestamps, and the targeting of universities likely of strategic interest to China.

Actions taken by AWS

Amazon Threat Intelligence notified the project’s maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory.

The affected organizations were non-AWS customers that AWS had no direct path to notify. Instead, AWS worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.

Adoption is growing

Gambit Security was one of the first organizations in the industry to document the use of Cairn by a threat group. Its research describes a separate, financially motivated actor using Cairn to target online retailers. Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations. Additional details are available in Gambit Security’s report.

What this means for defenders

The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints. To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.

Behind the scenes, AWS active defense systems use global honeypots (decoy systems that attract threat actors) and network traffic analysis to identify actors that are scanning for vulnerable systems, and then help restrict that activity at the network level. These protections are built into the AWS network at no extra cost to customers.

Indicators of compromise

The following addresses appear in records dated September 8 to 10, 2026.

142[.]4.98.145

142[.]4.107.34

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

CJ Moses

CJ Moses is the CISO of Amazon Integrated Security. In his role, CJ leads security engineering and operations across Amazon. His mission is to enable Amazon businesses by making the benefits of security the path of least resistance. CJ joined Amazon in December 2007, holding various roles including Consumer CISO, and most recently AWS CISO, before becoming CISO of Amazon Integrated Security September of 2023.

Prior to joining Amazon, CJ led the technical analysis of computer and network intrusion efforts at the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division. CJ also served as a Special Agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). CJ led several computer intrusion investigations seen as foundational to the security industry today.

CJ holds degrees in Computer Science and Criminal Justice, and is an active SRO GT America GT2 race car driver.

The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are "undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy," Signal president […]
item.content:encoded:
Why: Signal blocking AI agents from reading the screen touches security and AI agents. (score 8)

From The Verge.

Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.

Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen

Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”

Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system.

Signal’s app security settings on Android devices will display this message for the screenshot-blocking feature.

Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

item.content:encoded:
Why: VMware vCenter zero-day exploited by a China-linked group, a notable breach. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system.

It has been addressed as part of patches released on November 19, 2026, in the following versions -

  • VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.1.0200
  • VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0200
  • VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m
  • VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)
  • VMware Cloud Foundation - Fixed in 5.2.5
  • VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)
  • VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

"CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC)," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said.

"Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local."

An attacker can exploit the vulnerability to obtain an authenticated administrator session, execute arbitrary commands, and acquire files, such as the data.mdb database, by using the Directory Service ("vmdird"). The tech giant's threat intelligence and incident response teams said it observed the Chinese hacking group weaponizing the flaw using a utility dubbed BONESAW.

"BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang, which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account," Google said.

The activity is part of the same campaign that also involved the exploitation of a then zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to conduct reconnaissance, obtain administrative control, establish persistence, and deploy a bespoke proxy tunneler called BARECLAW.

From the Remote Support device, the threat actor is said to have moved laterally to an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and deployed additional payloads to broaden their access, map the environment, conduct data theft, and move into the virtualized environment.

"The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012," Google said. "Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of Armory Castle's remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW."

Deployed as part of the attack are six identified malware families and utilities -

  • SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, JSP web shells designed to run arbitrary commands, stage payloads, and establish a foothold on the Linux appliance.
  • BONESAW, the Golang-based remote exploitation utility for CVE-2026-123890 used to target an internal vCenter Server.
  • SAWSNAKE, a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, thereby making it possible to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW and allowing the attacker to forge authentication tokens, bypass multi-factor authentication(MFA), and impersonate any user. It's a Go-based port of an open-source Python script named "vcenter_saml_login.py."
  • BEARBONES, a C backdoor based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server that's capable of bypassing system password authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from the temporary directory.
  • LAZYBONES, a lightweight Go backdoor that uses Slack for command-and-control (C2) communications and has been previously deployed in a separate intrusion in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of a critical flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2025-22457, CVSS score: 9.0).

It's suspected that Armory Castle had knowledge of the flaw prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026, with the recovered BONESAW binary containing a build timestamp of July 13, 2026. However, it's worth noting that build metadata can be modified before compilation.

"After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, Armory Castle moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-<REDACTED>@vsphere.local," Google said.

"Notably, Armory Castle enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. After enabling SSH, Armory Castle connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account."

In the final stage of the attack, the adversary was found enumerating the ESXi file system, mounting Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and adding an SSH public key to the root account's authorized keys. It also conducted additional reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi file system, which were then archived and downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance for subsequent exfiltration.

Furthermore, the attackers have been observed dropping LAZYBONES to a separate Linux appliance, which periodically checks for commands from a designated Slack channel, allowing it to perform command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment.

CVE-2026-123890 is the second vulnerability in a VMware product to be exploited by Armory Castle as a zero-day this year alone. Late last month, CrowdStrike revealed it identified incidents where the hacking crew abused CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an insufficient logging flaw in VMware ESX, to reduce audit trail visibility.

"BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days," Google said. "The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each."

"The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting Armory Castle operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor's operational commitment to compromise high-priority targets."

Google News,

item.author: The Hacker News
item.description:

From The Hacker News.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Unpatched Windows lock-screen bypass is relevant to a Microsoft security PM. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

A newly disclosed unpatched zero-day technique called FastUnlock lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows computer start programs without signing in. Whoever uses it gets only a limited account, not administrator control of the machine.

The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker tested it the same day and found it works.

There is no fix from Microsoft yet, and nothing shows the method has been used in a real attack.

The technique does not work on every machine. It requires physical access to the computer and a Microsoft account accessible through the lock screen's recovery options, and it uses Windows' built-in screen reader, Narrator, to navigate the locked screen.

In its test, the firm reached a point where it could run a program from the lock screen in a limited account that ThreatLocker identified as WSIAccount and said is "not an administrator account."

The researcher's GitHub disclosure is a short post with a video and little written detail, so the clearest account of what the flaw does comes from the firm's independent test.

Many Windows computers encrypt their drives with BitLocker, but in a common setup, that does not make them immune to this technique. A chip called the TPM unlocks the drive automatically when the computer starts, so by the time the lock screen appears, the files are already readable, and the bypass runs at that point. Microsoft's own TPM documentation describes this mode, in which the drive unlocks "without having to enter a PIN."

FastUnlock does not break that encryption or recover the key. It runs on a computer that has already unlocked its own drive in the normal way, which is a smaller problem than cracking an encrypted disk, though still a real one for a machine someone else is holding.

The conditions above, physical access and a reachable Microsoft account, are what put a machine at risk. No official list of affected Windows versions has been published, so treat any machine that meets those conditions as possibly affected until one is.

What You Can Do Now

With no patch available, the useful steps are about physical control and startup protection.

  • Keep machines that can go missing out of the wrong hands. Lock away or closely manage laptops, shared desks, and front-counter computers that a stranger could reach.
  • On sensitive machines, add a startup PIN to BitLocker instead of letting the drive unlock on its own.
  • Shut down or hibernate devices when they leave someone's control. A startup PIN protects only a machine that has not yet started, not one already on the lock screen.
  • Do not treat a locked screen on its own as enough.

Microsoft's countermeasures guidance recommends using a startup PIN, along with shutting down or hibernating machines when faced with determined, hands-on attackers. Until an official fix or advisory appears, watch for one and apply it when it comes.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: A Seth Godin essay with a sharp metaphor about patience. (score 7)

From Seth's Blog.

No matter how high you turn the thermostat, your house will take just as long to get to 72 degrees.

Second metaphor: You can’t make a pizza faster in a 2,000 degree oven. In fact, you’ll incinerate it, not cook it.

Third metaphor: Two people can have one conversation and meet each other. For a group of 11, it’s 55 conversations.

Fourth metaphor: It’s easier to salt bland food at the table than to fix over-salted food in the kitchen.

PS Next week in the US is Thanksgiving. But wherever you are, I hope you’ll enjoy the Thanksgiving Reader, an annual tradition designed to be shared.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber on the retirement of the executive behind iPhone Camera and Photos, a notable Apple leadership change. (score 8)

From Daring Fireball.

Mark Gurman, reporting for Bloomberg today (gift link):

Jon McCormack retired at the end of October after more than eight years at the company, according to people with knowledge of the matter. He oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how users capture, view and edit their pictures and video.

Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to take over McCormack’s exact role. Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under another executive, said the people, who asked not to be identified while discussing internal moves. An Apple spokesperson declined to comment.

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year.

I’ve met McCormack a few times. He frequently led media briefings for new iPhone camera features. He was always thoughtful, insightful, and fair. Like, sometimes his demonstrations would involve comparisons between photos of the same subjects and scenes captured on iPhones and ones captured with flagship Android phones. The photos were all good. It was never “Here are some beautiful images captured on iPhones and some dogshit ones from a Samsung and OnePlus”. The differences were often subtle. He’d even make the case for why someone might prefer the Android ones. But he could explain why Apple — and he personally — preferred the ones from the iPhone. Not just how the iPhone camera captures and processes images, but why. He also knew when to let the images speak for themselves.

McCormack was deeply informed at a technical level. He reported directly to Craig Federighi and that level of engineering acumen showed. I can’t recall any question being too technical for him to have a ready answer. One of the best iPhone camera innovations in recent years is the redesigned Center Stage selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 (and Air) lineup last year. The square sensor is hardware, and McCormack was a software VP, but the feature exemplifies the way hardware and software are developed in tandem at Apple. McCormack was the public face for that feature — and internally, pushed to make it happen. That square sensor is bigger, which means (a) it’s more expensive; and (b) it takes up more space internally. Both of those require winning hard-fought arguments inside Apple in order to ship. The bottom line is that it helps iPhone users take better photos of themselves — and according to McCormack himself, over 1 billion selfies are taken with iPhones every day. The influence Apple’s Camera team has on the daily lives of billions of people is significant; McCormack understood that.

But what really struck me about McCormack, right from the start, is that he is clearly a serious photographer himself. That’s perhaps understating it. He recently published a book of his own nature and travel photography: Patterns: Art of the Natural World. He discussed the book in an hour-long interview with his Apple colleague Pamela Chen, whose job title is one of the coolest I’ve ever heard: Chief Aesthetics Scientist. (Chen, unsurprisingly, is also a talented photographer.)

Gurman:

His departure comes at a time when Apple is navigating a fundamental shift in photography. Competitors such as Alphabet Inc.’s Google and Samsung Electronics Co. have increasingly embraced generative AI features that allow users to make substantial changes to images. That has blurred the distinction between capturing a real moment and creating an artificial one.

Two years ago in his iPhone 16 Pro review, returning to his repeated theme of “What is a photo?”, Nilay Patel quoted, at length, the answer he got from McCormack. I, in turn, quoted Patel quoting McCormack, and added:

McCormack’s response is genuinely thoughtful, and resonates deeply with my own personal take. But it’s worth noting that Apple is the conservative company when it comes to generative AI and photography — and yet they’re still shipping Clean Up. I’m not complaining about Clean Up’s existence. I’ve already used it personally. I’m just saying that even Apple’s stance involves significant use of generative AI.

This year, Apple added “extend” and “reframe” alongside Clean Up. I don’t love either of those features simply because I don’t like how they change the meaning of “What is a photo?”, but I don’t hate them either. We can’t put the generative AI genie back in the bottle. Apple, still, is the conservative company in the generative AI phone photography space.

Jon McCormack had a knack for shepherding good new features into the Camera app. But also, based on conversations I’ve had with multiple people who worked with him at Apple, McCormack was great at keeping stupid ideas out of the Camera app. Good new features that ship get more recognition than stupid new features that never ship — but the latter, I would argue, is the rarer and more important management skill. It’s far more important to keep stupid ideas out of any app than it is to add good new features. McCormack was the protector of the Camera app. Under his leadership, it remains focused on the craft and art of photography.

Lastly, everyone I know who worked with him loves the guy. McCormack was the perfect guy for an essential job, and he leaves big shoes to fill.
