Applications using file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions may therefore expose passwords, authentication tokens, request bodies or transferred files to an attacker […]
item.content:encoded:
Why: A subtle real-world transport security bug where an uppercase S silently drops TLS in PHP streams. (score 8)

From Michael Tsai.

PHP (Mattias Geniar):

PHP’s HTTP and FTP stream wrappers can send data without encryption when an HTTPS or FTPS URL has an uppercase S in its scheme, for example HTTPS://, httpS:// or FTPS://. Applications using file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions may therefore expose passwords, authentication tokens, request bodies or transferred files to an attacker able to observe the network traffic.

[…]

Mixed-case URLs passed by an application have been affected since PHP 5.2.0, and redirects to a mixed-case URL since PHP 4.3.0.

That was in 2002. It’s now been fixed in PHP 8.5.13 and other versions.

There’s also a new PHP 8.6 (Hacker News). Lots of security fixes recently.

Previously:

  • PHP2Shell

item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber flags Google making its Gemini agent free as Tasks, a sign agents are going mainstream. (score 7)

From Daring Fireball.

By John Gruber

Ivy: Plan. Do. Reflect.
The to-do list that ends.

  • Google’s Spark AI Agent Becomes ‘Tasks’

  • Emma Roth, The Verge (gift link):

    Google is rebranding its Spark AI agent as “Tasks” and making it free to use. The feature, which is powered by Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model, can do things like create meal plans, manage your calendar, and dig through your emails to find recurring expenses you might not need.

    Users in the US will get access to a few other features, including the ability for the AI agent to call businesses to compare product pricing and check inventory, purchase items with Google Pay, and sign into accounts that support Google Password Manager. US users can also assign Gemini tasks by emailing [email protected] or texting it.

    New rule for Google: measure twice and cut once when naming anything. Is there a single product they’ve come out with related to AI that hasn’t gone through at least two entirely different names? And do these ding-dongs realize that “Tasks” sounds like a to-do app — in fact, so much like a to-do app that Google already has one named “Google Tasks”?

item.content:encoded:
Why: A clear explainer of how a race in PHP session writes can be chained into remote code execution. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

PHP's default file-based session storage can be made to return objects an attacker chose, by cutting off a session write at the right moment. When combined with a second weakness, such as a suitable gadget chain in the app, those objects can allow the attacker to run code on the server.

Today's PHP releases fix the flaw, called phpAfterShell.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-126714 and rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 scale by PHP's maintainers. Depthfirst, a security company, says it found the flaw and reported it to the maintainers.

The October 21 PHP releases, which fixed two critical flaws known as PHP2Shell, do not contain this fix. Servers updated then remain affected until they install today's releases. Neither the maintainers nor the company reports any attacks using phpAfterShell.

Who Is Affected and What to Do

These releases are affected, according to the maintainers' security advisory:

Branch Affected releases Fixed release
PHP 8.2 Before 8.2.36 8.2.36
PHP 8.3 Before 8.3.37 8.3.37
PHP 8.4 Before 8.4.28 8.4.28
PHP 8.5 Before 8.5.13 8.5.13

PHP 8.6.0, also released today, includes the fix.

The flaw is in the files session handler, which PHP uses by default. Sessions kept in Redis, a database, or another store are outside this defect, though each store's handling of a cut-off update needs its own check.

Whether an attacker needs to log in depends on how the app exposes its session handling.

On the path the company tested, the attacker uses upload progress, a PHP feature that records the progress of a file upload in the user's session. Where the feature is on, a multipart form upload that carries its field makes PHP write to the session before the app's own code runs. The app does not need an upload page, only any page that opens the session later.

PHP 8.1 and older are end-of-life. The official end-of-life mitigation branches for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are not affected, but older unpatched builds of those versions are, according to the company.

The company's remediation guidance sets out these steps:

  • Install the fixed release for your branch, as listed above. If you run PHP 8.1 or older, move to a supported branch.
  • Rebuild any container images and redeploy.
  • Check that the PHP version serving web requests is the new one.

If you cannot update yet and your app does not use upload progress, set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the server's PHP settings, then restart the PHP workers. Also limit the untrusted data your app stores in sessions.

Switching the feature off is not a full fix. It closes the upload path, but apps that put attacker-controlled data into sessions in other ways remain affected, the maintainers say.

The maintainers listed the same setting on October 21 as a temporary measure for one of the PHP2Shell flaws. Servers that have kept it off since then still need the update.

Moving sessions to a store that replaces records in one step also avoids this defect. The update is still the recommended fix for sites that keep the files handler.

Linux distribution packages may include the fix without changing the PHP version number, according to the company, so the version number alone may not indicate whether a server is fixed.

Once installed, the fixed releases empty the session file before each write and stop the write if that step fails. A cut-off write can still lose session data, but it can no longer leave old data behind for an attacker to use.

The updates also switch upload progress off by default. The Hacker News compared PHP's source code for the October 21 releases and today's. The built-in setting is on in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and off in 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0.

The release notes do not mention or explain the change. The sample php.ini files still show the old setting in a commented-out line. A php.ini file, distribution package, or hosting panel that switches the setting on will keep it on.

Where nothing else sets it, apps that rely on upload progress will need it switched back on after the update.

The same releases also fix other PHP security flaws.

How the Attack Works

The attack starts with the session write that upload progress makes before the app's code runs, Depthfirst's researchers say in their technical analysis.

A PHP session file stores each value as a name followed by serialized data. Length fields in that data tell PHP where each string ends, and nothing in the file marks a write as finished.

PHP locks the file while it writes, but the lock cannot undo a write that stops halfway. If the worker process dies partway through, the file can retain the start of the new data and the end of the old data.

By setting the lengths in the new data, an attacker can make text that sat harmlessly inside the old data read as a separate record, including a serialized object. The next request that calls session_start() loads that record and creates the object.

The researchers' public proof uses a harmless built-in object, stdClass, which appears in the session once the file is mixed.

The emergency PHP2Shell fixes on October 21 addressed an earlier attack via the same step.

"The original exploit stopped working, but the underlying problem was still there," the researchers say of the PHP2Shell patch.

That exploit needed objects to become active while PHP recorded upload progress, so the maintainers limited which classes can load at that moment. The change did not touch the file write. The object data still reaches the disk and becomes active later, when an ordinary request calls session_start().

The attack depends on stopping the write at the right moment. The maintainers say one way is a hard memory-limit failure in another thread of a threaded PHP build, which can kill the process mid-write.

Code execution then still needs a suitable gadget chain in the app, and the flaw can also corrupt session state.

In the researchers' own Linux tests, PHP's execution timeout fired only after the write had finished, so they used an out-of-memory kill to stop the worker mid-write instead.

The planted object appeared on the 11th attempt in a fresh run. That count measures getting the file into the right state on their servers, not how often code execution succeeds.

Their own chain needed no gadget from the app, the researchers say. It used a second bug instead, memory corruption in one of PHP's built-in classes.

They are holding back its details for coordinated disclosure and have not said whether that bug is fixed in today's releases.

The same trick can also replace ordinary session values, such as who is logged in, their permissions, or a CSRF token, before the app checks them, the researchers say.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: A former CISO unpacks the FBI ARTEX advisory and how attackers reach privileged access in hours. (score 7)

From Blog on 1Password Blog.

Gone in three hours: What ARTEX does with your credentials

Threat actors can now go from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. Your change advisory board takes longer to approve a firewall rule.

That figure comes from the FBI’s November 13 advisory, FBI FLASH-20261113-001, about a framework called ARTEX. The read as a recovering CISO: all the techniques in the alert are familiar, but the clock has changed. Every credential you left lying around just got easier to pick up.

What is ARTEX, and how does it automate cyberattacks?

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent pentesting framework written in Go. An operator types in an objective in plain language. LLM-backed agents turn it into commands, load the proper scripts, and run them.

The developer published it on GitHub in July 2026 for authorized testing. The FBI reports malicious use since at least August. A month from the initial release to abuse is, for an offensive security tool.

After reports of misuse surfaced, the developer pulled the repository on October 8. But, forks, mirrors, archives, and a commercial version keep it in circulation because the internet has never once given anything back. The Internet never forgets. By early November, researchers counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles.

The reported targets span at least ten market segments worldwide, including financial services, government, healthcare, and energy. One financially motivated campaign exfiltrated personal information on about 67,000 people. In another incident, a supply chain compromise at a cloud backup service opened access to more than 2,250 downstream tenants.

Where does ARTEX find credentials?

The alert maps the activity to 43 ATT&CK techniques. Read it by phase and one thing keeps turning up: a credential somebody forgot about.

  • Reconnaissance. Agents tested the permissions of Azure credentials, including SAS tokens, service principals, Kudu credentials, and storage account keys, with sub-second checks.

  • Initial access. Hardcoded administrator passwords in JavaScript bundles, weak administrative credentials, compromised vendor credentials through trusted B2B federation, and stolen VPN configurations with leaked credentials.

  • Persistence. Account takeover through password resets, new SSH key pairs, and credentials added to existing OAuth applications.

  • Privilege escalation. Cloud compute instances launched with high-value IAM roles, harvested Kerberos Service Tickets, DCSync to steal the Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (KRBTGT) key, and an administrator token forged with unrotated authentication keys.

  • Internal reconnaissance. More than 110,000 Active Directory objects enumerated, and Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords read.

On paper, an admin password in a JavaScript bundle is T1552.001. In practice, it is a sticky note on the monitor, served from a CDN.

One piece of good news: endpoint protection blocked attempted lateral movement to domain controllers through Pass-the-Ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay, and Pass-the-Hash. So boring controls are still earning their keep.

Why do AI-driven attacks make exposed credentials more dangerous?

Automation changes the price of one exposed credential. A hardcoded password or an unrotated signing key used to wait for a human with time and motivation. Now an agent tests it in under a second and feeds the result into the next technique.

Two variables decide how quickly an exposed credential can become a broader incident:

  • Standing access sets how far the credential reaches once it is used

  • Detection time sets how long you have, and three hours is less than some incident bridges need to agree on a severity level

So we have stopped planning around a patient attacker. Assume anything discoverable gets discovered, and anything valid gets tried.

Five ways to reduce ARTEX-related credential exposure this week

The FBI's credential recommendations are specific. The controls below are theirs.

  1. Sweep for embedded secrets. Review application configurations, environment variables, infrastructure-as-code, deployment scripts, and CI/CD pipelines. I would add shipped front-end bundles, since that is where the alert found admin passwords.

  2. Rotate what you find, promptly. Include signing and authentication keys. The forged admin token in the alert relied on keys nobody had rotated.

  3. Restrict deployment and publishing credentials. List every person and pipeline that can read them today. Cut the list to the ones that deploy.

  4. Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants. Revoke what nobody uses.

  5. Monitor credential additions and privileged role assignments. Monitor the speed of identity access, and spikes in API traffic.

Steps one and two fit in a week for most teams. Steps three to five need a named owner and a date, or they become a slide.

Where 1Password helps reduce credential exposure

Several 1Password capabilities are aligned with those recommendations. The FBI does not endorse products, and each capability has a boundary you should know before you count on it.

  • Developer Watchtower, in the 1Password desktop apps for Mac, Windows, and Linux, finds unencrypted or insecure SSH keys in ~/.ssh and .env files with plaintext secrets in nine named development folders. It only checks files on local disk that match .env naming patterns, so it doesn’t look at remote repositories or Git history, and other file types like a JavaScript bundle are outside its view even when they sit in a scanned folder..

  • Privileged Access provides just-in-time, task-scoped access to cloud environments with automatic deprovisioning, and discovers overprivileged cloud identities. It applies only to access granted through Privileged Access.

  • SaaS Manager finds apps with high-risk OAuth scopes and revokes their tokens in Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID.

  • 1Password Developer Tools, allow for JIT secret injection to coding agents and CI/CD pipelines including GitHub Actions, validates the workload identity against registered policy and releases only the secrets that are scoped to the task only for the duration of the workflow. Secrets are available to the job during the run. They are not single-use or bound to a runner.

None of this is a claim about the ARTEX intrusions themselves. A vendor telling you its product would have stopped a breach it was not present for should make you check your wallet.

What credential hygiene will not fix

Most of the ARTEX activity sits outside credential management: web application exploitation, Kerberos attacks, web shells, and command and control. The FBI's guidance also covers reducing the external attack surface, strengthening application protections, and preserving evidence for response. A vault does nothing for an unpatched web app.

The facts here reflect the FLASH as published on November 13, 2026. They may change as investigations continue.

Two actions to take before Today

  1. Read FBI FLASH-20261113-001 and send the mitigations section to the person responsible for your CI/CD pipelines

  2. Search your production JavaScript bundles for the string "password." A hit is your first rotation ticket and your opening story at the next all-hands

Secure hardcoded credentials

Explore 1Password Developer Tools to learn how to help your team find exposed secrets and keep live credentials out of code and pipelines.

The early ​exuberance, however, partly faded, signaling volatility ahead as investors locked in quick gains and the main indexes retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector’s outlook.

In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price.

Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Apple is staffing up to build an agent that uses apps and writes code, a big shift in its AI strategy. (score 7)

From The Verge.

Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent

Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

item.content:encoded:
Why: On your always-include list. (score 10)

From Cliff Mass Weather Blog.

This week, a very El Niño-like atmospheric pattern is bringing needed precipitation to central and northern California.

Reservoirs are filling, and a substantial snowpack will accumulate over the higher terrain of the Golden State.  Good skiing with a week.

But the weather gods have not forgotten us.    The large-scale pattern will shift this weekend,  bringing substantial precipitation and mountain snow to our region as well.

Let's look at the latest forecast!

Over the next 72 hours (through Saturday morning), California will be quite wet.  The watershead of the Colorado River will do well, in addition.


But subsequently, the precipitation shifts northward, with Oregon and Washington State enjoying substantial wet action (see below). 
This will continue the next 72 hr, with the Northwest coast being hit very hard. 
Northwest ducks will be happy.


What about snow?  

Over the next ten days, first the Sierra Nevada and then the Northwest mountains will get plenty of snow (see the 10-day totals below).  Skiing will begin at Whistler.


So why will precipitation shift from California to the Pacific Northwest?  

That is easy to explain by looking at the average upper-level (500 hPa pressure, about 18,000 ft) map, averaged over 5-day chunks.  

For the first five days, there is a low-pressure area off California, which directs the bulk of the precipitation south of us.  


But everything changes during the subsequent five days; the upper low moves offshore and to the north--a much wetter pattern for the Northwest.


You can see the change at the surface.  The sea-level pressure pattern at 4 PM today has a low off of southern CA.

Fast forward to Monday afternoon: a VERY potent low is predicted to be off our coast (below).   And many more lows are in our future.


Importantly, these storms are not making landfall and are staying out to sea... which is very much an El Nino configuration.   But much wetter for western Washington and British Columbia.

Some are very happy with the forecast

item.title: The trouble with serendipity
item.author: The Works in Progress Newsletter
item.description:
Why: Works in Progress on how scientific discoveries really happen, a big-ideas read. (score 8)

From The Works in Progress Newsletter.

Many scientific discoveries didn’t happen the way you think.
item.content:encoded:
Why: Works in Progress on how scientific discoveries really happen, a big-ideas read. (score 8)

From The Works in Progress Newsletter.

Saloni Dattani explores accidental discoveries in history, and comes away learning that scientists’ lives were messier than she expected.

This is a column: a lighter piece from the Works in Progress extended universe, designed to be enjoyed in print. If you’d like to opt out of columns, or any other section, you can do so here.

People love accidental discoveries. Penicillin’s discovery by Alexander Fleming is a classic example. Fungal spores wafted in through an open window, fell onto a plate of bacterial colonies, and dissolved them. Another is Louis Pasteur’s discovery of a chicken cholera vaccine, the second vaccine ever developed. After Pasteur left a broth overexposed to oxygen, it went stale. But he ran out of fresh broth, so used it anyway to study the effects of an infection, and found, surprisingly, that it protected the chickens. Or how about the discovery of X-rays? Wilhelm Röntgen was working with a cathode ray tube in a dark room when he suddenly noticed a screen glowing nearby, even though he’d wrapped the tube in cardboard.

Subscribe now

Though they’re great stories, I’ve come to believe none of them happened that way. Röntgen had his notes burned after his death, and the story is just a hypothesis. Pasteur was extremely secretive as well, and forbade his family from making his notes and letters public after his death. His grandson, however, did, and after poring over their contents, historians have found that the key experiments were done deliberately by Pasteur’s then-assistant Émile Roux while Pasteur was away for his daughter’s wedding.

And what about Fleming? His first paper describing penicillin in 1929 never says where the spores came from. Of course, it’s hard to see how he could have known, given they would have been microscopic. But Fleming first told the window story in an interview in 1945, sixteen years after his first report, and his colleagues testified the window was ‘seldom if ever opened’. They weren’t able to replicate the discovery as he described, either: penicillin would have needed to be present on the plate before the bacteria grew, because it blocks bacteria from building their cell walls, rather than killing them once they’ve grown.

Subscribe to print

Several people have tried to work out what really happened. Fleming’s would-be biographer Ronald Hare made dozens of attempts and found just one reliable way to reproduce the discovery that fit the facts. The spores, he argues, were an unusually productive strain; came from the lab of a fungal researcher on the floor below, rather than the window; settled on the plate roughly when Fleming seeded it with bacteria; Fleming forgot to incubate it; and all this happened during a cold spell in the summer that let the mold grow before the bacteria. Hare noted how much more serendipitous this sequence of events was: ‘the odds against the occurrence of the phenomenon become almost astronomical’, though he ultimately believed it. While writing this column, I read through many of his notes and letters archived at the Wellcome Library and have come to agree with his view: Hare was exceedingly careful in corroborating the events from multiple people and sources from the time.

Part of the reason I find the popular stories fascinating is because it’s jarring to realize how little they’re based on. I do expect some stories of accidental discovery will survive the test of time. In medicine, for example, it’s fairly common to test a drug for one disease and find, unexpectedly, that it works for another: colchicine was used for centuries to treat gout before it was found effective against cardiovascular disease, and sildenafil (Viagra) was being tested for angina when its more famous effect was noticed. Side effects are difficult to predict.

Subscribe now

But I wonder why the popular versions have survived so long. Maybe they’re more enjoyable? They’re certainly easier to recount than the other explanations, which are convoluted. A fungal spore floating through an open window to reveal a world-changing antibiotic is a far better dinner party story than a meandering one involving several more coincidences you’ve probably already forgotten. Or the stories make scientists feel just like us: anyone can stumble upon a discovery, and then the challenge is merely to... spend years turning it into something useful?

‘Chance favors only the prepared mind’, as Pasteur put it. I think there’s something to it: the brilliance of these scientists isn’t necessarily in their initial discoveries, but in seeing their potential and doing something with them. Edward Jenner, for example, wasn’t the first to notice that cowpox infections protected against smallpox, but he documented it thoroughly and popularized the method, spreading smallpox vaccination worldwide.

But what bothers me is that calling these discoveries accidents is sometimes the opposite of reality. Pasteur and Roux, for example, carried out hundreds of experiments to find reliable methods to create new vaccines – the popular framing is actively misleading and diminishes their work.

My friend Niko McCarty recently dug into other famously serendipitous discoveries in biology, such as those of green fluorescent protein and nanopore sequencing, and explained they came from systematic trial and error. He also describes the idea of ‘engineered serendipity’: in optogenetics, for example, ‘the key breakthrough came about because the inventors wrote down the exact requirements they were looking for [...] and then enumerated, or wrote down, all the ways they could possibly imagine to make this happen’. It makes me wonder if learning how they really happened could help understand how to make more discoveries systematically.

Yet I’m still left with questions. Why credit chance events instead of hard work? Why hide or burn your notebooks?

Messiness, mistakes, and privacy come to mind. But here’s another theory: competition and rivalry. Gerald Geison, a historian of Pasteur, suggests the method he ultimately used to develop chicken cholera vaccines was ‘remarkably simple’ and could be applied to other diseases too: ‘had he revealed immediately the method of attenuation through exposure to ordinary air, Pasteur might have faced a host of competitors in the search for other vaccines’. Pasteur was probably the best-paid scientist in France at the time, and sold his inventions commercially. His secrecy might have been rational: patents weren’t allowed on medicines in France then, so keeping the method secret would have helped him maintain his monopoly on producing them. Pasteur was so cagey that he didn’t allow his collaborators to take notes, took his notebooks with him when he traveled, and published his methods (without much detail) only months after announcing his discoveries.

Subscribe to print

Meanwhile, Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays and had his notes burned after his death, had been in a long dispute with another scientist, Philipp Lenard. Lenard had spent years researching cathode rays before him, and shared his methods and discharge tube with Röntgen. Once Röntgen became famous, Lenard accused him of having robbed him of the discovery. That dispute, historians suggest, could have motivated the note-burning, but it’s hard to know without being able to read them. (Incidentally, Émile Roux, too, had his notes burned periodically, and it’s only because Pasteur’s were released that we know what happened at all.)

Science seems like it should be above the messiness. It’s an institution we’ve built to guard against our biases. But it’s also just people – who forget, hide their notebooks from their colleagues, burn their papers, and spend years fighting over who deserves credit. It’s shaped by rivalries, incentives, obsessions, and years of unglamorous work, most of which is forgotten. That, to me, makes it far more interesting than a story about an open window.

Saloni Dattani is an editor at Works in Progress.

item.content:encoded:
Why: UK tribunal ruling keeps Apple's fight over an encryption backdoor order largely public. (score 8)

From MacRumors: Mac News and Rumors - All Stories.

Apple's challenge to a UK government demand for access to encrypted customer data can now be heard largely in public, after a tribunal rejected the Home Office's attempt to keep the order secret, according to the Financial Times.


The Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government had failed to demonstrate that confirming the demand would damage national security. The decision requires the Home Office to acknowledge that it served Apple with a technical capability notice (TCN), which is an order that can compel companies to make customer data accessible to UK security services, even when it is encrypted.

The government's position relied on its policy of neither confirming nor denying such notices. However, the tribunal found that disclosures to the media, including the Financial Times, and discussions with U.S. officials had already departed significantly from that policy.

In its judgment, the tribunal said the combined effect was that anyone following the dispute already knew Apple had received a TCN. It described the suggestion that official acknowledgment would threaten national security or give a malicious actor fresh information as "fanciful."

The ruling means that much of the legal action brought by Apple, alongside a separate challenge from Privacy International and Liberty, can proceed in open court.

Apple filed its latest legal challenge in July, following a second TCN. The Home Office had previously agreed to withdraw an earlier demand covering UK and U.S. customers after a dispute with the American government. The replacement notice is believed to focus on UK users specifically.

The dispute led Apple to stop offering Advanced Data Protection to new users in the UK in February 2025. The iCloud feature provides end-to-end encryption for additional categories of data, including device backups, photos, and notes, meaning Apple does not hold the keys needed to decrypt them.

UK users who had not already enabled ADP can no longer turn it on. Apple says it cannot switch the feature off on their behalf, so it can remain active on accounts where users previously enabled it and have not turned it off. The company said affected users will be given a period to disable ADP themselves to continue using ‌iCloud‌, but a deadline has still not been provided.

Without ADP, those additional categories of ‌iCloud‌ data use standard protection, under which Apple holds the encryption keys and can provide data in response to valid legal demands. iMessage and FaceTime remain end-to-end encrypted, as do categories protected by default, such as passwords and Health data.

The tribunal will now be able to hear much of the arguments over the government's encryption demands in public, with the legality of those demands still to be decided. Privacy International lists the substantive hearing for its separate challenge as scheduled for December 2026.
Tags: Apple Privacy, Apple Lawsuits, United Kingdom

item.content:encoded:
Why: Snell on using YoLink sensors for household alerts, a thoughtful home tech piece. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

I was at Casey Liss‘s house over the weekend, sitting in his living room, when suddenly I heard a chime and a voice said, out of nowhere: “The wash is done.”

It turns out that Casey has connected an array of sensors to his Home Assistant setup, and somehow his family accepts that occasionally a disembodied voice will shout out home status information. (It’s not as subtle as his other approach.)

What’s wilder is that the box Casey’s using to do this is actually one I have in my own home! It’s a YoLink Speaker Hub, which I bought along with three leak sensors (affiliate link; I bought a three-pack of sensors with the hub for $60) a year and a half ago. And while I haven’t automated my speaker hub to announce things (yet!), I realized I haven’t sufficiently sung the praises of these YoLink sensors.

In short: They are very good, with tremendous range and battery life, and extremely easy to install. You don’t actually need anything like Home Assistant to use them—they come with their own, entirely functional app for configuration and alert purposes.

The leak sensors themselves are tiny plastic pucks you just put in potential trouble spots—for me, that’s under the kitchen sink, next to the washing machine, and next to the condensate pump that doubles as the outlet for my dehumidifier in the winter months. When they register a leak, I get an emergency notification on my phone and (optionally) the Speaker Hub can make an unmissable alert noise.

We’ve previously had under-sink and washing-machine disasters, so this was an easy purchase for me. And since I installed them, I’ve been alerted once about a serious issue—the drain hose from my dehumidifier had come out of the pump housing and was dripping freely.

Casey’s also taking advantage of the long battery life and range of YoLink’s system to do things like use contact sensors to alert him when his mail has been delivered, and the company offers a wild array of sensors that work with the hub.

And, yes, once you plug the Speaker Hub into Home Assistant, you can drive its built-in audio features, which include built-in text-to-speech, a library of alert tones, and even custom MP3 sounds, from any automation happening in your house. (Casey’s laundry alerts are, impossibly, not from smart appliances, but from inline energy-consumption monitors he’s attached to his washer and dryer.)

If you’re so inclined, you can really go to town with these sensors. But if you just want basic operation, such as making sure that the next time your sink leaks it’s not a total disaster, I can’t recommend the YoLink sensors and hub highly enough.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Hackett on Voyager 1 nearing one light-day from Earth, a hopeful science moment. (score 7)

From 512 Pixels.

Yesterday was a big day:

The Voyager 1 spacecraft, traveling for nearly 50 years, will soon cross a mile marker reached by no other human-made object — one light-day away from Earth. That’s the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equaling about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), a point that Voyager 1 will reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST.

One of the most interesting things — among many — about the Voyager probes is their on-board gold records.

Robert Pearlman dug into them for Ars Technica:

In the one light-day that humanity’s most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.

Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter’s moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a “commemorative phonograph record,” in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.

About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs’ overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.

“So much has been written about the contents of the record—the message in the bottle, so to speak—whereas I was more interested in the hardware, the bottle itself, because so very little is known about that,” Swanson, former chief historian for NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston and founding editor of Quest: The History of Spaceflight Quarterly, said in an interview.

From Seth's Blog.

It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on. But this skips the key question: What’s it for? The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other […]
item.content:encoded:
Why: Seth Godin on chasing trophies versus the real work. (score 7)

From Seth's Blog.

It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on.

But this skips the key question: What’s it for?

The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other team.

Your favorite episode of the Mel Robbins show might not be the one that got the most views. And of course, the best video on YouTube is unlikely to be the one that went the most viral. That’s simply the easiest to measure.

High school sports seems to be about solving the trophy shortage, but is that what it should be for? Are all the other teams and all their athletes failures? Or is it simply a shortcut that lets the coach off the hook when they hesitate to do the hard work of developing their students?

If it’s easy to measure, it might not be the thing you ought to be measuring. In fact, it probably isn’t.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Overview of Azure announcements at Ignite, relevant to an Azure security PM. (score 7)

From Microsoft Azure Blog.

Azure at Microsoft Ignite 2026: The headlines
  • Azure AI core: AI on infrastructure you control.
  • Azure Cobalt 200: Our highest-performing general-purpose virtual machines (VMs).
  • Azure Catalyst: Agent-led modernization from plan to code.
  • Agentic cloud operations: Agents that keep your cloud running well.
  • Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB: PostgreSQL for AI apps and analytics.
  • Fabric apps: Governed apps built on trusted data.
  • Microsoft IQ: Context for every agent.

Over the past year, my conversations with customers have changed. A year ago, the question was which model to choose. Now it’s how to put agents to work on the processes that run the business, and how to trust them to do it.

With the same frontier models available to everyone, the advantage comes from what no one else has: your context. It’s how your business runs, what your people know, and the systems and data you’ve spent years building. That’s your IQ. It’s your intellectual property, so it should stay yours, and it should work wherever your people and agents do. Our job is to make every layer beneath your agents better, from the infrastructure that runs them and the estate they act on to the apps they power and the business context that tells them how your company works.

Azure is the foundation of Frontier Transformation. We engineer Azure as one system, so the knowledge an agent needs stays governed and the security you use to protect your people extends to the agents acting for them. And because we’re evolving the open, cloud-native platform you already rely on, you don’t have to start over.

See what Azure can do for your business

As Satya Nadella shared at Microsoft Build in June, we added more datacenter capacity in 18 months than in Azure’s first decade. Combined with more regions than any other cloud provider, you can scale your AI workloads globally with confidence as demand grows.

This week at Microsoft Ignite, we’re sharing what’s new across every layer of the platform. New capabilities spanning compute, storage, and networking let you run AI at scale with the control of your own infrastructure, without having to build, secure, and operate all of it yourself. Azure Catalyst brings agent-led modernization together in one experience from estate to code.

PostgreSQL now has two homes at Microsoft: Azure HorizonDB, generally available for mission-critical scale, and the new Fabric HorizonDB, which connects your PostgreSQL apps to analytics and AI. And Fabric apps, now generally available, let your teams turn trusted enterprise data into working apps.

We’re also introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform that helps you build your own IQ and put it to work in every app and agent. It also gives your teams a path on Azure to build, run, and continuously improve those agents.

Run AI at scale with the control you choose

It starts with the infrastructure that runs your agents. As they take on real work, you should be able to run them on your terms, with your choice of models, your data, and where they run. That control lets you find the right balance of performance and cost for each workload and adapt as models and needs change.

But control comes with real work and risk. Platform teams end up assembling and operating much of the AI stack themselves and stretching GPUs to keep up with shifting demand. Agents that reach models, tools, and data and run code on their own open new security gaps, putting sensitive data at risk.

Teams want the control of running their own AI infrastructure without taking on all the manual toil of building, securing, and operating it.

Building the AI core on Azure

That’s what we’re bringing to Azure. New capabilities across compute, storage, and networking come together as one AI foundation, so you keep control of your models and workloads while Azure takes on the work underneath. Build AI with Microsoft Foundry in a fully managed experience and run it at scale with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) when you need more control over performance, security, and cost.

Ignite session: AI infrastructure from cloud to Edge

Watch now ↗

Azure sets up and tunes the infrastructure for you, so your teams spend less time on configuration and more time moving models and agents into production. Workloads are placed based on available capacity, so your GPU investment goes further as demand grows. Security is enforced centrally across agents, models, and tools, giving security teams consistent controls wherever agents run. And because it’s built on open-source projects, your workloads stay portable, including to your own servers outside Azure, keeping your options open as your needs change.

The result is AI that scales with your business, on infrastructure you control.

To hear how organizations are operating AI at scale, join Mark Russinovich and Pavan Davuluri in the innovation session “AI Infrastructure from cloud to edge.”

Strengthening every layer of your AI estate with Azure Cobalt 200

Agents reason, make decisions, and run continuously, and that’s reshaping what cloud infrastructure needs to deliver. That’s why we design Azure as one system, from silicon to servers to services. We pair our own Maia and Cobalt chips with the latest from NVIDIA and AMD, so every workload runs on the right silicon for the job. Our strategy focuses on building performance, efficiency, and security into every layer. The result is AI that’s faster and more economical to run at scale, on a roadmap you can plan around.

Ignite session: cobalt 200…

Watch now ↗

Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines, our highest-performing general-purpose VMs, are now generally available. Designed from the ground up for scale-out, cloud native, and agentic AI workloads, these VMs deliver up to 50% better CPU performance compared to our Cobalt 100 VMs. Together with Maia, they give you an infrastructure you can plan around.

Read about the latest Azure Cobalt updates in this blog

Agent-led modernization and operations, from estate to code

Agents are only as useful as the systems they can act on. Much of what makes your company unique is built into your applications and databases and years of business logic your teams rely on. Modernizing puts existing apps and data to work in new AI-powered experiences, helps teams ship faster, and lowers the cost and risk of running older systems, creating a more adaptable foundation for growth.

Getting there isn’t easy. Modernizing can mean mapping complex systems and changing code that few people fully understand. Keeping the estate running well means sorting through constant signals with little knowledge on what matters most. And as agents take on more of that work, teams need to let them act while keeping the oversight your business requires.

That’s why we’re bringing agents to both, from estate to code. Azure Catalyst helps you modernize applications, code, and databases from plan to execution. And new capabilities in Azure Copilot, Azure SRE Agent, and Azure Monitor help keep your cloud and databases running well, with people in control.

Modernize for AI with Azure Catalyst

Azure Catalyst is a new unified experience for agentic modernization. It brings discovery, planning, migration, modernization, and code intelligence together, so IT teams and developers work from the same plan across infrastructure, applications, and data. Azure Catalyst modernizes the technology you already have into a foundation for AI, putting the business logic in your existing applications to work in new AI-powered experiences and agentic business processes.

Ignite session: rethink modernization…

Watch now ↗

For IT teams, Azure Catalyst agent extends from migration planning into deeper modernization and execution. For developers, GitHub Copilot modernization carries that plan into code in the tools they already use, with agent governance rulebooks and bring-your-own-model support that customizes your modernization project to the specifications of each business. And Azure Catalyst delivers a deeper understanding of how enterprise applications work, so teams can assess the impact of changes, modernize faster, and find where legacy processes could be reimagined with AI.

Ignite session: modernize faster with ai…

Watch now ↗

Modernization can also close security gaps. End-of-support runtimes, unpatched dependencies, and aging code widen your threat surface. Azure Catalyst works with Microsoft Security to fix that: Microsoft Perception and MDASH rank vulnerabilities across your estate and code, Azure Catalyst identifies vulnerable code and databases to modernize first, and GitHub Copilot turns those findings into fixes in the same pass. Each app comes out more secure than it went in.

Learn more about Azure AI foundation and Azure Catalyst in this blog

Keep your cloud running well with agentic operations

As applications scale across hybrid infrastructure, microservices, and AI workloads, leading organizations are moving to operating models where insight flows directly into action. That’s the idea behind agentic operations: AI agents, guided by your intent, continuously observe, reason, and help take action across the cloud lifecycle. Signals feed coordinated workflows that improve performance, cost, and reliability as systems run, with people kept in control.

At Microsoft Ignite, we’re bringing that model to more of your estate. Azure Copilot‘s deployment agent, now generally available, helps you go from requirements described in natural language to deployed cloud workloads. You can even extend agentic operations to Oracle and SAP with Azure Workload Center, now in limited preview.

Ignite session: put ai agents to work…

Watch now ↗

Azure SRE Agent brings agentic operations into secure production environments, with new enterprise controls in preview, while Microsoft Entra Agent ID and Agent 365 give central teams a consistent way to discover, govern, and audit agents throughout their lifecycle. We’re also giving agents richer data and understanding so they can detect issues earlier, diagnose problems faster, and take more effective action. Azure Monitor health models, now generally available, give agents a real-time view of your application architecture and business priorities, so they can recommend fixes.

Learn more about agentic operations in this blog

Build the next generation of AI apps

Then there are the apps your agents power, where business data becomes business value. The question for every organization is how quickly it can move from idea to an app the entire business can rely on. Today, the people building AI apps span the whole organization. Developers are creating mission-critical systems and new apps with agents, while teams across the business are describing the app they need in Copilot. Each needs something different from the platform, but every app needs to connect to business data and run under governance IT can trust.

We’re building one foundation for all of them, and it starts with PostgreSQL, the database of choice for a growing share of developers. With Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB, you can run PostgreSQL wherever your apps need it, from mission-critical systems to analytics and AI. Fabric apps builds on that foundation, so teams can turn business data into working apps, whether they start in code or in conversation.

Power your AI apps with PostgreSQL on Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB

The apps developers build now reason over data, call models, and act for users, so the database underneath has to bring transactions, vectors, and AI together at mission-critical scale. Azure HorizonDB, now generally available, is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database built for that work. It delivers millisecond latency with built-in vector indexing, so your apps can find, reason over, and act on data in one place. Enterprise-grade security comes built in, and developers can work in tools they already know, including GitHub Copilot and Visual Studio Code.

ignite session: data foundations for modern apps…

Watch now ↗

We’re also extending the power of PostgreSQL directly into Microsoft Fabric. Fabric HorizonDB, now in public preview, brings a serverless, Fabric-native PostgreSQL experience alongside SQL database in Fabric and Cosmos DB in Fabric. By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps.

To simplify database management across environments, Database Hub in Fabric is now generally available. It provides a unified experience to discover, monitor, and manage databases across Azure, on-premises environments, and Fabric, with Fabric Copilot highlighting what needs attention.

Read the latest Microsoft Databases announcements in this blog

Turn ideas into governed enterprise-ready apps with Fabric apps, now generally available

Great ideas for apps come from every corner of the business, and with Copilot, people can build one in minutes. But taking it from prototype to production on trusted data remains the biggest hurdle. Fabric apps, now generally available, bring together the backend services applications need with direct access to trusted data in Fabric, built-in security, and enterprise governance. Developers and coding agents build in code with open-source tools, and Fabric provisions everything from databases to authentication, with no infrastructure to manage. This makes it easier to turn ideas into enterprise-ready applications that can scale across the organization.

ignite session: build like a startup…

Watch now ↗

We’re also extending Fabric’s role as the data foundation for AI-powered applications. With the new Microsoft Copilot integration, now in Frontier public preview, anyone can describe the app they need and bring it to life, with the option to use Fabric as a ready-to-use data backend providing databases, storage, and data APIs. We’re also introducing Copilot Credits as a new usage-based billing option for Microsoft Fabric, providing greater flexibility alongside existing capacity-based options.

Power BI creators can now build more than static reports. With a new agentic app creation experience in Power BI Desktop, now in preview, they can turn their existing semantic models into interactive apps that capture input, update data, and support operational workflows.

Learn more about Fabric apps in the Ignite Microsoft Fabric blog

Ground every agent in your business context with Microsoft IQ

Most organizations already have the knowledge their agents need. It lives in the semantic models your analysts built in Power BI, the documents and procedures your teams rely on, the conversations happening across Microsoft 365, and the systems of record you run every day, like SAP and Oracle. The problem is that it’s scattered, so every new agent starts from zero and every team rebuilds the same context.

That’s why we’re introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform for building your organization’s IQ. It brings together Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, Web IQ, and more than 350 connectors, so the knowledge your agents need is captured once, governed in one place, and reused by every agent and app.

At the heart of Microsoft IQ are new business plugins, now available as part of the Frontier program. Business plugins turn what your teams know into trusted context, skills, and tools that anyone across the business can reuse. Take a supply chain disruption. A business plugin can tell an agent to use the components and orders semantic model in Fabric IQ to find the affected orders, the supplier contracts in Foundry IQ to check late-delivery terms, and Work IQ to find who owns the decision. Your domain experts write it once, and every agent across the organization inherits it.

Teams can also reuse proven evaluations across agents instead of rebuilding them. The foundation underneath Microsoft IQ brings Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Fabric together in one path, built on Azure, to build, run, and continuously improve agents. And Agent 365 gives IT one place to observe, govern, and secure them.

ignite session: Harnessing Your IQ…

Watch now ↗

Your IQ stays yours, and it isn’t locked into one assistant. The same context and business plugins reach your agents wherever they run, in Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT, through model context protocol (MCP) and APIs. Your permissions and governance go with it. Agents can also draw on the business context in your systems of record, like SAP and Oracle, so they work from the data your teams already rely on. Learn more about Oracle’s latest integrations with Microsoft IQ.

See how the Australian Energy Market Operator uses Microsoft IQ to help keep Australia’s power grid secure:

Nearly 60,000 customers already use Microsoft IQ today. And because every agent builds on the same context, each one you add makes the next one better.

Learn more about Microsoft IQ in this blog

Experience these innovations at Microsoft Ignite

Every agent you build is only as good as what it knows about your business. That’s why we’re making sure your IQ, the context that makes your company unique, is available to your agents across every layer of Azure, with governance and security built in. It stays yours, and its value grows with everything you build on it. To learn more about Microsoft IQ, I encourage you to join my Microsoft Ignite session, “Harnessing Your IQ with a continuously improving agent platform,” in person or online at no cost, or watch the recording afterward.

For a closer look at all the innovation we are bringing to Azure, explore the full list of sessions on the Microsoft Ignite session catalog.

Explore Azure at Microsoft Ignite

See how Azure Catalyst, Azure HorizonDB, and other Azure innovations help you modernize your estate and build AI apps.

See all sessions

item.content:encoded:
Why: iPhone Duo camera review from an iPhone photography specialist. (score 7)

From Lux — iPhone camera apps, camera reviews and more.

iPhone Duo Camera Review: Form Brings Function

With its debut, the iPhone Duo was dinged by critics for having a camera system that's a step-down from the iPhone Pro. It seemed like this wasn't the camera to use on once-in-a-lifetime trips. I guess Halide users didn't get the memo.

While it lacks the iPhone 18 Pro's camera, the Duo still captures amazing photos. If you're considering the Duo but take iPhone photography seriously, the ultimate question is whether the small tradeoffs are worth what the Duo gives in return.

This review is not an epic trip across the globe. We're saving that for the 18 Pro. Instead, we're taking a trip to the New York Botanical Gardens for its annual Holiday Train Show.

The show featuring 200 miniatures, carved from real plant parts, which recreate famous New York landmarks

With computational photography, it's easy for software to compensate for poor hardware. That's why we're starting this review with photos that skip the shenanigans, so we can see how the hardware stands on its own.

These are very good cameras, which makes sense, as they're about on-par with the iPhone 17 Pro.

And Now For the Mandatory AI Discussion

None of the above photos were touched by the new AI photo editing that Apple launched in iOS 27. I have to admit, I have an aversion to this stuff. Maybe I just prefer the honesty of flaws. That said, I won't fault you for using AI to alter photos you share with friends and family.

At the train exhibit, there were two cases where the cleanup tool could save the day. I gave it a whirl, and wow, it's come a long way. Can you tell what was altered here?

There used to be a guy at the door in the background. The clean enough tool is now smart enough to fill in the occluded door panel.

In another instance, someone snuck into my frame and I didn't notice. I try my best to avoid photographing strangers, but sometimes I get tunnel vision and this happens.

Is it acceptable to use clean up to protect the privacy of someone else's kid?

Regardless, the cleanup tool has come a long way. I was used to smudgy slop, but with iOS 27, the results look seamless.

The Reframe tool makes me feel even more uncomfortable, but also gave me a good laugh. I tried to reframe this miniature of the botanical gardens, the AI confused it with the real botanical gardens, and it inserted a New York skyline.

And then we get to Extend. Please forgive me.

I spent an hour staging and lighting a "hero" photo for this review. No matter how I positioned the camera, even standing on a ladder, I couldn't get quite the composition I wanted. It felt too tight.

I began wondering how Apple Photos' Extend would handle it.

Well, I'll be damned.

I feel dirty, and I don't know why. Would I feel better if I didn't use AI, and I extended the shot in Photoshop by hand? I don't have answers. Right or wrong, Apple's AI photo editing has gotten really good.

This concludes all the AI you'll find in this post.

The Hardware and Low Light

When comparing the main camera of the Duo and Pro, it all comes down to light. Based on a teardown by Wekihome, the Duo's main camera sensor is 30% smaller than the iPhone 18 Pro, and its aperture opens to ƒ/1.48 compared to the Duo's ƒ/1.6. In total, you're looking at around 75% less light on the Duo.

The Duo uses the first generation sensor shift stabilization, while the 18 Pro uses the second generation introduced way back in the 14 Pro. That makes the Duo on-par with the budget iPhone models. It's safe to assume that this wasn't a cost cutting measure, but a technical requirement to keep the device thin.

In theory, you should expect the iPhone Duo to use higher ISO. Will this lead to more noise reduction and that "watercolor look" that screams iPhone photo? In practice, I didn't see this.

Consider this spectacular rainbow at dusk, skipping over Apple's noise reduction.

Zoom into the sky, and there you go.

This photo was ƒ/1.6, ISO 160, 1/60 exposure. This is about what you can expect shooting an interior at night. I think it's pretty good! I think sensor noise became much less of a concern on iPhones with the introduction of the 48 megapixel sensor, which "bin" adjoining pixels to cut noise.

Here's the same shot with the first party camera. It uses the 'Standard' photographic style, with default settings, and then tweaked in the Photos app to better match Halide's shot.

If we zoom into the sky, we see it's completely noise free.

But once you zoom in details, things feel a bit plastic.

A good friend of mine who works in visual effects describes noise as, "analog dithering." In the real world, whenever light hits a photo sensor, there's a natural randomness that orbits around the truth. When you leave the noise in an image, your brain pieces together the fine details, even better than software. When you apply aggressive noise reduction, you wipe that information.

Noise comes down to taste, and Apple defaults to heavy noise reduction. However, with the latest version of photographic styles, they added a "grain" option to bring back texture. Let's turn it on.

From the looks of it, Apple is adding a synthetic layer of grain after noise reduction, as opposed to preserving the original noise. If that's really what's happening, I strongly disagree with this choice.

I don't think there's anything wrong with letting users bump up texture. That's why we give you that option in Halide.

But if you're going to have noise, I think you should preserve the original noise. Noise reduction strips information, and adding new noise afterwards amounts to an optical illusion. You're robbing Peter to pay Paul.

Anyway, if you want to reduce the noise in low light, the Duo benefits from its size and inertia. Open it up, hold it with both hands, and brace it against your body. I was able to slow down by an extra two stops and still get acceptable shots.

Unfortunately, you're going to have to use a third-party app to do this. Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo lacks "Pro Controls" in the first-party app. That's too bad, because slow shutters are fun.

We round out our sensor discussion by flipping things around. All front-facing cameras have the same sensor size as the iPhone 17 and 18 Pro. The exact size is… complicated. While Apple describe the front sensor as square, it's actually octagonal! You just don't see the awkward corners because iOS crops your photos into portrait or landscape.

The inner front-facing camera is worse off because it's hidden behind the display, which is like taking a photo behind a screen door. It's going to cost light and detail.

Apple does not allow RAW capture from the inner front-facing camera. Developers can only access the final, processed image. Maybe Apple knows that the unprocessed image is so bad that it's a waste of a photographer's time.

The inner front-facing camera is fine for FaceTime calls. If you want to take a good self-portrait, you should at least use the outer front-facing camera. Better yet, unfold the Duo and use the back-facing camera.

The Tele-phant In the Room

So the biggest omission, and most valid criticism of the Duo, is the lack of a telephoto camera. Will you miss it?

If you only shoot with Apple's camera app, you probably use the telephoto camera less often than you think. When there isn't enough light, or you try to capture something too close for it to focus, Apple's camera app quietly switches over to the main camera and crops its results. It doesn't matter if you had the 4× button selected.

Fortunately, Apple's camera app saves metadata telling you the actual focal length used. This makes it easy to check in Apple Photos using a Smart Album.

In the last two years, I've shot over 5,000 photos, and about 12% used the telephoto lens, and a good chunk were purely test photos for developing Halide. This made me comfortable trying the Duo as my daily driver, and in the last few weeks, I haven't had a single moment like, "Man, I wish I had a telephoto right now!" Then again, I've been pretty busy working on these Halide updates, so I haven't had time for any scenic trips.

The Lack of Pro Formats

I will say that the Duo's biggest weakness is the inability to capture ProRAW. ProRAWs give you incredible latitude when editing high dynamic range scenes like this one.

If we zoom in, you'll notice sensor noise.

Unlike the low-light example earlier, here we have too much light in our scene. If we expose the shot to raise the shadows, we'll very likely clip details in highlights. We have to starve the shadows of light, which brings with it noise.

On the iPhone Pro, this is no problem. Deep Fusion takes multiple exposures, and packages it into a ProRAW for editing flexibility. Unfortunately, the Duo (and the rest of the non-Pro iPhones), only support native, Bayer RAWs. I'll also note that Night Mode is only available in the first party camera app, and it doesn't shoot Bayer RAW.

That's a longwinded way of saying that when shooting high dynamic range scenes, or using Night Mode, you are strictly limited to Apple's photographic styles.

Whether that's a dealbreaker is a matter of personal taste. Apple's photographic styles are not my cup of tea, but if you love them, great. I'm mostly disappointed that they're your only option, when I don't know a technical reason for it. ProRAW debuted in 2020 on iPhones with significantly less memory and processing power.

That said, third-party apps like Project Indigo build their own computational photography pipelines from scratch. It won't be consistent with Apple's camera app, but it might be a fine substitute when you have these itches.

The same can't be said of Apple Log, which is only available on the Pro lineup of iPhones. Even if a developer wanted to build their own version of Apple Log, Apple doesn't provide the APIs to do it.

Judging the Tradeoffs

The iPhone Duo is a great camera that allows you to produce amazing photos. It just isn't an iPhone Pro. In return, you get the benefits of an iPhone Duo. Is the Duo for you?

Since I began using the Duo as my daily driver three weeks ago, a number of strangers have struck up conversation asking what I think of it. This isn't the same level of curiosity as the first iPhone, but there's definitely interest. If you got this far into the review, clearly you're considering it. For all its 1.0 flaws, I really dig this device. I think it'll be popular. I just don't think it's the next step of phones.

You came for a camera review, so let's use a camera metaphor…

That's 35mm film. It dominated mass market photography until the move to digital in the 2000s. If someone says "film," you probably picture 35mm.

When NASA needed to capture the moon landing, they reached for "medium format," which is about 60mm. That film requires bigger, chonkier cameras.

A normal iPhone is like 35mm camera, and it hits the perfect sweet spot between size and utility for most people. An iPad is medium format. It's great when you need to watch a movie or do some light productivity, but iPads are annoying to carry everywhere.

A few decades into mass market photography, we saw interesting experiments with transforming cameras. The Mamiya 6 had a collapsible lens design, bringing medium format to a portable form factor. In 1998, Hasselblad released the XPan, a bizarre camera that takes 35mm film, but let you capture photos as wide as shooting medium format.

These cameras didn't set the world on fire. They were expensive, and solved a niche problem. However, they were still profitable. These companies sold these products for years, and even released updates like the Mamiya 7 and XPan II. These cameras have developed a bit of a cult following.

Foldables will always be more expensive and bulkier than single screen phones. Still, using a Duo for the last three weeks, I discovered a new itch alongside the scratcher. It's amazing to shoot a photo and then edit it seconds later on a screen with abundant space.

Niche cameras can thrive because film follows standards. If cameras were like apps, then all the film companies would have to update their film stocks whenever a new camera comes out. This is exactly the challenge Apple faces.

Apple needs companies to take the time to optimize apps for the Duo. Nobody wants a situation like Instagram, who waited 15 years before launching their iPad app. Even worse, some apps were outright janky on the day of the Duo launch.

That's because lots of apps were built on decades-long assumptions about iPhone interfaces, such as toolbars sitting at the bottom of the screen. I don't fault anyone for coding their apps around reasonable assumptions, and even Halide looked wonky on launch day. My penance was working through the weekend to ship a fix by Monday.

Three weeks later, Apple says over 200,000 apps have been updated for compatibility. My bank's app is not one of them, but hey, big corporations move slow. For most apps, the transition should be fairly painless if you paid attention to the to the "adaptive" APIs Apple introduced well over a decade ago. I'd wager all the popular apps will be serviceable before you can just walk into an Apple Store and walk out with a Duo.

That said, there's a difference between building an app that works on the Duo, and building a great experience for the Duo. While Apple's design guidance is a great starting point, it's deliberately generic. It can't tell you how your app can make the most of the new form factor, so it feels more than an iPhone app blown up to a big screen.

Making the most of the Duo for Halide has been an iterative, but fun, experience. When it was unveiled, the first idea that came to mind was "waist-level viewfinder," similar to a Hasselblad or Rolleiflex.

By half-closing the Duo and swapping from right to left, you can shoot from the hip.

This has some ergonomic perks, like capturing your kids at eye-level without hunching over. Alternately, raise it above your head and look up, to get shots above crowds. Just please, please don't do that at concerts.

Some photographers find that changing their perspective gives them a fresh take on the art form. In portraiture, lowering the camera removes a barrier between you and your subject, and can lead to more candid results.

Another idea for the Duo was the ability to review your last photo side-by-side with the viewfinder.

Caught someone blinking or looking away? Just delete it. Nailed the shot? Favorite it now, rather than hunt through your camera roll later.

We shipped our first update three days after the Duo's launch, and then listened to user feedback. Some users found the reviewer distracting, so we shipped a quick update that let you hide it. We also ran into more edge cases in the UI, such as needing to flip the toolbar from right to left in its split-app mode. That brings us to our second major update.

In today's update, we've found the perspective spot for the histogram: the crease. It's a bit of a "no man's land" for interaction when half-open, which makes it a good spot for auxiliary information.

When you hide the reviewer, we show our "XL" mode, maximizing the viewfinder to make the most of the big screen.

Lens controls move to the left, and it feels great to adjust focus with one hand while your other keeps your finger on the shutter button, just like a standalone camera.

Finally, we've added modes to the outer screen when fully open. You can mirror the camera view, which is great if you need to take a selfie with the best camera. Alternately, you can display a preview-only to avoid the distraction of controls.

We've also added an option to use the outer-screen as a softer alternative to the flash. Consider this shot.

Let's say I want to lift my face out of shadow, which is the job of a flash-fill. Unfortunately, the tiny flash on an iPhone is not great in this situation, unless you're going for a vintage Y2K look.

A larger light source, like the outer screen, yields more natural results even if it lacks the same power.

This is not going to work miracles, but if your subject is fairly close to the screen, you'll find that it provides softer, more even lighting.

Today's Halide Duo update is available now for all Mark III users.

I love the Duo. I'll find the tradeoffs worthwhile if I can be a little more productive on my phone. However, as someone who builds camera apps for a living, I'm far from giving up my iPhone Pro. Stay tuned for our 18 Pro review.
