item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber weighs in on the Huang and Nvidia scandal with real commentary. (score 8)

From Daring Fireball.

Ever since the Huang/Nvidia scandal erupted, I’ve been thinking about a short post I wrote back in March, under the headline “Jensen Huang Doesn’t Smell Anything”:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, during an on-stage interview at The Hill & Valley Forum last week, was asked “What do you see as America’s unique advantages that other countries don’t have?”

His answer, after taking a moment to think, “America’s unique advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump.”

Huang, newly appointed to the aforelinked President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, seemingly doesn’t smell the growing stink.

The stink was the historically low (and sinking) popularity to which Trump’s 2.0 presidency had sunk. Undeniable to anyone in touch with reality. Huang’s obsequious Trump-fellating answer to that question would have been eye-catching even a year prior, when Trump first rolled back into office with an aggressive agenda and a surplus of political capital from a clear election victory — but it was, frankly, a startling thing to say in March 2026. It makes a lot more sense, though, given what’s come to light in the last 10 days.

[Update: This event was in July 2025, not March 2026, but while I regret that error, my points stand.]

If you’re not paying close attention you might think Huang’s was the sort of answer any major tech CEO might have given. But it’s not. That was a really unusual thing for Huang to say, way out of line with how corporate leaders typically approach politics. The typical approach for large publicly held corporations is to avoid partisan politics. Advocate only for policies directly related to the company’s business, and otherwise stay out. The political winds change direction every few years. George Bush senior in 1988 was the last new president elected from the same party as the outgoing incumbent, and he only lasted one term. It makes no sense for a corporation that intends to continue thriving for more than the next few years to closely align itself with one party — unless they believe that party will remain in power for the foreseeable future, à la the FDR/Truman Democrats, who won five consecutive presidential elections from 1932 to 1948 (and seven out of nine through 1968).

One metaphor I use for politics is a football field. Democrats on the left, Republicans on the right. CEOs typically stay as close as they can to the 50-yard line in the middle of the field. That way, when an election puts the other party in power, they don’t have to move — they just need to turn around. That’s how someone like Tim Cook could maintain good relations with the White House from Obama to Trump to Biden back to Trump again. He just stayed close to midfield and turned around after each election.

Remaining as close as possible to political midfield under Trump required unseemly obsequious tribute, unprecedented in modern U.S. history. Million-dollar tickets to his inauguration. That ridiculous gold trophy. Embarrassing stuff. But that’s ultimately a reflection of Trump’s avarice, not the politics of Cook personally or Apple as a company. That was the price to stay on the 50-yard line. Cook has often repeated that his two personal heroes are Martin Luther King Jr. and Bobby Kennedy (senior, to be clear). He keeps portraits of both of them in his office. He never swapped them out for portraits of, say, Ronald Reagan. Apple never changed its internal policies or language regarding racial and LGBT equality. The Apple homepage never stopped celebrating Martin Luther King Jr. Day — even when it coincided with Trump’s second inauguration.

And yet Trump remains so enamored of Cook that he floated his name to succeed Huang at Nvidia. Tim Apple remains the apple of Trump’s eye. Yet Apple had nothing to change or apologize for when Biden came into office, nor will they again if, as now seems likely, Trump is succeeded in 2029 by a Democrat elected to clean up his kakistocratic kleptomaniacal mess. (Presumably Apple will gladly pony up at least another $25 million to restore the East Wing after Trump’s architecturally ungodly ballroom edifice is torn down.) And Apple certainly won’t need lawyers to defend them from charges of corruption and/or breaches of national security. Nvidia, not so much.

This is what we should want: business leaders who endeavor to stay out of partisan politics, not hopelessly enmesh themselves in it. Industry and politics cannot operate in isolation, but they should avoid intertwinement except where necessary. Great companies stand the test of time. That’s not feasible if you hitch your corporate wagon to one party or the other, no matter the political moment. We don’t think of Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola, or Berkshire Hathaway as being Democratic or Republican companies. You cannot chart their fortunes over time based on which party was in power in any given decade. You may well have strong political opinions that are far from the 50-yard line, on one side or the other. I do. But you shouldn’t look for those opinions to be validated by industry executives, any more than you should look for business and product-design decisions to be made by elected government officials. True American values put country over party when it comes to business. And, as Calvin Coolidge aptly put it, “The chief business of the American people is business.”

America does possess unique advantages that other countries don’t have. Personal liberties enshrined in our Bill of Rights. A vibrant, diverse, ever-changing melting pot of a citizenry. A strong tradition of the rule of law, placing no man above it. Competitive markets that allow new entrants to supplant entrenched incumbents. Any CEO worth their salt should have an answer to the question of America’s unique advantages that holds true no matter who, from which party, is currently president. And they should believe it.

What makes Huang’s answer so off-putting isn’t that it was so abjectly partisan — politically tone-deaf to the inevitability of Democrats coming back into power, and perversely obsequious to Trump personally — but that Donald Trump is the antithesis to the entire above list of things that actually give America unique advantages other countries don’t have. Trump and the MAGA movement are also decidedly American and uniquely so, but they represent what’s worst about America.

But I give Huang credit for honesty. Clearly, he believed what he said. Huang didn’t just stray from the 50-yard line — he broke for Trump’s end zone.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Tsai rounds up the Apple iCloud outage and the lessons from an internal update gone wrong. (score 8)

From Michael Tsai.

Juli Clover (Hacker News, John Gruber):

Apple has largely resolved outages affecting iCloud accounts, retail stores, and more, the company said in a statement to Bloomberg. Apple said the outages were due to an unspecified “internal update” and were not caused by a cyberattack. The company is working to get remaining systems online “as soon as possible.”

Developer services like notarization were down for another 5 hours or so after that—but, then, notarization seems to go down every week.

I don’t know whether it’s related, but around the time the outage started, my Apple Watch stopped functioning. It would only show a small, white analog clock, and I couldn’t get to the main watch face. Restarting didn’t help. This had never happened to me before with any Apple Watch. I had to erase it and restore from backup.

I also wonder whether there’s any connection with the other recent outages.

Yahoo News (Hacker News, Slashdot):

While U.S. officials continue to investigate last week’s nationwide ground stop that caused thousands of flights to be delayed or canceled, the Federal Aviation Administration said on Tuesday that it is pausing the installation of routers linked to the outage.

CNN (Hacker News):

The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.

AP (Hacker News):

Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

CNN (Hacker News):

A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at US airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a rare FAA ground stop that caused massive disruption.

Natalie Musumeci (Hacker News):

Charles Schwab’s website briefly went down for some users on Tuesday.

Previously:

  • Microsoft Outage
  • Apple Service Outages

item.content:encoded:
Why: Visual Intelligence comes to the iPad Camera app in the 27.3 betas. (score 7)

From MacStories.

Apple added a dedicated Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app with iOS 27, which you can read more about in Federico’s annual review. Now that same feature is set to come to the iPad.

Earlier this week, Apple released developer beta two for the 27.3 OSes. I wrote about many of those upcoming changes earlier this week but missed the changes to the iPad’s Camera app. As with iOS, when you open the Camera app in iPadOS 27.3, there will be a dedicated Siri mode. Switch to the new mode and the shutter button becomes a Siri icon. Tap it, and Siri will analyze the scene, describing what it sees. From there, you can use your finger or an Apple Pencil to circle or scrub over individual items, activating Visual Intelligence to search Google, Amazon, and other Visual Intelligence-enabled apps. Here’s a quick demo of it on the latest iPad mini that I recently reviewed:

Visual Intelligence is one of those iOS and iPadOS features that I’ve had trouble remembering to use. However, as you can tell from the video, it works really well for things like recognizable products. I’m glad to see this coming to the iPad, especially the mini, which I’m much more likely to use as a camera for capturing my surroundings.

item.title: How I got my recipes on HomeView via Safari
item.author: Six Colors
item.description:
Why: Snell finds a clever workaround for recipes on HomeView and critiques Apple app strategy. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

It’s close, but not perfect (note the blank center image). One of my disappointments in Apple’s app strategy for the HomeView is that its choice to not support third-party apps—except via CarPlay—freezes out an entire class of apps that should be right at home on the device: recipe apps.…
item.content:encoded:
Why: Snell finds a clever workaround for recipes on HomeView and critiques Apple app strategy. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

One of my disappointments in Apple’s app strategy for the HomeView is that its choice to not support third-party apps—except via CarPlay—freezes out an entire class of apps that should be right at home on the device: recipe apps.

HomeView features a fun recipe browser inside Safari, but if all your recipes are stored in an app—my preference is Silvio Rizzi’s Mela—then they are locked out of HomeView.

Or are they?

Before I get to my solution to this issue, I want to tip my cap to the inspiration I received from other quarters. Stephen Robles, motivated to solve this same issue, built an entire recipe-keeper app for HomeView. And I heard from Aaron Gold, the developer of Saucepan, another recipe app that has figured out HomeView integration.

Here’s the long and short of it: If you want your recipes to show up on the HomeView, they need to be web pages that open in Safari on the HomeView. That’s the only pathway right now. Robles and Gold both solved this problem by building apps that upload recipe data to a web server that generates and opens a private URL in Safari, which you can then just AirDrop directly to the HomeView.

This is probably what every developer who wants to support HomeView right now will have to do.

That said, while I hope Rizzi is on the case, I wasn’t satisfied with waiting and I didn’t want to move house to a different app. So I decided to see if I could solve this problem another way, namely by building a solution that would encode the HTML exported natively by Mela and open it in Safari in a way that would be transferable to the HomeView.

Here’s the result: a Shortcut you need to add, and a single HTML wrapper page you need to download and put on a web server you have access to. Download them both here.

When you’re in Mela, open a recipe and then tap the … menu, then Share: HTML… and from the resulting share sheet, choose the shortcut Mela to HomeView. It will open the recipe by loading the recipes.html file at the URL you chose (when you put it on the web server you have access to, remember?) and then passing all the data from the recipe into that web page via encoded data appended to the URL in Safari. The HTML file is just a wrapper; all the recipe data is included in the URL.

Then when Safari opens, bring your device close to the HomeView and it’ll transfer it over and load it in Safari, complete with a button to enter HomeView’s Recipe mode.

There’s one catch: Try as I might, I couldn’t get Recipe mode to display the pretty “cover image” of a recipe. Apparently for that you need to load the image from a remote server, and for this simple approach I don’t want to encourage people to build an extensive web back-end that’s capable of accepting uploads. (You can do it, to be sure, and I might—but for this solution I wanted it to be as simple as possible. Frankly, I don’t love that you have to put an HTML file on a web server at all, but here we are.)

Anyway, that’s my solution—for today. I hope that Mela and other recipe apps will solve this with hacks similar to those of Robles and Gold in the short term, and that Apple will provide better access to third-party recipe databases in the long term.

item.content:encoded:
Why: A decade-old unauthenticated RCE in NGINX HTTP/2 is a big deal for nearly every server fleet. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

A flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in.

The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today.

F5, the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port.

Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg.

In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container.

Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today.

Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.

Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories. That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6.

Wiz PoC

NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory.

Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0.

Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup:

Flaw What it needs
CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 turned on
CVE-2026-123633HTTP/2, with requests passed to a backend server while the worker is running low on 
worker_connections
CVE-2026-123634A proxied server name built from variables, plus a server-side include (SSI) or 
mirror
subrequest to a location that looks up the same name
CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 turned on
CVE-2026-113425 NGINX used as a mail proxy

HTTP/2 is on where a 

listen
directive includes 
http2
, or where 
http2 on
is set. Running 
openssl s_client
with 
-alpn h2
against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads 
ALPN protocol: h2
if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2.

Fixes, Workarounds and Signs of Attack

These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5:

  • NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 to 1.31.8 (mainline): fixed in 1.31.9
  • NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6, including older branches such as 1.28: fixed in 1.30.7
  • NGINX Plus 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1: fixed in 37.3.0.1
  • NGINX Plus 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1: fixed in 37.0.8.1
  • NGINX Plus R34 to R36: no fix listed

Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes. On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1.

After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes.

The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants.

Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that 

nginx -v
reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory.

Xint PoC

The vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and 

mirror
directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks.

CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs.

On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set 

http2 off;
in each affected 
server
block and remove 
http2
from its 
listen
directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove 
http2
from the 
listen
directive, so 
listen 443 ssl http2;
becomes 
listen 443 ssl;
. Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the 
openssl
check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2.

Until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line 

install sctp /bin/false
to a 
.conf
file in 
/etc/modprobe.d/
. That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel.

For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own.

Rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis. The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail.

The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the 

avx512f
and 
avx512vl
features.

Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post.

Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: Big school districts push back on Google forcing Gemini features, a notable AI adoption fight. (score 7)

From The Verge.

New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search

Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

item.content:encoded:
Why: TPM lockout bypass cracking BitLocker and Windows Hello PINs is squarely in key management territory. (score 9)

From The Hacker News.

On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say.

That leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way.

Both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries. From the speeds they measured, they calculate a worst-case of 40 hours for a four-digit Hello PIN, compared to 69 days with the lockout working as documented. For a default six-digit BitLocker PIN, the worst-case time drops from 19 years to 20 days.

AMD confirmed yesterday that its processor firmware has a flaw that allows the attack on some PCs with its chips. It plans fixes for most of those chips between November and February 2027. For now, the researchers advise adding at least two digits to Hello and BitLocker PINs.

The TPM in these PCs is a firmware TPM, built into the processor. Unlike a separate TPM chip, it has no secure storage of its own, according to the research paper the researchers posted late last week. So it keeps its saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, encrypted on the mainboard's flash chip.

If someone copies that saved state and later writes the old copy back, the count goes back too, unless the PC detects it. Newer PCs try to catch this with counters inside the flash chip, called RPMC, that can only go up.

On AMD PCs that use these counters, the processor's firmware never verifies that a counter actually increased. A small board placed between the processor and the flash chip can block the update and report success, causing the PC to accept the old state.

RPMC chips from flash maker Winbond have a different weakness, the researchers found. A brief drop in the chip's power supply, called a voltage glitch, can cause the chip to reveal the secret key that signs its counter values. With that key, which took about a second to extract with their best settings, the board can forge any counter value.

On the Intel laptop they tested, one glitch was enough: the laptop's firmware feeds the chip the same value at every boot, so the leaked key kept working after each restart.

For the Hello test, the researchers attacked a locked HP OmniBook 3 with an AMD Ryzen AI 5 330 processor and a BitLocker-encrypted drive. Their setup typed PINs from 1000 upward and reached the correct one, 1235, after 236 tries in 57 minutes.

Windows still forced a restart after every 5 incorrect PIN attempts on that laptop, but no lockout delay was applied. Microsoft's lockout defaults lock the TPM after 32 wrong tries and forget one failure every 10 minutes.

The BitLocker test ran on a Framework Laptop 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H processor and Winbond flash. BitLocker's startup prompt adds no limit of its own, so each reset gave a fresh 32 tries. The setup found the PIN, 123457, after 236 tries in 6 minutes and 55 seconds.

In both tests, the researchers took the flash chip off the mainboard and wired in their own board. A script read the screen, typed PINs, and restarted the laptop through a KVM switch. They also changed firmware settings to slow each laptop's link to the flash chip, because their board could not keep up at full speed.

The researchers make two further claims that their tests did not cover. Either method could be used against either PIN. A recovered Hello PIN can also unlock keys tied to the device and enable Hello-based single sign-on at work, and, in some configurations, pass a multi-factor check.

The researchers have published their attack firmware, board designs, and scripts. They say reproducing the RPMC attacks is not plug-and-play and needs one of their boards. Neither the paper nor the vendor notices published so far describe attacks outside the lab.

Which PCs the Attack Works On and What Vendors Say

Whether the attack works depends on the processor and the flash chip:

  • AMD-based PCs with RPMC flash: open to the board that blocks counter updates. The chipmaker has confirmed the firmware flaw behind this and plans to fix it.
  • AMD-based PCs without RPMC flash: on two AMD desktops in the researchers' tests, writing an old copy back with an ordinary flash programmer reset the count, requiring no board. They conclude that AMD processors likely have no other protection against this, though two desktops may not be representative of all AMD systems.
  • PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the researchers say these are open to the leaked-key method whatever the processor, and that only a new chip design can fix it.
  • Intel PCs without RPMC-like flash: three Intel systems detected the same write-back in those tests.

The researchers expect the AMD firmware flaw to affect AMD PCs that use the Microsoft Pluton security core as their TPM, but did not show this.

On an AMD PC, the owner can boot Linux, for example from a live USB stick, and run the command grep . /sys/bus/pci/drivers/ccp/*/rpmc_* from the researchers' exposure check. The output indicates whether RPMC flash is present and enabled, which tells the owner which of the two methods applies. Missing files do not mean the PC lacks RPMC.

For Intel PCs, the researchers know of no such check. Owners would have to open the PC and look for a Winbond chip marked 25R or 74M.

AMD tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-43613 and assigns it a CVSS score of 5.1 in a security bulletin published yesterday.

The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack." The researchers first told it about the flaw in February.

The chipmaker's fix targets run from November to February 2027 across Ryzen, Ryzen AI, Ryzen Threadripper, Athlon and EPYC chips, and one unnamed product has no date yet. These are planned dates for its own firmware, not updates already out for PCs.

The bulletin does not cover AMD PCs without RPMC flash. It also does not say whether the update will prevent an attacker from installing older, unfixed firmware on the PC, which the researchers say a fix must prevent.

Intel, whose processor was in the BitLocker test laptop, said in a security announcement earlier this week that the research "did not demonstrate a vulnerability in an Intel component". That matches the tests, in which the attack on the Intel laptop needed the Winbond chip's flaw.

According to the researchers, Intel's security team called the reused value a weakness rather than a vulnerability.

The researchers told Microsoft in April. According to them, the company rated the Windows Hello report as "moderate severity" and below its bar for an immediate fix, issued no CVE or bounty, and committed to raising its recommended minimum Hello PIN length to six digits.

At the company's request, the researchers filed the BitLocker finding as a separate report for a different team. The company declined to give them any further written statement for the paper.

Separately, a Windows 11 test build released late last week makes six digits the minimum for personal-account Hello PINs, with an option to use four. The release notes give no reason, and features in that test channel may never reach regular releases.

According to the researchers, Winbond was first told about its chips' weakness to voltage glitches in January 2025 and received a second report in April showing that a glitch also leaks the key. The flash maker is studying the issue, possibly including a new chip design, but has not committed to a fix or a date.

What Owners and Admins Can Do

Two extra digits make a large difference in the researchers' figures:

Worst-case time to find a numeric PIN
PIN length With the documented lockout Hello attack (AMD laptop) BitLocker attack (Intel laptop)
4 digits 69 days 40 hours 5 hours*
6 digits 19 years 168 days 20 days
8 digits 1,903 years 46 years 6 years

* BitLocker accepts a four-digit PIN only if an admin lowers the six-digit minimum. The times are worst cases calculated from speeds measured on one laptop each.

In May, Microsoft advised moving BitLocker from TPM-only to TPM+PIN to block the YellowKey bypass, as part of its YellowKey mitigation. The same TPM lockout guards that PIN.

Steps for each setup:

  • Windows Hello for Business: raise the Minimum PIN length policy, under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > PIN Complexity. If it is not set, Windows requires six digits, a worst case of 168 days in the table above, and admins can set it as low as four. The PIN policy settings page lists it on the PIN settings tab.
  • BitLocker: raise the Configure minimum PIN length for startup policy, which allows 4 to 20 digits and requires six by default. Turning on "Allow enhanced PINs for startup" lets letters and symbols, which the BitLocker PIN guidance recommends for older hardware.
  • AMD-based PCs: install the firmware update with the chipmaker's fix when one is available for your PC. Until then, the chipmaker advises keeping PCs under physical control and watching for signs of tampering.
  • PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the flash maker has not committed to a fix, according to the researchers. Intel advises its customers to ask their PC maker about updates.

Google News,

item.title: Casting an expert eye on Apple’s AI photo-retouching features
item.author: Six Colors
item.description:
Why: Snell's expert analysis of Apple's AI photo retouching tools. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

In its 27 operating system releases, Apple added loads of generative image editing tools, and the tools have incrementally changed since they were introduced over the summer.…
item.content:encoded:
Why: Snell's expert analysis of Apple's AI photo retouching tools. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

In its 27 operating system releases, Apple added loads of generative image editing tools, and the tools have incrementally changed since they were introduced over the summer. I’m going to take my 20-plus years of experience in visual effects and talk about how well those tools work in practice.

I’m not going to get into a whole preamble about how I really do think it’s OK for you to edit a photo, or the video comparing the initial release of Clean Up with comparable retouching tools. People can do bad things with image editing tools, but I don’t believe that photos people take of their lives should be treated like courtroom evidence.

Having said that, it’s important that tools set users up for success by guiding them toward making good choices that preserve as much of their original images, and their original intent, as possible. Data loss of original pixels can be a trade-off to get an adjustment that people want, but tools shouldn’t hide the data loss from users.

Lesson number one in VFX is that you’re only changing the pixels you have to change for the effect the client wants. You do not de-noise (or de-grain) your entire image (or image sequence) to do your work and then send that back to the client. You do not re-noise the entire de-noised image either; if it can be helped, you control the region you are editing in your image to confine your work. As much of the original image as possible should pass through.

Apple doesn’t always disclose to the user how its generative tools are impacting the images. That includes things like maximum resolution caps, filtering the pixels that are being kept, blurry boundaries, and potential color and value shifts. There is the Show Photo Without Edits button, which Apple provides to let people see before and after a generative edit has been made. I strongly encourage everyone to use that button. But it won’t tell you about lost resolution, and when the image is scaled to fit to the window, you may not be able to see the damage.

It’s totally fine if you’re happy with the zoomed-out version, and it suits the purpose (a lock screen image, a desktop, whatever). For a lot of people, they’re the same picture. Just know that these tools don’t really match your original sensor noise, and as of the 27.2 release the images are now watermarked with SynthID, even though Apple does not disclose that to users in the interface, so they can’t decide if the change they’re making is worth the image being “AI” since SynthID doesn’t disclose the editing chain.1

Pretend extend doesn’t just append

Cutting off the edges of a photo, and adding on to the edges of a photo, are unsurprisingly related. So much so that Apple reused its aspect-ratio crop selection code for the interface of its Extend tool. (This should be in the Crop interface.)

At the very least, Apple should change the code it’s reusing from the aspect ratio bounds resizing so that it fits to the bounds of the input as a minimum dimension when toggling between 3:4 and 9:16. Because right now, changing the aspect ratio in Extend can crop the image, which is what you want for Crop… but not for Extend.

I don’t like the hazy blur effect at the edges, because users should be able to manipulate a single edge of their image without messing with pixels all the way around. There’s no useful way to snap to fit the original bounds in order to use as much original image as possible. You just have to kind of eyeball where you’re dragging the reticle.

The unfortunate truth is that Extend throws away image data. It only looks like it keeps your original pixels when you’re zoomed way out. It perceptually reads like you’ve extended your image, but what’s really happened is that the original image is actually scaled down and resampled to be a smaller resolution so that your generative border, plus your original pixels, all fit in a 12.19-megapixel canvas.

It appears that Apple is using a soft filter to resample the image—not even a sharpening filter, because everything is definitely softer and there are no ringing artifacts associated with sharpening.

The blurry border from the crop preview is also true to what’s happening, because the entire border is blurry. There seems to be about 200-300 pixels of a feathered mask operation that takes your scaled-down photo and combines it with the generative edge.

Imagine that I said that I wanted to add a room to a one-story house that had no property boundary constraints, and the contractor did it by demolishing the house and building a scaled-down replica of the house, then adding the extra room on so the whole house took the same square footage. That’s some Nathan Fielder behavior.

If the generative maximum is 12.19 MP, or something around that, why not take those generative pixels and scale those up to match the increased bounds so that the original core can be preserved? Don’t blend any borders that aren’t actually being extended! Forcing everything to fit some technical constraint rather than making preservation of data the constraint is backwards.

Another place where data could be pulled from to improve quality is other neighboring photos you’ve taken. Extend doesn’t use other photos in your camera roll from the same time frame, or location, as context. You can easily see this for yourself if you duplicate a photo, crop the photo, and then use Extend on the crop, you won’t get buildings sourced from the neighboring image. It’s a silly test, but it just confirms it’s not happening.

Context is very important to getting good results, because it’s what a real photo retoucher would do, or a VFX artist. It’s one thing if you don’t have the data, in which case filling in what was probably there is much more impressive, but if you could have filled in what you have photos of, then you should do that.

Which brings us to…

Reframe to blame for eye strain

The Reframe feature is the most “we repurposed something” of the models. I would argue that it is not a creative image editing tool at all, but it is very clever. If you look at Apple’s ML Sharp, or any of its other myriad projects around 3D computer vision, you can see a lineage of sorts. (This means that things like reflections and refractions do weird stuff. Pond surfaces, shop windows, wine glasses, and the like.)

Reframe lets you move around quite a bit, and you’ll see all the stretchy weird stuff, and holes, from areas where the camera did not have line of sight. Reframe does not use context from surrounding photos, or video, to fill in those missing pieces, unfortunately. Instead those holes are filled in with speculation from some kind of model.

Reframe doesn’t retain any of your original images, even scaled down, like Extend does. It’s filling in everything seemingly guided by its extrapolated 3D view that’s full of holes. It doesn’t have access to the original imagery to paste back in.

However, where Extend mostly softens and mushes original pixels, Reframe also has tone and color shifts that are not anchored to your original image.

These color and value shifts are not uniform, and aren’t restricted to certain file types. The SDR image from my Sony a6400 has shifts, and the egret photo was taken with Project Indigo, not the Camera app. There isn’t an entirely consistent and predictable direction of color and tone shifts. Sometimes it’s more drastic than others, or a defect might be similar with shots taken around the same time of day.

To take the angle adjustment out of the calculation I took a bunch of shots with gray and white to measure color cast changes and only changed the image by 0.99 zoom. This artificially small adjustment also shows how much Reframe hammers the image since all pixels need to be redrawn, but it’s much easier to compare directly to source than if I was wildly swinging the camera around. If you want to do your own tests I would recommend a tiny adjustment like this to make comparisons easier.

This is technically very sophisticated, and the part where you can just drag your mouse, or finger, around to move things is pretty neat. Unfortunately, my critique of the control scheme is that people can’t quite do the kinds of recomposition that they might want to do to a photo from a 2D perspective. “Move this person to the left” has to be “Move the camera around this person” instead.

Here’s my partner Jason in front of Tower Bridge in London. I like the photo just fine, no regrets, but it’s arguable that it would have been helped if Jason was standing slightly to screen right. These controls can’t move Jason. If I shift the perspective until Jason’s body is no longer overlapping with Tower Bridge then Jason is no longer facing the camera, and we’re looking at him from a three-quarter view instead of front on.

I struggle to think of a use case for orbiting around a person unless you’re Michael Bay.

In another example, where I took a selfie of Jason and me at the Eiffel Tower, I tried to use Reframe to make it look like less of a selfie (again, I don’t care that it looks like a selfie, but I know normal people will do these things). I’m not swinging wildly off axis, but more of the background is revealed from parallax, and not sourced from context. Most importantly, Reframe caught my knuckles and turned them into some kind of cotton candy cancer.

Big nope. Surely, I can use Clean Up to remove my knuckles?

Clean Up re-up

The new Clean Up is not what I would consider to be two years better than the original Clean Up. It couldn’t paint my knuckles out without inserting a flesh-colored seam in the shoulder, or other streak artifacts. I don’t understand why this is quite so bad at simple requests.

But it turns out that there are two Clean Ups: when the Image Quality is set to Fast and when it’s set to High Quality. (There’s also an “Auto” setting that usually gave me Fast results.) The High Quality pass involves using a server-based model, so it’s slower… but it’s also much better.

A flaw in both Clean Ups is that there’s image segmentation that tries to intelligently only select the hand I want to remove, which always leaves a few pink pixels where the hand pixels are at their thinnest just as they disappear over the shoulder edge. I had to hit that with another round of paint. This isn’t a model limitation, like when Fast Clean Up added pink pixels; this is a selection issue.

The good news is that Clean Up is the only generative tool in Photos that doesn’t alter the entire image. It does seem to dilate out from the paint operation and blend back to the photo, so the trees above my hand shift, but that’s more in line with what I would expect from this tool than what Extend and Reframe do.

It would be nice if I could more precisely paint where I wanted it to work, not where I wanted it to selectively decide to work, though.

Crop shop image plops

The concerns I have about unnecessary modification to original pixels are not the kinds of things that everyone in the general public would notice or object to. It might look a little shifted, but they just wanted this for some lock screen, photo frame, or highly compressed Instagram carousel. I do think it’s up to Apple to do its best since there is no technical reason for Apple not to.

The real obstacle for most people will be tool use.

Providing these individualized models to people that have some overlapping function exposes the models Apple has ready to ship, not the workflow it sees people using. (The most basic example being the need to provide a one-stop shop for cropping and composition tools.)

I would also remind Apple that it doesn’t ship a competitive set of tools for boring, deterministic, 2D operations like straightening, perspective operations, and subject-aware cropping. How many times have we collectively clicked the “auto” button in the Crop panel and it didn’t do what we wanted?

Why are we fighting with center-weighted vertical and horizontal perspective tilt operations instead of having an automated perspective adjustment like Lightroom? Instead, we have an assortment of nondeterministic image diffusion models running on servers, which is way more complicated. We can’t just hit a button to fix some skewing lines with a simple 2D operation? Something that doesn’t put the scarlet letters “AI” on the image?

I get it that generative models sound fancy, but this is for a public that is not going to scrutinize the tools as much as image-editing nerds are. The tools aren’t good enough just because normal people can’t tell how much of their original image was destroyed. I know that Apple wants these tools to seem magical, but they’re all still kind of just demos that have escaped containment. I’m not sure they solve as many real-world problems as Apple would like them to.

  1. Provenance is really important and I’m glad that Apple added a way to identify synthetic images, but it doesn’t disclose that to users. A support document says that users can verify SynthID at synthid.com, but there’s nothing in the interface that communicates this. ↩

item.content:encoded:
Why: Microsoft's agent framework package was compromised to steal cloud credentials, a supply chain lesson. (score 8)

From The Hacker News.

Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido, Chainguard, Endor Labs, OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Google-owned Wiz.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access.

Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python.

"Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report.

Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported.

"Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs said. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework."

The names of the .pth files are below -

  • agent_framework_meta.pth in version 1.26.1
  • af_runtime_diag.pth in version 1.26.2

The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then launches the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data -

  • Environment variables based on substring-based matching
  • Credential files associated with Azure CLI (~/.azure/*.json), .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, Hugging Face, Microsoft Azure DevOps agents, and .env and JSON files
  • Azure DevOps OIDC tokens
  • Azure managed-identity tokens
  • Azure instance metadata and retains up to 8,000 characters of the response

"Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue new ones," SafeDep said. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those."

"In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata."

It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service (IMDS) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token.

All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb").

Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables.

Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps -

  • Isolate affected hosts and runners
  • Pin the package to the most recent safe version (1.26.0) and restore from a clean environment
  • Check for exposure to the malicious versions between 8:35 and roughly 9:20 p.m. UTC on November 17, 2026
  • Search proxy and DNS logs for requests to webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb
  • Rotate exposed credentials from a clean system
  • Audit Azure identities and review sign-in and activity logs
  • Audit GitHub Actions workflows that deploy to Azure

"The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside."

Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year. In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm.

Google News,

item.title: In the Microsoft employee price list, why did the BASIC compiler cost less than the BASIC interpreter?
item.author: The Old New Thing
item.description:
Why: Raymond Chen on Microsoft history and pricing, right up your alley. (score 8)

From The Old New Thing.

Understanding the pricing scheme. The post In the Microsoft employee price list, why did the BASIC compiler cost less than the BASIC interpreter? appeared first on The Old New Thing .
item.content:encoded:
Why: Raymond Chen on Microsoft history and pricing, right up your alley. (score 8)

From The Old New Thing.

One of the questions in response to the Microsoft employee price list from 1987 came from Peter Cooper Jr.:

Why is the MS-DOS BASIC Compiler cheaper than the MS-DOS BASIC Interpreter?

That’s a good question. You’d think that since the compiler is more powerful, it should cost more.

And it probably did cost more in stores.

But this is the employee price list, and the policy for employee pricing at the time was to charge for cost of goods plus some administrative overhead for running the employee software program itself.¹

I don’t know why the MS-DOS BASIC Compiler packaged product cost less to produce than the MS-DOS BASIC Interpreter, but I can guess.

I bet the manual is thinner.

The compiler product assumes you don’t need a tutorial on the BASIC language itself. The compiler manual concerns itself with instructions on how to run the compiler and details on how the compiled version of the language differs from the interpreted version. (For example, there may be some interpreter features that aren’t supported. Or there may be special comments you can put in your program that are used as directives to the compiler itself and which are ignored by the interpreter.)

A thinner manual requires less paper and a smaller box, and it weighs less, which means that it costs less to produce, ship, and store.

¹ This is no longer the policy for employee pricing. Employees can no longer, say, get Windows Server Datacenter Edition for the price of a cardboard box and a DVD.

The post In the Microsoft employee price list, why did the BASIC compiler cost less than the BASIC interpreter? appeared first on The Old New Thing.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber commentary on the Nvidia leadership drama. (score 7)

From Daring Fireball.

Jensen Huang, on X yesterday, hours before Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report:

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Doing this in public is pathetic. There are in fact a lot of simps out there — largely on X — clamoring for Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang. Here, for example, is Jason Calacanis, who works as David Sacks’s pool boy:

China Hawks are going to get a chip ban, and Americans are going to get a recession.

To believe Calacanis, the only thing holding up the entire U.S. economy is Nvidia’s chip sales into China in violation of national security law. This, too, is a pathetic opinion to express in public.

All of these bring-back-Jensen stans are stuck in the denial stage of grief. The national security China hawks won. It’s over. Huang is out, done in by his own staggering hubris. Huang’s miscalculation was that after his side lost the debate over what U.S. national security policy should be regarding AI chip sales to China, he wrongly presumed Nvidia could just ignore the spirit, if not the letter, of the law and just sell banned Nvidia chips into China anyway, because he had Trump on his side. That cronyism had won out, and if you had Trump on your side, you could do whatever you wanted. People who think this way often overestimate the permanence of their erosions of the rule of law and liberal democracy. The Nazis thought the Third Reich would last 1,000 years — it lasted 12.

Turns out U.S. national security officials still run U.S. national security policy. Turns out Democrats weren’t out of power in Congress for long.

Link: x.com/JensenHuang/status/2122726005219737649

item.content:encoded:
Why: Big Think essay on awe and consciousness fits your big ideas interest. (score 7)

From Big Think.

Years ago on the way to New Zealand for my doctoral studies, I stopped in Los Angeles to visit a friend. He organized a trip to Joshua Tree, where we hiked and camped. Come nightfall, I gazed at the stars and clouds — or so I thought. My friend pointed out that the cloudcover was, in fact, the Milky Way. 

I didn’t realize our galaxy was ever visible to the naked eye, and I was deeply moved. The vast stillness of the desert, the free-roaming coyotes and the thick blanket of stars reminded me that we humans are only a tiny part of it all, yet also unbreakably connected to this stretching, expansive universe. More than a decade later, the awe of that experience remains important and vivid in my life.

Now, as a psychological scientist, I study awe for a living. Last summer, my colleagues and I asked 200 people in the UK to document their encounters with awe over six weeks. Because such experiences are often linked to a sense of purpose and flourishing, we wanted to know what mattered more: their frequency or intensity.

What we found surprised us. As we’ll explain in a forthcoming John Templeton Foundation-supported paper, those who experienced moments of awe that induced strong feelings of amazement and wonder reported a greater sense of meaning and wellbeing by the study’s end. It wasn’t how often people felt awe that mattered, but whether they had an experience which strongly evoked it.

What, exactly, happens to us when we experience awe, and what makes the feeling so significant, in such a lasting way?

We researchers know that it has something to do with feeling simultaneously small and connected to something larger. During awe, analytical thinking recedes; we simply experience, transcending the cerebral way in which we ordinarily engage with the world.

After years investigating this phenomenon, I’ve come to believe that awe offers a window into an overlooked aspect of human consciousness — one of science’s most elusive mysteries. If we can isolate and study the state of awe and similar self-transcendent experiences, we might deepen our understanding of our species, and of how we experience the world.

The problem with the thinking mind

When we think of consciousness, we imagine a conscious voice that says, “This is now” —  an idea that goes back at least as far as the 17th-century French philosopher René Descartes, who famously stated, “I think, therefore I am.” But what if this thinking (literally) has led us astray?

My inquiry into consciousness started in 2015, when I began researching analytical versus intuitive thinking. Having trained as a cognitive neuroscientist during my PhD at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, I’d always prioritized the rational mind, dismissing intuition as a lesser agency — one reserved for guessing games or New Age spirituality. It’s a predictable bias: Since Descartes, the Enlightenment and the Scientific Revolution, much of Western culture has privileged logic over the supposedly mercurial feelings of the body.

It wasn’t until I began working with Dr. Miguel Farias on the psychology of religion and spirituality that I questioned my assumptions about intuition. Our research challenged the idea that religious belief is necessarily rooted in intuitive rather than analytical thinking, and made me reconsider whether the preference for rational thought might be limiting how we understand the human mind. Even for an academic like me, who saw the body mostly as a way to transport my brain from place to place, experiences of awe like the one I had at Joshua Tree seemed too consequential to ignore. 

Research suggests that intuition plays an important role in how we perceive the world and make decisions, even when we’re not consciously aware of the processes guiding us. In a foundational study, neuroscientists Antoine Bechara, Antonio Damasio and their colleagues asked participants to choose cards from four decks — two advantageous and two disadvantageous. They found that subjects began showing subtle physiological signs of stress when approaching the unfavorable decks, even before they could consciously identify them as risky. The researchers interpreted these findings as evidence that the body can influence decisions before we can consciously explain them.

Psychologist Jonathan Haidt has made a similar argument about moral judgment, likening the rational mind to a press secretary: Rather than making decisions, the brain may simply explain and justify conclusions we’ve already reached intuitively. In a way it makes sense: Working memory, which supports analytical thinking, has a limited capacity. Yet there is a whole world around us that we need to take in, which the body does holistically through its various senses.

For me, these findings raised a larger question: How much of our experience of the world unfolds beyond the reach of reflective thought? And if we fail to fully study this intuitive, non-reflective dimension of our minds, how complete can our understanding of consciousness really be?

The self that thinking cannot capture

This question brought me back to an idea proposed more than a century ago by William James, widely regarded as the father of modern psychology. In his 1892 text, Psychology: Briefer Course, James distinguished between two aspects of the self, which he called the “Me” and the “I”:

“Whatever I may be thinking of, I am always at the same time more or less aware of myself, of my personal existence. At the same time it is I who am aware; so that the total self of me, being as it were duplex, partly known and partly knower, partly object and partly subject, must have two aspects discriminated in it, of which for shortness we may call one the Me and the other the I.”

In line with philosophical discussions, I developed modern definitions for the two aspects of James’s “total self.” His “Me” is what I call the reflective self-state: conscious awareness, where we think about ourselves, reflect on what we are doing or have done, interpret how we are perceived, and so on. It’s the type of thinking that can be described in language, and thus be made explicit. James’s “I” is what I have come to think of as the experiential self-state: the part of us that simply is — in the here and now, as a sensing entity. 

The experiential self-state is difficult to describe, because the moment we try to put it into words we shift toward the reflective self-state, making ourselves the object of our attention once again. But this doesn’t mean the experiential self is simply an absence of thought or intention. Rather, it’s a form of awareness in which bodily sensations, emotions and sensory information come together to guide our perceptions and responses, without deliberate thought. Deep meditation offers a useful example of the experiential self-state, as does awe.

What science might be missing about awe

This distinction between reflective and experiential awareness could help resolve a longstanding puzzle in the study of awe itself. To measure the awe we feel during concerts, psychedelic trips, collective rituals, mystical encounters and the like, researchers use the Awe Experience Scale (AWE-S), a survey tool developed by Johns Hopkins University psychologist David Yaden and his colleagues. 

I’ve used this scale extensively in my own research, and encountered a recurring puzzle. Participants sometimes describe feeling small or insignificant during awe, as I did at Joshua Tree, only for that sensation to give way to an overwhelming sense of connection. I wonder whether retrospective surveys capture this lasting connectedness more readily than the fleeting feeling of self-diminishment.

If so, it could be problematic. For example, in one study of nearly 500 ravegoers, my colleagues and I found that connectedness predicted how transformative participants considered their experiences, while self-diminishment did not. I suspect these seemingly contradictory sensations — feeling small yet big — may occur in a specific temporal sequence, such that feelings of connectedness remain, to the time of a survey, whereas self-diminishment does not.

My dual self-states theory offers a helpful framework: As the reflective self recedes, the experiential self becomes more prominent. Rather than contradicting each other, feelings of self-diminishment and connectedness may reflect two crucial dimensions of consciousness. As we become less focused on ourselves, this allows us to become more immersed in sensory experience, after the perceived boundaries between ourselves and the world begin to dissolve.

This distinction matters, because the way we measure awe determines what we can understand about it. If we capture only the sense of connectedness that people remember afterward, we may overlook the changes in self-awareness that unfold during the experience itself. Studying how these two self-states interact in real time could reveal not only what awe feels like, but also how it shapes and enriches our experience of the world and even the universe.

New windows into what it means to be human

Awe, meditation, and other self-transcendent experiences should not elude scientific inquiry simply because they are difficult to describe. I propose developing a psychological scale to measure the experiential self-state, so we can better understand these experiences.

Doing so would help us investigate experiences often described as ineffable, or beyond words, and ask more precise questions about powerful moments of awe that seem to deepen our sense of purpose and well-being: When does self-focused thought diminish, and when does a sense of connection emerge? Do bodily boundaries become less distinct? How do bodily signals shape our judgments before we can put reasons into words? And could becoming more attuned to these signals help us use them more effectively?

Perhaps the moments when we are least focused on ourselves — whether we are lost in music or immersed in nature — offer some of our best opportunities to understand what it truly means to be conscious.

This article was developed in partnership with the John Templeton Foundation.

The most transformative discoveries often begin by questioning the boundaries of what we think we know. The John Templeton Foundation’s Future of Intelligence venture supports research and dialogue that challenge what was once taken for granted: What is intelligence, and what might our conventional definitions miss in the worlds of plants, the cosmos, and AI? Learn more, apply for a grant, and sign up for the newsletter here.

This article The surprising science of awe — and what it reveals about consciousness is featured on Big Think.
