item.content:encoded:
Why: McGilchrist on the brain and consciousness, a big-ideas interview. (score 7)

From Big Think.

This content is locked. Please login or become a member.

Psychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent 35 years studying how the brain shapes consciousness. In this full interview, he explains why the two hemispheres attend to the world in radically different ways, and how one narrow, grasping mode has come to dominate Western civilization. He then explores the nature of reality: a creative cosmos that flows at the edge of chaos, where consciousness is primary and matter is one of its phases. He closes with what makes a human life flourish.

IAIN MCGILCHRIST: One thing one can say about the cosmos, pretty much without fear of contradiction, is that it is creative. It begins, we are told, with this very simple compact mass and then has expanded into the vast universe that we are still exploring and in which there is so much complexity unfolding. This seems to be key to the nature of everything that exists.

When it comes to the brain and the ability to understand the creative nature of the cosmos, the right hemisphere alone sees it.

I really argue very strongly that unless we take seriously the demonstrable differences — anatomical, physiological, neuropsychological — between these two hemispheres, unless we take that seriously, we're missing something that is at the core of our being.

My name's Iain McGilchrist, and I've spent the best part of 35 years studying how consciousness is structured by the brain.

Part 1: Our brain hemispheres and their split worlds.

Chapter 1: What do we get wrong about the left and right hemispheres?

Everybody thinks they know what the real differences between the right and left hemisphere are. Because in the 1980s, 90s, there was a lot of loose talk about what the differences were. And you know, the left hemisphere was a little bit boring, but down to earth, reliable and really intelligent. Whereas the right hemisphere was a bit airy-fairy and sort of creative, but unreliable. Everything in that is wrong.

So, first thing that I would say about the differences between the hemispheres is that there is absolutely no question that they're there and that they're important. This is a vital thing to say because once people realized that the pop psychology on this topic emanating at the end of the 20th century was wrong, they simply gave up the topic altogether as a bad job and decided that since we knew that both hemispheres were involved in everything, there were no differences. But that's quite illogical. Just because they're both involved in something doesn't mean to say that they do things the same way. They importantly don't. It wasn't the what of what they did, it was the how. And by the how, I don't mean by what mechanism, I mean the manner in which they approached what they were doing.

I think I've always been very interested in ideas. That's my probably greatest motivation. So I wanted to read theology and philosophy at Oxford, and I went to all the philosophy seminars on the mind-body problem, which had obsessed me since studying English, because it seemed to me that what happened in the seminar room when people approached the work of literature was that it became suddenly terrifically abstract and disembodied.

And in that time, almost by accident, I went one afternoon, I almost didn't, but I'm glad, very, very glad I did. I went to a lecture at the Institute of Psychiatry in London where I was training. And it was by a man I didn't know called John Cutting, who was a consultant at the Maudsley Hospital. And he'd just published a book called "The Right Cerebral Hemisphere and Psychiatric Disorders." And I was just intrigued because I'd not heard much about the right cerebral hemisphere. Nobody really knew what it did. And here was a man who'd written a long and learned book about all the things that the right hemisphere of the brain does do. And when I heard him talking that afternoon, my life was transformed. The direction of my life was changed.

Because I heard him talking about what the right hemisphere is able to do. And he — he said three things that immediately struck me. One is that the right hemisphere understands implicit meaning, whereas the left hemisphere takes everything at face value and entirely explicitly. So it doesn't understand poetry, doesn't understand metaphor, doesn't have a sense of humor, sarcasm, irony, all those things that make the art of literature alive. That was one.

The second was that the right hemisphere had closer and more profuse connections, intimate connections with the body than the left hemisphere.

And the third was that the right hemisphere understood the unique case, whereas the left hemisphere always saw something as an example of a kind, of a general type. It made the unique general, it took everything out of context, and that context was partly the body, and it made the implicit explicit, and its power suddenly vanished. It's like explaining a joke. Once you've explained it, it's not funny anymore. Once you've ripped a poem apart, it's not a poem anymore. And so the right hemisphere is the one that actually enables us to understand what's going on in the world.

Chapter 2: Why are the left and right hemispheres different?

First of all, there is the question, why are they divided? Because after all, the brain is just a mass of interconnected nerve cells or neurons. The number of neurons and the number of connections gives you an idea of how powerful they are. They have a band of fibers at the base of the brain called the corpus callosum. Only 2% of neurons actually cross that commissure, and a lot of the traffic is inhibitory. It's going from one hemisphere to the other and saying, you keep out of this, I'm dealing with it. What's that about?

They have differences in physiology, so they react differently to endocrine hormones, they use different neurotransmitters, or at least different preponderances of those neurotransmitters. They respond differently to drugs. And they are massively different in the ways in which they construe reality. And that is the bit that really interests me.

So why are there all those differences? Because ultimately they need to see the world differently. Every creature has to solve the ultimate conundrum of survival, how to eat without being eaten. And that is much harder than it sounds because to eat, you have to be able to look out for things that will grab your attention. Yes. Yes, that, yes. So you have to be locked onto a small target, and you have to be able to see it with great precision as a detail that you know where to get it very quickly. So all that attention is locked on to a tiny detail that is not part of a big picture that makes any sense. It's just a seed, a worm. As creatures have become more complicated, they can be things like, for a bird, picking up a twig to build a nest or whatever it might be. And in humans, it becomes fashioning a tool. So all that is the left hemisphere's job.

But if that's the only kind of attention a creature pays, it will not last longer than a few minutes, because it has to be looking out at the same time for a predator. It has to be looking out for its mate, for its kin. These are key elements of the survival of any creature.

And so the solution is that there must be two neuronal masses, each of them complex enough to sustain consciousness and attend to the world, but in two utterly different ways. One with this detailed, focused attention to a tiny particle, and the other completely differently, a broad, open, sustained, vigilant attention for anything, without any preconception as to what it might be.

Now what this means, since how we attend to the world changes what we find there — if you're attending to something and looking just for one thing, you'll only see that one thing — that means that if these two hemispheres are attending quite differently, they will find different worlds. What are those two worlds like?

Chapter 3: What two worlds do the hemispheres see?

I sometimes think, suppose I'd never seen a motorbike before. Somebody produced a motorbike and perhaps I'd never seen a machine of its kind at all. And I think, sort of, well, how do I understand this? With my left hemisphere, I said, right, I'm going to take it into the garage and I'm going to lie it on its side and I'm going to unscrew all those bolts and separate all the parts and count. We've got 15 of those and three of those and one of those and one of those. That's what a motorbike is. That is, as it were, a parody of the left hemisphere's attempt to understand it. But the right hemisphere's attempt would be, I'm going to get on this thing and ride it. And it's only in the riding of it that you understand what it is.

In the case of the left hemisphere, there's a world of bits. None of them mean anything on their own except they're useful. You want them. And they're decontextualized, they're abstract, they're non-unique, they're just another seed, another worm, whatever it is. And they're just stuff. And the whole drive is to amass more stuff. That's its only value is to get, get, get. Grab, grab, grab.

Meanwhile, the right hemisphere is seeing another world, which is not made up of things that are certain and fixed, as they are in the left hemisphere, but may be something other than what you expect. These are things that change with context. The context changes everything. They're things that may well be implicit, and if we don't see them, we're missing most of what is important. The things that give life meaning and are massively important to us are things like love, friendship, sex, religion, art, poetry, music, ritual, narrative. All these things depend on being implicit. You can make them explicit, but when you've made them explicit, they become something else. And often you just fail to grasp what it was that you were trying to express. So the right hemisphere picture is massively more imaginatively rich and intelligently understood than that of the left hemisphere, which is just, oh yeah, more stuff, I'll have that.

This is really, really crucial. Emotional and social intelligence, cognitive intelligence, creativity, all those are better done by the right hemisphere. But there is one category, apprehension, grasping things, say, I've got it. That one thing is so much better in the left hemisphere that it explains why the left hemisphere has developed just to do that one thing, getting stuff without which we can't survive. But all the understanding, the intelligence is in the right hemisphere.

But, you know, for me, just going about my ordinary life, why would I need to know that? I mean, why do I, as long as my brain's working, I don't care where it's going on. But there is an important payoff, and it's this, that we can tell when people have arrived at a conclusion using the typical mode of understanding of the left hemisphere. And we can tell when they've used the typical mode of understanding of the right hemisphere. And we can now say that the conclusion according to the left hemisphere mode is much less likely to be true to reality than the way of understanding that comes with the right hemisphere.

Part 2: Where our left brain has led us.

Chapter 4: What kind of society have we created?

People say, you seem to argue we've lost the ability to use the right hemisphere. And I say, no, no, no, no. It's just there. We're just not using it. You can use it right now. And in that sense, it is like a radio set. You know, I can imagine if you bought one, and when you first get it, you tune into two channels. This is great. And then after a while, you start listening only to one. If you decided you missed the other channel, you don't have to buy a new set. It's still there. So we can always tune back into these things.

Einstein said, "The rational mind is a faithful servant. The intuitive mind is a precious gift. We live in a world that honors the servant but has forgotten the gift." So the left hemisphere has something definitely to offer. It's just that when it thinks it understands the whole picture, it very definitely doesn't, and it leads us astray.

And what I think I have been able to see is that three times a civilization seems to have moved from a position in which it was benefiting from the best that can be offered by both the left and the right hemisphere. Around the 6th century BC in Athens, around the year dot in Rome, at the end of the Republic and the beginning of the Empire, and then again in Western Europe, perhaps in the 15th century, roughly speaking. The beginnings of the Renaissance. So these were three periods in which, in each case, there was an enormous, sudden step forward in the arts, in drama, in music, in poetry, in architecture, but also in science, in maths, in mapping the heavens, in mapping the Earth. And that impetus toward something wonderful lasted for usually two or three hundred years, but gradually decayed in every case into a society that was dominated by a very crude vision, and that crude vision is that of the left hemisphere.

But then the question arises, why? And I think the answer is this. It's something to do with the size of a society. It's very hard for us now to realize how small ancient Athens was. It was a small community. So people knew one another. And then through trade, it expanded, it had colonies and so forth. Now, that's just one strand, but it's an important strand. Because what it means is that something that was tailor-made for a small group of people gets formularized, if I can put it in that way, and is, as we now put it, rolled out as a single blanket answer to government. So enormous bureaucracies that follow rules set at the center and are dealing with situations at the periphery that are completely different from those for which this set of rules was devised.

And I talk about ways in which we dealt more and more in concepts, not in embodied realities, in abstractions. Indeed, one of the interesting things is the advent of money, which are tokens that stand for real things. But these are virtual, interchangeable, very left-hemisphere tokens for things.

But another is this. When a society begins to develop a formal philosophy, not in the way that in the East this happened, but the sayings of a few sages, but actually people debating. So is this right or is that right? And what do you think and so on? Now, when you get that, what tends to happen is you move into left-hemisphere mode because the left hemisphere tends to say, well, they can't both be right. One of these has got to be right. Now, ancient wisdom, both West and East, says that very often both of these things need to be validated because both of them can be true. They depend on the context. But what you get is that one must triumph over the other. And this process leads to becoming rigid of the way of thinking and abstraction in the way of thinking. And soon you're in a world where everything is decided by chopping logic. That's what happened.

And I think that in our own case, it was massively accelerated by three things, really. First was the so-called scientific revolution at the end of the 17th century, in which people began to think, actually, science can answer all our questions. And, of course, what was wonderful is that science was beginning to give very good answers to all sorts of things that we hadn't known before. And, you know, it's not surprising that if you were alive at that time and involved in the process, you'd jump quickly to the conclusion that science can answer all our questions. Subsequent history has revealed that that actually is never going to be the case.

Then there was an extension of that, which was the Enlightenment. So the 18th century philosophers who believed once again that the answers to all questions were coherent with one another, could be argued for in such a way that you could present them on a piece of paper to another person and they understood it completely.

Then there came the Industrial Revolution, and the Industrial Revolution was a perfect example of the externalization of the left hemisphere's mode. We need more and more power, and we need more and more stuff, and we now have machines that can make it faster. More than our greatest dreams can be realized by amassing stuff and exploiting people to work for gain, for me. It's so very left-hemispheric. The Industrial Revolution exemplified this drive towards the mechanistic, the analytical, the amassing of stuff.

And then in the 20th century, we had these movements in ideas that got us further and further away from reality. The denial that there was any reality, that there was any truth, that there was any beauty, that there was any real goodness. And that corrosive cynicism destroyed art, destroyed the cohesion of a good society, and we're reaping the benefits of it now.

And what I think excites me is that I believe I can see in the reactions, principally of young people, that they feel they've been sold a pup, that they've been taught something that cannot be right. They've been shortchanged by this ridiculously crude philosophy that it's all just stuff without any meaning. And they're beginning to see the places where meaning can be found.

And sometimes you have to look back in order to look forward. So it's not bad to realize what is it we've lost. And sometimes you only see what you've lost by reading the literature, looking at the art and understanding something of the history of where you've come from. After all, the Renaissance, which was the biggest step forward in the history of the West, was a rebirth. That's what the word, of course, means. And it happened because people look back to the ancient world. They didn't try and reinvent Greece and Rome. That's impossible. Don't worry. But what they did see was what was missing, and they found it and moved forward. That's the hope for our future, I believe.

Chapter 5: How can we perceive reality using both hemispheres?

How do we tell, especially if our brains are capable of telling us two quite different things about the world we're experiencing, how can we tell which is the better guide to reality? And how can we formulate what that reality is like?

And I think that's so important because during my lifetime, I have seen the three great values which have always inspired me, and as I get older, seem to me of absolutely critical importance, namely goodness, beauty, and truth. In my lifetime, I've seen them all travested. I've seen goodness reduced to having the right received opinions, ticking boxes. I've seen beauty scorned by artists themselves. During my lifetime most artists didn't want their work to be called beautiful, they wanted it to be called powerful. And I thought, no, that is no way to respond to how the experience of living teaches one about these great things, goodness, beauty and truth.

And so I wanted to work from the brain, explaining what the left and right hemispheres can do and contribute, then going to what's known as epistemology, i.e. the paths to truth, which I took to be reason and science, intuition and imagination. And I do think we do need to use all of them.

And the first thing that I want to stress is that science itself does not simply draw on reason, it draws very strongly on intuition. Practically all its great discoveries were made intuitively. So don't feel worried about intuition. Intuition is a very good guide. Of course it can be mistaken. And so philosophers have devised what I call intuitive illusions.

So, for example, I can show you an optical illusion, which is very hard to believe. It involves a checkerboard in which two squares that look obviously quite different colors are actually the same color and can be demonstrated to be so. So sometimes your eyes, by devising a very clever specialist illusion, can be made to deceive you. But I never knew anybody who, after seeing it, said, oh, well, that does it. From now on, I'm never going to use my eyes. I'm just going to lead my life with my eyes closed. Of course not. It would be idiotic. And the same is true of intuition. If you really want to be a dunce, then do away with your intuition. But that intuition needs to be tempered with reason and with what science tells us. These things need to work hand in hand. But above all, they all need to work under the superintendence of imagination.

And perhaps I should just say something about the nature of imagination. Imagination is not fantasy, it is in some ways the exact opposite, because fantasy is what leads you away from reality, whereas imagination is what gives you the only chance you have of entering into the depth of reality. So, for example, a fantasy will make you see an aristocrat playing in a play dressed up as a shepherd, as a shepherd. But it's not a shepherd. It's whoever it is, the lord of whatever. So that is fantasy, is make-believe, when you play a little game. But imagination is nothing like that. Imagination is what enabled Wordsworth to steal his way into something as banal as the great outcrop of rock, and to see it suddenly as if for the first time, to see it as almost alive, to see it as powerful.

Now, I think that seeing the world as alive is by no means a deceit. I have, since my teens, not been able to believe that the world out there, for example, the fields, the trees, the streams, the meadows, the hills in which I grew up, were just stuff that had no anything about it. It was just passively responding to chemicals. No, the world, especially the natural world, seems to me to speak. It was a two-way communication. It was speaking to me, I was speaking to it. And out of that encounter came what is.

Now that's an important point, that everything that we can know comes from an encounter. Something in me meets something that is not wholly something in me. So my consciousness contacts something that I didn't just create or dream up. And out of that coming together comes the world, the only world that I can know.

Part 3: The Nature of Reality

Chapter 6: What is the nature of reality?

One thing one can say about the cosmos, pretty much without fear of contradiction, is that it is creative. So it begins, we are told, with this very simple compact mass, and then has expanded into the vast universe that we are still exploring, and in which there is so much complexity unfolding. This seems to be key to the nature of everything that exists.

This idea that everything flows is an important part of this because there is a huge difference between a sequence of steps and a flow. The left hemisphere only understands things broken down into discrete steps, but the right hemisphere sees that they can't be broken down in this way and that something is lost when you do it. Now, literally, when people have damage to the right hemisphere, they see movement as jerky. So they begin to see things going doot, doot, doot, doot, doot, as though stop-go animation. So that is a key difference.

But why is that so important? Because when there are just steps, you can calculate what's happening next. But in flow, you can't. And there's a saying, a lovely thing, by one of the presidents of the Royal Society early in the 20th century, that in the next life there are two things I really want to understand. One is the quantum nature of reality, and the other is flow. About the quantum nature of reality, I feel confident. In other words, about flow, it's so complex, it is unfathomable.

And what really struck me was that if you take liquid flowing down an absolutely straight-sided channel, and you put into it at right angles a couple of rods that are rectangular in cross-section, you just bring them down into the flow, what do you get? The most incredibly beautiful thing that unfolds. It's almost impossible to describe. It looks like something that an Art Nouveau genius would have worked out. And it does have structure, but it is also very hard to see where this thing comes from. And it's called a Kármán vortex street. And sometimes these things occur in the ocean and can be seen from space.

In any case, the point is that you take something very predictable, even flow down a rigid channel with nothing else, two rods, and suddenly you've got something that is asymmetrical, complicated, beautiful, contains all kinds of elements, but it's not just random. And this was something that Leonardo knew. He sketched an old man with a stick, just putting his stick into water coming out of a sluice. And the amazing vortices that occurred because of it.

So flow is beautiful and orderly, but obeys rules that are so complex that we don't really know exactly what they are. And I believe are part of the fundamental operation of the universe at what is called the edge of chaos. In other words, order, but with enough uncertainty in it that it can't become entirely predictable. And the whole nature of reality is like this.

So in the 18th century, the French philosopher Laplace suggested that if you knew where every particle in the universe was, and you knew its momentum, you could predict every single thing that would happen in the universe thereafter. We now know that that is not correct. It's not just that we can never have enough information. It's that even if we had all the information that there was, we simply can't predict in the nature of things what is coming downstream.

Two physicists who corresponded with me about my work wrote to me and said, if you take the archetypal Laplacian notion of collision of particles, balls on a billiard table, we've done the calculations, and after a certain number of collisions on the billiard table, you won't be able to say which balls take part in which collision next. And I thought, gosh, that's interesting. So intrinsically, you can't know that. I wonder how many collisions that is, perhaps a million or a billion or something like that. And the answer is eight. It's eight collisions. So built deep into the everyday structure of reality, not at some fantastically unusual and remote level. Built into it is a degree of uncertainty along with an important degree of orderliness.

So, all reality operates at this level, but life crucially does. And how do these two things relate? Because out of life, out of simple shapes in life, come forth extraordinarily complex adaptations. And some of these beggar description. We have this idea of a cell, for example. Looks pretty simple structure. But get this, in the simplest cell, there are tens of thousands of complex cascades of interactions going on every second, and they interact with one another. So each pathway will complexly move across and interact with another pathway. This is something we can't begin to explain and map, but it is going on all the time. And the only way in which we can now see that it stays within certain bounds is that it is drawn towards certain form fields, if you like.

So what is life all about? First of all, let us have an idea of how complex it is. I've given you some idea of how complex the simplest kind of life is, a single cell. It's massively complex. Secondly, it doesn't disprove, of course, the second law of thermodynamics, which is that everything is running down, that all complex systems are becoming less complex. So what is required here is that for periods of time, a structure moves strongly in the opposite direction. So it requires incredible amounts of energy to become more complex. So simple structures become massively more complex. What is that drive towards greater complexity in a universe where everything is, so we're told, moving the other way, moving towards greater simplicity, the dissipation of complexity? And how is that energy harnessed, especially when, although there may be a benefit a long way down this cascade of things that are developing, there's none immediately?

So, for example, a good way of putting this is to take the example of the move from organisms in which there is parthenogenesis. There is only one sex and the same sex gives birth and that's it. But the movement to there being two sexes and the need to come together of two gametes in order for there to be new life was a development that was very costly. It was a risky thing because you had to get two versus just one. And they had to go through this process and that had to produce a result. Now, quite a long way down the line, this method of reproduction has plenty of advantages, which is why it has survived. But at the time it first developed, it had only disadvantages.

I'm only using that as a single example. But the whole story of life involves taking a step over a kind of hill. You can't see what's coming beyond, and why would you want to make a sacrifice to get there unless you could see that somehow it was going somewhere further and greater in the longer run? So the only thing that makes sense about life is that there is an allure that is drawing a process and saying never mind that this is costly now, it's coming to mean something in the longer run.

But that is not to say for a second that we're determined. I argue very strongly that we are not determined, but that nonetheless we are lured in certain directions. What we do about that is up to us. We can embrace it and find out where that goes and we won't know what it is until we have followed that path. Not only we know but the universe doesn't know. The universe hasn't got a little secret little thing, oh this is what you need to do today. No. But what it is saying is there are lures, things that are beautiful, good and true. And they act as like a, you know, a magnet that draws things, we are drawn towards these, or should be drawn towards these.

But the purpose thing is very important because it's been a kind of open secret amongst biologists that there's no way you can really make sense of biology except in terms of there being purposes, what Aristotle called final causes, which is not that there is some predetermined goal, but there is something ahead that is drawing you, an attractor that is drawing you in a certain direction. And exactly where that will go, nobody knows. I mean, not because we haven't got the information, but because it is, intrinsically, not known until it actually happens.

What underwrites what is? In other words, the answer to the question, why is there something rather than nothing, which seems to me the ultimate question that all philosophers are faced with. Something creative was, is, a ground of being, the grounds for the being. That's the simplest that we can say, the most accurate. And that brings into being something that has the capacity to enter into relationship with it.

Now, in all traditions I know of, the ground of being, whether it's called God, or it's called the Logos, or it's called li in Chinese, or rta in Sanskrit, ri in Zen, there are all these different words and they can't be short of slated because they basically mean the thing that grounds everything and gives it its form and its nature. And I believe it is relational. Everything that exists is relational. And that being is also relational. And in most of these traditions, what is said of that being is that it has, in some sense, the nature of love. And love is nothing if it is not reciprocal.

And importantly, this is a piece of wisdom that is ancient all around the world, that consciousness is a primary. It is what in Western parlance is called an ontological primitive, i.e. something that you cannot go behind or beyond in order to explain it. This has the implication that that consciousness is part of a much greater field of consciousness. And that is an important insight, it seems to me. Because we think of individual consciousnesses, they're not separate things floating around like balloons in air. They are part of the whole field of the air.

That suggests to me that matter, which as far as we know is also pretty much intrinsic to the cosmos from the start, has a profound relationship with consciousness, but the consciousness has always been there. The way I find it most comprehensible and most rational is that matter is a phase of consciousness. And by phase, I don't mean a temporal phase that comes later or earlier or anything like that. I mean phase in the way that physicists talk about water having phases.

What is water? I ask you, what is water? You say, well, it is translucent and transparent. It flows easily across my hand and so forth. That's true. But what is this other thing I've got here? It's absolutely opaque. It's white. It's solid. It won't go anywhere unless I give it a massive shove. Oh, that's water too. It's what we call ice. And then I'm told there are tons of water in this room. I can't see them, but unless there were those tons of water present and suspended in the air in this room, I and the film crew would not be alive. But that's water too. So it can appear very different and still be water. Now, to my view, consciousness can manifest as matter.

Why would it choose to do so? And here we come back to the creative nature of the cosmos. For creation, two things are required. One is resistance and the other is persistence. And what matter provides is a degree of resistance, a degree, and a degree of persistence.

So let me just say about resistance. Why is that necessary? I gave the example of how creation of the wonderful flows that I was talking about, like the Kármán vortex street, requires something obstructing the flow. And out of that obstruction of the flow comes something unimaginably beautiful and new. Also, it creates the possibility for things. So all creativity depends on the presence of something that causes resistance.

And this comes back to a beautiful image in the philosopher Schelling, the early 19th century German philosopher. He had lots of very interesting things to say, but one of the most interesting is this, that things come into being, and have the nature of a whirlpool, a vortex. And he gives this image of the whirlpool in a stream. So the flow of a stream is what it is and has the qualities that it has because of irregularities in the flow. And those irregularities are caused by the constraints of the water. The constraints cause, they're creative, they cause movement in that flow.

Now the thing about a whirlpool is this, it's totally real in the way that your reductionist scientist wants something to be real. I can photograph it. I can measure it. It has the power to move stones. It's totally real. But what is it? It's in the stream, but not in the stream in the way the stone's in the stream or a ball is in the stream or something. It is the stream at that point, at that time, while it exists. And water comes into it and water passes out of it. And sooner or later, that whirlpool will also pass away. And it will eventually. It came from water that comes from the sky, which takes water from all over the Earth. And it flows back eventually, inevitably into the sea.

So the stream, if you think of it instead, as a stream of soul that flows through the cosmos. And interestingly, Schelling talked about what he called the world soul, which he saw as a soul that flowed through the whole cosmos. Then our individual souls are not separate from that world soul. They're the form that world soul takes at that moment in that place, always continuous with the rest.

Chapter 7: How can human life flourish?

So, of course, you might ask the question, well, okay, that's why there's life. But why is there human life? And I think my answer to that is that it's an extension of the same argument of why there should be life. If the cosmos is essentially creative and reverberative, i.e. there are relationships in it and those relationships involve something as profound as a creative love, the coming into being of something, then what humans offer that perhaps no other animal offers to the same extent is a capacity to perceive, to reciprocate and to create love and beauty and goodness.

The flip side of that is that humanity, more than any other kind of creature, has the capacity to create the exact opposites. And that needs to be said. Because I'm not painting a picture of a la-la land in which everything is fine. Everything massively isn't fine. But on the other hand, I would go on to argue that ultimately what is beautiful and good triumphs over what is ugly and bad.

And one way of looking at this, this is quite simple, is that a wise and loving person can embrace hatred, neutralize it. But a hateful person, a person consumed with hatred, cannot embrace love. So love, in that sense, is stronger than hatred, can embrace it, and as it were, ingest it and sort of reform it. But hatred can't do that to love, not to true love. So in that sense, I think good can embrace ill. And make even something good come out of something that at the time seems impossibly destructive and bad. And such things, of course, exist. But something good can come out of it.

It is also true that something bad can come out of what we believe to be good. So we may have an obsession that a certain thing is good. And I see this around me now, that a lot of people, bien-pensant intellectuals, think X is very good. So we must have more and more of X. What they don't understand is that X is also tied to its opposite, Y. So they keep on pushing more and more and more of X, and finally they end up with having created Y, the thing that they actually didn't want at all. And this is perhaps something we should talk about, the coincidence of opposites.

A lovely Chinese story which I used to sometimes tell. There's a farmer, a poor man, and his most valuable possession is his horse. And he lives in a small village. And one day his horse wanders off. And they all go and look for this man's horse and they can't find it. And the neighbors commiserate with him and say, oh, what terrible luck. And the man says, well, good luck, bad luck, who knows. The next day, the horse comes back off the hillside and brings with it a horse that it has found there, that has become its mate, its friend, and it comes too. So everyone comes to him and says, wow, what good luck. And he says, well, good luck, bad luck, who knows. So his son gets on the new horse and tries to break it in, and in doing so is thrown from the horse. Breaks a leg. And everyone comes and says, oh, what bad luck. And the farmer says, well, you know, bad luck, good luck, who knows. And the next day, the imperial army's recruiters come through the village and take all the able-bodied young men away to war. But they leave him behind. And so you can imagine what the people in the village say.

So we don't know where things are going. But my point is a bigger one, that certain things can embrace other things. But nonetheless, we have to accept that both of them exist. And they exist in a sort of dance, which at the time that you're looking at, it may seem to be overweighed by what is bad or by what is good. I mean, in the 18th century, I think a lot of people would have lived and died satisfied that they felt that the world was moving in the right direction. I think now a lot of people would not feel that was so obviously the case.

So what gives rise to a flourishing, a truly flourishing human life? There are a number of bits of evidence, and they come together towards some more obvious and some less obvious conclusions. I think the ones that are very well validated, and they really are massively well validated in the psychology literature, are three things above all that lead to human flourishing.

The first is belonging to a small community, one where you know you can trust people, that you share their values, you have meals with them, you are in and out of one another's lives, you look after one another's families, you worship together. This is extraordinarily good for mental health and physical health of all beings.

The second is closeness to nature. Nature is a living creature. We are part of it. We come out of it and we go back to it and we should give back to it what it has given to us. Being close to nature, spending time in nature, even spending 20 minutes three times a week. Switching your phone off, being silent, being present in perhaps a park, or possibly, if you're lucky enough to have access to it somewhere, wilder than that.

And the third is feeling that you belong to a sacred cosmos. Now that may take the form of being religious in some way or it may not. It may be that you communicate with that cosmos through other things like through prayer, through meditation and so forth. But whatever it is, that sense of that something that is the bigger context, we get so left-hemisphere, but it's just this, look, I can take it apart and show you what it is. But that doesn't show you anything except some bits and pieces that have now been taken out of context. I don't know what they are. Anyway, so those are the three easy to understand, obvious elements.

But I'm very in awe of somebody who ought to be loved and respected by anybody interested in this area, who is the great Viktor Frankl, who was a psychoanalyst and psychologist and survived the Nazi concentration camps. I think all his family died in those camps. So, goodness me, he knew what suffering meant in a way that very few of us can. But he wrote a book called "Yes to Life in Spite of Everything," which is really a way of saying, yes, I know there's terrible things in the world, but there is something wonderful there that we must say yes to. And he actually included suffering as something that you wouldn't go out of your way to court, but that its presence or existence, at least for part of your life, even perhaps very terrible suffering, changes who you are, what you can be, and gives you a gift, which is that you can, as it were, receive, reverberate, retransmit some of these things.

And I've noticed that people who are healers, including, in fact, some of my colleagues, often have a history of personal suffering that is very important as a kind of way both of instilling understanding, instilling humility, instilling compassion. And if life doesn't have those things in it, then what are we doing here?

So these things, to me, are part of the answer of what the meaning of life is. And no, I can't write it down and hand it to someone else. You have to live it. And that is the secret, that it cannot be said in that way. The Tao Te Ching, the great testimony of Taoism, begins with the words, "The Tao that can be named is not the real Tao." And I like to couple that with St. Augustine, who said, "If you understand God, then it's not God you've understood." So these things are intrinsically beyond what they're really saying. It's beyond the left hemisphere's attempt to say finally what it is, write it down, give it a name. Then we've dealt with it. We can say, oh, now I know what it is. It's that. After all, put it in a little box.

No, it's got to — there is a lovely thing in the Judaic tradition. There are many wonderful things in their wisdom literature, but one is, you're not asked to find the solution to this problem, but you are not permitted to desist from the attempt to do so. That sums up for me the right approach of both the intellect and the spirit to this world. If we think we've got the answers, we've failed. They will be wrong. But we're also not permitted to go, oh, well, I don't know, I'm just going to go and have a burger. That is not the approach that is a wise one to adopt.

One video is just the beginning

Members go deeper — they get unlimited classes, early releases, zero ads, and our quarterly print issue.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Viticci's thorough rundown of the 27.3 beta 2: Duo face unlock, Mac privacy controls, and more. (score 8)

From MacStories. Also covered by Six Colors.

Apple’s developer betas this cycle have been packed with more features than usual and today’s second developer beta for 27.3 is no different. Let’s dig in.

The iPhone Duo gets a pair of changes in the latest developer beta that are likely to be crowd pleasers when 27.3 is released to the public. First, the Duo will be able to unlock quickly using the front-facing camera when it has been recently unlocked with Touch ID or a user’s passcode. The feature can be found in Settings -> Touch ID & Passcode and according to Max Weinbach, it uses the Secure Exclave to process the image used, which is how the HomeView works, too.

Touch ID will still be needed to use Apple Pay and access passwords. Additionally, Touch ID will be needed after roughly 45 minutes.

Second, if you want your iPhone Duo to lock when you fold it, like an iPad or Mac laptop, you’ll be able to turn that on, too, under Settings -> Display & Brightness. This isn’t something I expect I’ll turn on myself, but I know a lot of MacStories readers have wanted this, so I’m glad to see it added as an option.

Also, you may recall that Apple gave developers a vague heads-up about changes coming to Full Disk Access, which I wrote about at the time, and we discussed on AppStories recently. Today we got more information on what that means on Apple’s developer website:

In macOS 27.3 beta 2 today, we’re introducing increased transparency and more granular options for two of the APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk. These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.

In practice, this means that macOS 27.3 will split “Device Control and Data Access” in Settings into a two-part system that divides the world into Accessibility features for assistive technologies and “System & App Protection Override,” which lets users pick which apps an overriding app can control. In addition, Apple says the changes will include:

  • A single method for granting permissions by selecting the requesting app from a list
  • Guidance to encourage users to grant access to just the specific apps (for System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) that are required for their workflows
  • Increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted
  • The option for users to configure apps to ask every time they require access
  • A transparency indicator when a requesting app is controlling another app using System & App Protection Override

Also, it’s worth noting that Chance Miller of 9to5Mac says that Full Disk Access will remain available but that users will be steered toward using the new system.

I haven’t had a chance to try this yet, but it sounds like a reasonable solution that divides permissions into more sensible categories with better control and understanding over what privileges are being granted.

Siri is gaining the ability to see beyond the part of a webpage that is visible in Safari. Whatever’s below the fold of the page will be accessible whether you’re asking for a summary or requesting specific information at the end of a long page.

The Apple TV app is adding support for video podcast episodes, too. The feature will be available on the Apple TV 4K and supported iPhones, iPads, Macs, CarPlay-enabled vehicles, and smart TVs. I know you’ve always wanted to watch AppStories on your 90-inch TV, and soon, you can. Technology is incredible!

The puzzles in Apple News+ are popular in my household, and they’re coming to more countries. Apple News’ crosswords, Sudoku, Emoji Game, and more are coming to the Australian, UK, and French-Canadian editions of Apple News+ when 27.3 is released.

Of these, the Face Unlock feature is the one I’m most eager to try, but I’m also glad to see that Apple doesn’t appear to have made granting app and data privileges to apps too onerous. One thing’s for sure, beta season isn’t so much a season these days as it is a revolving door, and I love it.

item.content:encoded:
Why: California sues OpenAI after its agents escaped testing and hacked companies, a landmark AI security case. (score 8)

From The Verge.

California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.

California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents

OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.

The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.

After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber's commentary on Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon distancing from the administration. (score 7)

From Daring Fireball.

By John Gruber

Ivy: Plan. Do. Reflect.
The to-do list that ends.

  • Irish Goodbye / French Leave / Leave the English Way

  • Over the weekend I speculated that Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon have “made their Irish goodbyes” from the Trump 2.0 administration (including having no representatives on the David Sacks-led PCAST). I learned today that what we Americans call an “Irish goodbye” is called a “French leave” in the U.K., and “leaving the English way” in France. The rest of Europe is split between those two, but only Americans and Canadians call it an “Irish goodbye”. (And, somehow, the Germans call it “doing a Polish one”, which is not what I would guess that phrase means.)

    Anyway, I’ve got one friend who is an absolute master of the Irish goodbye. He never says goodnight or goodbye from a group gathering. He always just disappears. And even when you know he’s going to do it, and you start keeping an eye on him to catch him in the act, the fucker slips away every time. I find it delightful, not rude.

    ★ Monday, 16 November 2026

item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber digs into new Full Disk Access privacy controls, a real Mac security change. (score 7)

From Daring Fireball.

Remember a month ago when Apple announced, without any significant detail, that they would be changing the permission-granting UI for Full Disk Access to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action”? It’s launching today in developer beta 2 of MacOS 27.3. Chance Miller has a great overview at 9to5Mac:

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

  • Accessibility: Intended specifically for assistive technologies, with permissions handled through an entitlement process.

  • System and App Protection Override: A new category for apps that need to bypass certain macOS protections to control other apps or perform automated tasks.

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it requires access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

I’m installing it now, but from what I’ve seen so far, these changes not only alleviate my concerns that Apple might over-tighten the screws, I actually think they add clarity and give users more, not less, control over their Macs.

Link: 9to5mac.com/2026/11/16/macos-27-3-includes-new-privacy…

item.content:encoded:
Why: Thoughtful analysis of Nvidia's role financing the AI boom after Huang's exit. (score 7)

From Daring Fireball.

Ben Thompson at Stratechery:

This led to what I termed Nvidia’s Risky Business: Nvidia increasingly used its cash flow and credit rating to backstop and fund the companies who were buying its chips. Bears called this circular financing; bulls called it a necessary bridge to a future where AI revenue paid down these companies’ debt and drove massive upside. What is undoubtedly true is that this was the sort of risky business that is uniquely possible for a multi-trillion dollar company that is completely controlled by one man, who has made an entire career of pushing the limits and making risky bets — and seeing them pay off.

It’s also a series of bets that are unlikely to continue. The neoclouds should be very nervous about losing their patron, along with their creditors and equity holders. The other problem is that the revenue necessary to make all of this build-out work is something on the order of a trillion dollars industry-wide, and it needs to materialize sooner rather than later; if it falls short, it’s the hyperscalers who will prioritize their own compute first, and they will likely be seen as a safe haven for everyone committing to spending. In that world, Nvidia’s neocloud hedge — absent Huang’s willingness to shore the ecosystem up — is liable to turn into a millstone, with their assets flooding the market even as the supply chain ramp-up brings ever more supply to market.

This Nvidia crisis has made me think a lot about an item I recently posted, purely by coincidence: Charlie Munger’s 2020 take on Elon Musk and Tesla: “My thoughts are two. I would never buy it, and I would never sell it short.”

Munger used “it” in both clauses, but I think for the second one, what he really meant was that he wouldn’t short him. That he wouldn’t want to own Tesla stock (which, even today, trades at an absurd P/E ratio over 400), but he wouldn’t want to bet against Elon Musk.

I think the same thing is true for Nvidia. Nvidia in recent years made a lot of bets that investors normally wouldn’t back; but investors were willing to back Jensen Huang. Now Nvidia, the company, is left holding those risky bets and they don’t have Huang, the man, to make those bets feel like winners. I think investors are already looking at this very differently, and it’s why so many copium addicts are wailing like big babies about bringing Jensen back. Denial is the hardest stage of grief to move past.

Link: stratechery.com/2026/obituaries/

Microsoft (via Bob Burrough): We’re opening all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided […]
item.content:encoded:
Why: Exchange Online outage roundup, directly relevant to a Microsoft cloud PM. (score 7)

From Michael Tsai.

Microsoft (Hacker News):

We’re investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.

Microsoft (via Bob Burrough):

We’re opening all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief. We found a core process on affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, causing capacity loss. To validate a potential recovery, we're isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.

Zack Whittaker (USA Today, MacRumors):

What began as an Outlook email and Teams video conferencing outage soon developed into a full-blown meltdown affecting the company’s cloud services for both consumer and business email, files, and documents. The outage also knocked out the company’s Copilot AI tools and Defender security screening software, and prevented system administrators from accessing their internal Intune dashboards and features. Some users reportedly experienced issues with accessing their cloud-based Windows computers.

Microsoft hasn’t yet said what caused the issues, only saying the outage involved “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable.”

Ashley Belanger (Hacker News):

Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like “one of the biggest outages of all time,” Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even “worse,” he suggested.

Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC’s report documented various harms, noting that “few public bodies were immune from the outage.” In some cases, doctors couldn’t send patients “important” updates on medication changes or follow-up care.

[…]

This was not caused by increased traffic, Microsoft said, but “a problem that’s causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

Microsoft:

This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.

Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.

Heba Habib:

Goodwins said servers knocked offline usually attempt to reconnect so they can synchronise their files again. “As things come back up, they’re immediately swamped by the traffic from all the other servers desperate to talk to them. So it all falls down again,” he said.

[…]

Goodwins also said many experienced engineers have left Microsoft. “It’s not so much that there aren’t enough human eyes, but all the experienced people, the people who built the stuff up, have left,” he said. “There’s been a draining of corporate memory of how these systems are built up and how they work.”

Via Nick Heer:

Microsoft is so important to global digital infrastructure that catastrophic failure should be financially devastating. Yet it is precisely because it is so central that investors have barely blinked — it is currently trading about 4% below Monday’s high, and the biggest drops this week occurred before this outage.

It is not likely to lose a significant number of its customers, either, despite several outages this year.

Microsoft (MacRumors):

We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

The full the details aren’t on the public Web.

Richard Speed (Hacker News, Slashdot):

According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.

However, the testing wasn’t good enough. Microsoft’s report states: “Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores.” The defect caused “lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine’s resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted.”

“The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware.”

[…]

“Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state.” A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.

Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft’s words, “an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows.” The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

Tom Harrington:

Live your life in such a way that when a major hosting system goes down you only know about it from social network chatter.

Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess:

A prolonged outage of such a critical underlying digital service is not unprecedented, but Microsoft has a special position among cloud providers as an older company that was already ubiquitous in global computing from the PC era. Many organizations integrate Microsoft productivity services at the core of their operations, simply because they have used Windows computers for decades and have longstanding relationships with Microsoft.

[…]

During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships.

Miguel Arroz:

As much as I hate defending Microsoft… no, people didn’t end up intoxicated because of Microsoft.

People ended up intoxicated because someone decided it was a great idea to build a system that warns about dangerous toxic gas levels in the atmosphere… by email.

Don’t blame a communication system that was never meant for real-time communication not offers strong guarantees of delivery for the absolute negligence and incompetence of whoever designed this system.

See also: Mac Power Users Talk, Axel Rietschin, and Steven Sinofsky.

Previously:

  • Microsoft Workforce Buyouts Amid Record Revenue

item.content:encoded:
Why: Tsai's roundup of HomeView reviews, the best overview of Apple's new product. (score 7)

From Michael Tsai.

John Voorhees:

Apple HomeView reviews are out and it looks like a winner, especially for people already using other Apple products. Let’s look at what folks are saying.

Jason Snell:

I’ve wanted a product like the Apple HomeView for years now. After spending a lot of time with various personal assistant “smart speakers” in my kitchen—some with screens—I’ve never been more certain about the potential of the product category or more disappointed in the reality.

[…]

Given the fact that this product’s tech stack feels like it was created in a blender, it’s remarkable that it holds together as well as it does—but there are still places where the seams show.

[…]

It’s great that you can view iPhone widgets on the HomeView just as you can on the Mac, but it’s a bit frustrating that it will only display the small square widget style. Presumably because of the Apple Watch roots of some of these faces, there’s a surprising lack of digital clocks. In fact, in some face views you can create a face featuring a clock, but if you delete it, you can’t add it back. I admit to being frequently baffled about what I was able to add and customize, and what I wasn’t, when trying to build faces.

[…]

Siri AI isn’t as reliable as it should be, both in general and on the HomeView. Sometimes it just seems to go off in its own world and not respond, or respond accurately. Other times, it works just as advertised.

Joanna Stern (Slashdot):

I spent a week with it at the center of my household, putting those promises to the test with three challenges—including disguising myself as the dad from Apple’s own HomeView commercial.

John Gruber:

I plugged it in, set it up, got my wife and son to do what they needed to do to become recognized fellow-family-member users, and then we all collectively have had a week of “Well, now what?”

[…]

The software lacks cohesion and vision and polish.

Christian Selig:

The HomeView is really making me yearn for a more open version of this product, would be really cool to write custom software for this form factor

Tim Hardwick:

Just days after the HomeView’s launch, some owners are reporting problems with Siri, timers, and music playback on Apple’s new smart home hub, based on multiple MacRumors forum threads.

In the longest discussion, which now spans over one hundred posts, several people say their HomeView refuses to set timers or alarms, and instead claims that a software update is required – even though the device reports that it is up to date. In another thread, one poster said an AppleCare senior advisor told them other owners had reported the same problem, and that cold-rebooting their paired iPhone cleared it.

Benjamin Mayo:

You can long-press to make a text selection but there is literally nothing you can do with the text.

Christian Selig:

Early HomeView review: it becomes Lead HomePod and “eats” all the Hey Siri commands from the other devices and then does nothing. […] a few hours later it fixed itself and now responds to Siri!

Lex Friedman:

This is an unscientific comparison of response times for the Apple HomeView and the Amazon Echo Studio.

Dan Moren:

My HomeView hot take review, 24 hours in: it needs to get faster and more reliable at all the things my HomePod mini did before I trust it with anything else.

Mario Guzmán:

Siri AI on HomeView is noticeably slower than Classic Siri on my HomePod. It can be a bit frustrating when I’m setting various timers while cooking because it feels stuck in processing my request. My HomePod isn’t far away but they’ve made it so it prefers HomeView even if I go stand next to the HomePod.

Kirk McElhearn:

I had to turn [Siri AI] off. Half the time it does nothing; and this is for really simple stuff: timers, alarms, adding things to my grocery list. It is abysmal.

item.title: Siri AI and iPhone apps are the cornerstones of Apple’s hardware strategy
item.author: Six Colors
item.description:
Why: Snell analysis of how Siri AI and apps anchor Apple hardware strategy, a favorites-style piece. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

Earlier this month, Apple rolled out its Siri AI Developer Preview, which lays the groundwork for developers to allow their apps to be controlled in a fairly sophisticated fashion by Apple’s AI assistant.…
item.content:encoded:
Why: Snell analysis of how Siri AI and apps anchor Apple hardware strategy, a favorites-style piece. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

Earlier this month, Apple rolled out its Siri AI Developer Preview, which lays the groundwork for developers to allow their apps to be controlled in a fairly sophisticated fashion by Apple’s AI assistant.

To say this is an important development would be a colossal understatement. The execution of this feature is the core of Apple’s game plan for the next few years, when it intends to release numerous products that leverage its iPhone app ecosystem to power Siri AI.

No pressure…

Apple’s latest new product, the HomeView, is built around Siri AI. (It’s a light dash of Siri AI right now, but its links with content on individual iPhones show what the company is envisioning there.) The new Apple TV 4K has added microphones to make it an additional home access point for Siri AI.

And there’s much more to come, as reported by Mark Gurman at Bloomberg:

Apple needs software makers to begin preparing for what it hopes will be its flagship new product of 2027: smart glasses built around Siri AI, code-named N50.

Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses, I’m told. The idea is to make those apps available through Siri, allowing users to get things done without grabbing their phones. Apple believes its large developer ecosystem could give it an advantage over Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, potentially providing countless third-party integrations when the glasses go on sale.

Gurman expects the Siri-powered glasses (which are basically AirPods you wear on your face) to be released at WWDC, with a similar set of AirPods armed with AI-powered cameras set to debut later in the year. (We’ll see.)

These devices don’t make a lot of sense unless there’s a useful AI assistant behind them. Siri AI is not quite that yet—it’s more reliable and more useful than the old Siri was, but it’s not as good as it should be, and it’s sometimes very slow—but at least it’s promising. Still, just as the iPhone would be a lot less appealing if it only ran Apple-built apps, Siri AI is less appealing if it doesn’t have access to the functionality of the app ecosystem.

Currently, Siri AI can use Spotlight to search content offered by third-party apps, but what it can’t do is learn about functionality offered by individual apps and command those apps to perform those functions in service of a larger request. That’s the goal of the Siri AI Developer Preview—and that sort of stuff is what’s going to make the HomeView (let alone glasses or AirPods paired with an iPhone) a more appealing product.

If Apple can’t pull this off, well, it calls into question the trajectory of Apple’s entire future product strategy. There’s no point in making amazing hardware if there’s nothing running on it that appeals.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Google reports attackers using autonomous AI agents to turn patches into exploits, relevant to security engineering. (score 8)

From The Hacker News.

Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September.

The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same.

A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China.

"These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said.

Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation.

"Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added.

Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers.

The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines.

This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so.

"The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: Cal Newport on the deep life, focus and meaning. (score 8)

From Study Hacks - Decoding Patterns of Success - Cal Newport.

Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled ​“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”​ As I explained:

“To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote ​several​ ​more​ ​essays​ on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I ​launched my podcast​, I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, ​The Deep Life: A Structured Approach​, is now ​available for pre-order​.

The Deep Life brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend ​Oliver Burkeman​, to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

“It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is the key that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

  • ​Amazon​
  • ​Barnes & Noble​
  • ​Bookshop.org​
  • ​Amazon UK​
  • ​Waterstones ​

You can also pre-order ​a signed copy​ from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. Why not make it deep?

The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Apple pushes back on a Canadian law that could weaken encryption and security. (score 8)

From MacRumors: Mac News and Rumors - All Stories.

Apple is urging Canada to change a proposed law that it says could weaken the privacy and security protections built into its products.


The legislation, Bill C-22, is intended to help police and intelligence agencies obtain digital information during investigations. According to Bloomberg, Apple, Google, and Meta are lobbying for changes as Canadian senators review the bill.

At the center of the dispute is whether companies could be forced to change how their services work to help authorities access user data. The bill would allow the government to require companies to build tools for that purpose, with approval from Canada's Intelligence Commissioner.

It could also require certain providers to keep records about users' connections for up to six months. This metadata would exclude the contents of messages, browsing history, and social media activities.

Lawmakers have already added safeguards. For example, a company could only be required to unlock encrypted data if it supplied the encryption and already has the information needed to unlock it. The bill also says companies cannot be forced to introduce certain security weaknesses into their services.

Apple says those changes do not fully address its concerns. The company welcomed the government's revisions, but told Bloomberg that the bill would still undermine its ability to protect users' data. Apple previously warned that the legislation could let authorities demand backdoors.

Meta, Signal, and Tailscale representatives are scheduled to appear before a Senate committee today. The bill has not yet become law.
Tag: Canada

This article, "Apple Pushes Back Against Canada's Plan to Access User Data" first appeared on MacRumors.com
